#3429. There's a New Way to Automatically Back Up Your Android Photos for Free

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you're an Android user looking for a way to save your photos and videos without maxing out your cloud storage space, your device may soon be able to back up automatically to your PC. As spotted by Android Authority, Google included automatic backups from Android to Windows via Quick Share in its release notes for Google Play services v26.43.

Quick Share is a wireless file-sharing feature for Android that allows users to send photos, videos, and documents to nearby devices, including Windows computers and iPhones with AirDrop. The new automatic backup feature, which is likely to roll out gradually, uses Quick Share's functionality to transfer copies of photos and videos on your phone to your PC when nearby.

Since these backups happen locally, you don't need to rely solely on cloud storage in your Google account, nor do you need to remember to initiate transfers of photos and videos between devices. Plus, this is all free and doesn't require a separate cloud service subscription. While you can back up your media to Google Photos, as of earlier this year, more data from your Android backups count toward your Google Account storage cap unless you exclude specific types. Alternatively, you can also cobble together a decent amount of cloud storage from other providers at no extra cost, but automatic backups between Android and Windows minimize the likelihood that you'll forget to save data, and your PC provides plenty of space for free.

Once the feature is available on your device, you'll be able to initiate backups in the Quick Share for Windows app. Your Android and Windows devices must be in close proximity and signed into the same Google Account. You can toggle Automatic backups on and change the settings for what gets backed up and to where. The transfers will then occur wirelessly in the background.

As Android Authority reports, early hints at this feature suggested that Samsung phones and PCs would be excluded from automatic backups, but the release notes don't specify any further details.

#3428. Magic Is Bringing Back Its Most Controversial Creature Type

Magic: The Gathering's Aaron Forsythe tells Polygon he knows when more Sliver cards will come to the game

Whether you love or hate Sliver decks in Magic: The Gathering, you should prepare for more Sliver cards to make their way to the game soon. Vice President of Design Aaron Forsythe revealed as much during an in-person interview with Polygon at MagicCon: Atlanta 2026.

During an interview at MagicCon, Polygon mentioned how a couple of Sliver-related cards that were part of Edge of Eternities, and asked if the Magic: The Gathering team is thinking about bringing the cards back in a big way or if they are too broken to actively support. In response, Forsythe confirmed that "we know when they’re coming back," although he wouldn't share a specific timeline for their return.

"They will be back," Forsythe elaborated. "We know when they're coming back, and I'm not going to tell you. But we know people love them. They are hard to develop. They are hard to make work unlimited, but we have a plan."

Slivers have a long history in Magic: The Gathering as one of the most fun yet controversial creature types that a player can use in their decks. Sliver cards actively boost or benefit from other Sliver cards, enabling decks that can quickly scale up in power in a way that's tough to counter or beat.

As Forsythe mentions, that makes them particularly tough to develop, since they can be very overpowered. That is likely why we haven't seen as many Sliver cards in recent years. Wizards of the Coast now seems up to the challenge of bringing Sliver cards back in a big way, though, and it'll be fascinating to see what form the comeback that Forsythe teased takes.

While we have no idea when more Sliver cards will come to Magic: The Gathering, Wizards of the Coast did debut the Nauctis: The Sunken Realm set of cards at MagicCon: Atlanta 2026. That set will be released on Feb. 5, 2027, and will introduce a whole new oceanic realm to the game's multiverse.

#3427. 5 Forgotten '80s Sitcoms That Still Hold Up Today

The 1980s were stacked with classic sitcoms. "Cheers," "Taxi," "The Golden Girls" and so many more had us pinned to our couches during primetime. Of course, there was also formulaic garbage like "Who's the Boss," "Full House" and "Growing Pains." This is always the state of play in television. But the quality-to-trash ratio was pretty favorable throughout the entire decade.

Nevertheless, there were many terrific '80s sitcoms that got axed before they had a chance to flourish. In most cases, they were flouting formula, which meant viewers had to adjust to different comedic rhythms. Audiences proved malleable with variety shows like "The Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour," "Rowan & Martin's Laugh-In," and "Saturday Night Live," but the sitcom structure was sacrosanct: set-up and punchline all the way to a tidy finale in 30 minutes. Every minor crisis got resolved with a closing laugh (unless it was "a very special episode"). Deviating too far from the norm was typically fatal.

The '80s sitcom graveyard is littered with coulda-been classics, most notably "Police Squad!," which died a quick death after six episodes, but later spawned the wildly successful "Naked Gun" franchise. Alas, there are others that were so unsuccessful and/or controversial that they're only streamable on YouTube via old VHS rips (if they're streamable at all). Here are five '80s sitcoms that undeservedly got a quick hook.

Martin Mull was a brilliant comedic performer whose television career got off to a promising start in the 1970s. He was a scream as the detestable Garth Gimble on Norman Lear's "Mary Hartman, Mary Hartman," which earned him a spinoff as his character's brother Barth Gimble on the influential talk show spoof "Fernwood 2 Night." The show was something of a lark, but got a second season as "America 2 Night." After that, it seemed to be only a matter of time before he got another network show.

It took six years after the end of "America 2 Night," but that opportunity finally arrived in 1984 with "Domestic Life." The show had a seemingly can't-miss pedigree with Steve Martin as a co-creator, but CBS lost confidence in it quickly when it got off to a rocky ratings start as a mid-season replacement. Mull starred as Martin Crane, a Seattle TV news commentator who — along with his wife, rebellious 15-year-old daughter, and business-whiz 10-year-old son — encounters a variety of stock sitcom complications.

"Domestic Life" wasn't a parody per se, but, for 10 whole episodes, it was a hilarious vehicle for Mull's droll sensibility. Robert Ridgely was a delight as pompous anchorman Cliff Hamilton, and the series upended expectations at every turn. One of the best episodes found Mull scrambling to come up with $4,000 due for a balloon payment on his house, and being forced to ask his investor son for a loan. Mull plays the scene with an uproarious mix of flattery and outright shame. "Domestic Life" should've run for many seasons, but, despite critical acclaim, the ratings were never there.

When I watched the premiere of "Frank's Place" on CBS in 1987, I was simultaneously grateful that such an idiosyncratic sitcom could exist on network television and saddened that it was almost certainly destined for an early cancellation. The show reunited "WKRP in Cincinnati" creator Hugh Wilson with Tim Reid, who played DJ Venus Flytrap on the hit series, and was blessed with a nifty premise. Reid stars as Frank Parrish, a Boston college professor who's inherited a New Orleans restaurant. Frank wants to sell the restaurant, but is forced to stay on when one of the eatery's waitresses puts a voodoo curse on him. How will this erudite New Englander adjust to life in the Big Easy? On one level, this is basic fish-out-of-water stuff, but it goes places racially and culturally that no series dared to explore during that era.

Wilson adopted a single camera approach, and eschewed a laugh track. The latter threw a lot of viewers at the time, but, judging from solid Nielsen ratings over summer reruns, people were getting used to this approach. That's probably because the show was dripping with New Orleans atmosphere; it was every bit as lively and enchanting and delicious (oh, the food porn) as the city itself. Why was it canceled? According to Walter Kronkite, the legendary CBS newsman (who was a huge fan of the show), then-CBS CEO Laurence Tisch took offense to an episode that was critical of junk bonds (a major source of Tisch's wealth).

Why isn't this beloved series available via streaming or physical media? Much like "WKRP in Cincinnati," the music licensing is crazy expensive, and soundalike zydeco would rob the show of its soul. So the blurry VHS rips on YouTube are, sadly, the best we're going to get.

Three years before they brought the mean-spirited "Married... with Children" to the upstart Fox network, Ron Leavitt and Michael G. Moye caused a caustic stir with the blithely nasty "It's Your Move." The show starred Jason Bateman as a conscienceless teenager who scams everyone in his orbit, but takes particular pleasure in torturing his neighbor (David Garrison), a struggling writer who commits the cardinal sin of dating Bateman's mother. The two quickly engage in a tit-for-tat battle intended to discredit each other, but, until the series veered away from this format, their petty battles always ended in a stalemate.

Bateman landed this leading role on the strength of his smarmy work as Ricky Schroeder's friend on the NBC sitcom "Silver Spoons." He's matched every step of the way by Garrison, who toes the line between decency and sheer malevolence. There wasn't a nastier sitcom on network television at the time, and that, in part, proved to be its undoing. NBC found itself inundated with letters from concerned parents, who were alarmed to see their children mimicking Bateman's corrupt/criminal behavior. Pair this with the show trying to compete in the same timeslot as ABC's popular nighttime soap "Dynasty," and NBC opted to cut bait.

In the end, it worked out for everyone: Bateman smoothly segued from slappable kid to flustered adult (shining in "Arrested Development"), while Garrison turned into a confidante for Ed O'Neil's Al Bundy on "Married... with Children." But "It's Your Move" was a sharp (perhaps unintentional) satire of the greed-driven Reagan era. The characters on this show are either naive dopes or venal predators.

For five weeks in the spring of 1982, ABC burned off episodes of a sitcom that must've melted the brains of people who stumbled across it in a crowded time slot. Created in part by Michael Jacobs, a sitcom machine who would reach high highs with "Dinosaurs" and deep lows with "Boy Meets World," "No Soap, Radio" aimed to turn an inside-baseball comedy non-sequitur (on par with "The Aristocrats") into a successful sitcom. Had it debuted on HBO, it might've become a sustainable critical sensation. As a network series, it was dead on arrival.

The very loose premise of the show revolved around Steve Guttenberg as a manager of a failing Atlantic City hotel. These segments present the series as a slamming-door farce a la "Fawlty Towers," but it detours into absurd bits that, like its title, have nothing to do with whatever threadbare narrative it's trying to advance. People have compared the show to "Monty Python's Flying Circus," but it's clearly inspired by "Kentucky Fried Movie." The intermittent news breaks are straight out of the chaotic David Zucker-Jim Abrahams-Jerry Zucker classic. I'd love to talk to the creators of this show, because I simply don't understand how it was greenlit in 1982. "No Soap, Radio" is a shotgun spray of silliness. As a late-night show, devoid of the Guttenberg anchor and with a better recurring cast, it could've been a sensation. Instead, it's a fun little show that couldn't.

When Clint Eastwood's "Dirty Harry" film series sunk to a vile level of self-parody with the putrid "Sudden Impact," the conditions were perfect for a straight-up, ZAZ-type spoof of the star's judge-jury-executioner shenanigans. Comedy wunderkind Alan Spencer, who broke into the industry at the age of 15 as a joke writer, delivered the goofy goods in 1986 with the splendidly silly "Sledge Hammer!" The series starred David Rasche (Karl Muller from "Succession") as a trigger-happy San Francisco cop who's carrying on a near-relationship with his .44 Magnum. He sleeps with the gun (which rests on a satin pillow"), showers with it, and talks to it. Unlike Dirty Harry, Sledge Hammer is generally an affable guy, who, despite his extrajudicial bent, is liked by his partner Detective Dori Doreau (Anne-Marie Martin). He drives his supervisor Captain Trunk (Harrison Page) nuts, but typically gets the job done — albeit messily at times.

"Sledge Hammer" received mostly positive reviews and initially posted solid ratings. This changed when ABC began moving it around the schedule. When the show's numbers plummeted, ABC placed "Sledge Hammer!" squarely on the chopping block. Knowing they were doomed, Spencer and his writers ended the series finale with Hammer botching the disarming of a nuclear warhead, thus leading to the destruction of San Francisco. Amusingly, this episode did surprisingly well in the ratings, so ABC greenlit a second season (set five years in the past). The network promptly did "Sledge Hammer!" dirty by pitting it against "The Cosby Show." This was the end, but unlike the other shows on this list, you can currently stream "Sledge Hammer!" on Prime Video (it also received a physical media release). It's still a riot 40 years later.

#3426. Windows Laptops Just Closed a Major Gap With the MacBook Neo

To say the MacBook Neo disrupted the laptop market would be an understatement. When the Neo dropped, former Apple CEO Tim Cook said Apple had its best-ever launch week for first-time Mac customers, and the company is reportedly planning on doubling the MacBook's sales for 2027. It's not hard to see why the MacBook Neo is such a hit: Apple is offering the essential Mac experience at a fantastic price point. You no longer need to spend $1,000 or more for a MacBook, so long as you're okay making some sacrifices to get there—which, it seems, many customers are.

While the MacBook Neo has been a boon for Apple and Apple fans alike, I can only imagine the stress it brought to PC manufacturers—especially those with budget or midrange machines. Windows PCs have long won the price war against Apple. While MacBooks have their passionate customers, buyers looking for the best value have had to weigh expensive Apple laptops against many far cheaper options from companies like Dell, HP, ASUS, and Lenovo. But with the Neo, suddenly a MacBook was competing in this space, and well.

Part of the issue for PC manufacturers was Apple's control over its own ecosystem. Unlike most PC makers, which only produce the hardware for each machine, Apple makes both the hardware and the software for its MacBook lineup. As such, the company has the advantage of optimizing that hardware. It can design macOS to run more efficiently on weaker hardware, in a way that companies like Dell or ASUS can't. You might be comparing the MacBook Neo against a Windows laptop with similar specs, or even better specs, but because Microsoft makes Windows, not the laptop manufacturer, it's possible the Neo ends up with the better overall experience. While that might still be the case, Microsoft may have just closed that gap in a meaningful way.

This week, Microsoft announced key upgrades to memory-management efficiency, particularly for machines with 8GB of RAM. This is the amount of memory the MacBook Neo has, as well as many budget and midrange Windows laptops. That's not much memory for 2026, regardless of platform, but Apple seems to have squeezed a lot out of it for the Neo. Now, Microsoft may have just done the same for PCs, as Windows is reportedly 20% more responsive, with 40% faster multitasking.

In its blog post, Microsoft highlighted improvements that users with 8 GB of RAM can expect from Windows going forward. First, Microsoft says it focused on better utilizing the RAM your machine already has. The company compares its memory management to a desk: Anything on the "desk" is stored in RAM; anything in your "drawer" is stored in your drive. As you use your PC, Windows used to move more of your apps and tabs to your drawer to free up more RAM for other things, meaning you'd need to reload those items whenever you returned to them. Going forward, the company says that Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM instead of moving it to slower storage elsewhere. That means apps and tabs should refresh less frequently when you leave and return to them.

Microsoft also says that small actions should be faster across the board. When you open the Start menu, search across your PC, right-click, open Settings, launch the Snipping Tool, and open File Explorer, those actions may be up to 20% faster than they were in January. Microsoft Edge may open up to 33% faster, while Teams can enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which means it can launch up to 20% faster too. Microsoft put together an interesting stress test to compare multitasking performance between today and January. It opened 20 tabs in Edge, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, then Outlook and File Explorer, all without closing any windows. That experience was 40% faster following this latest update.

Microsoft says it also improved the memory efficiency in its apps: The company claims it reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB, and saved up to 360 MB in RAM across Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook. That extends to third-party apps as well: Microsoft says that WhatsApp has double-digit memory improvement now. Widgets also only load when you open the app, which saves 200 MB of RAM when the app is closed, while Edge tabs go inactive after 15 minutes instead of two hours.

Microsoft isn't making these upgrades in a vacuum. Hardware costs, particularly for RAM, have skyrocketed in the age of AI. Microsoft knows that people are likely going to hold onto existing hardware for longer than they usually do, or that they'll opt for less-expensive configurations, including, perhaps, machines with 8 GB of RAM.

PCMag's Chris Hoffman was adamant before this latest Windows update that buyers should steer clear of PCs with 8 GB of RAM. Now, he's pulling back a bit. In his testing, Hoffman noticed improvements when multitasking on an 8 GB PC when compared to similar tests from months ago. He could run multiple Chrome tabs, a Microsoft Word window, and Spotify without bogging down the computer much. Hoffman isn't a lightweight user, so he still wouldn't personally choose an 8 GB machine, but he admits, "If I were an average PC buyer looking for a reasonable desktop experience and could save hundreds of dollars by opting for 8GB of RAM, I might be happy with the performance."

To that point, I think this new Windows update makes 8 GB PCs competitive, especially against the MacBook Neo. We'll still need direct comparisons to know how well this new Windows experience holds up across the board, but these updates are promising. Users with 8 GB machines just got a free, valuable update overnight; new customers can opt for a more affordable PC without feeling like performance will take a nosedive just because they opened one too many Edge tabs.

As Hoffman says, 8 GB of RAM is not ideal for any user looking for serious multitasking or professional workflows, regardless of whether they choose a Mac or PC. But for the average computer customer looking for a solid machine without breaking the bank, I no longer see the Neo as necessarily the default choice. After all, Apple has slowly raised its price, too, from $599 to $699. If you're platform-agnostic, or even prefer Windows to macOS, these updates from Microsoft are quite promising. If you're in the market, check out PCMag's excellent list of budget laptop recommendations.

#3425. How To Rob A Bank Shares A Major Theme With This Iconic '90s Keanu Reeves Movie

Throughout history, cops and robbers have been inextricably linked. This comes with the territory, of course, yet the closeness between the two leads to the lines between them inevitably becoming blurred. So, naturally, the crime movie has a long standing tradition of exploring this mercurial, murky relationship, with filmmakers like Michael Mann making it a specialty of theirs.

Part of the tension inherent in the relationship between cop and thief is one which stems directly from a tenet of drama, which is that the villains are often more interesting than the square heroes. This issue becomes compounded when the heroes represent a flawed and unjust system of governance, something which the so-called villains only seek to rage against.

"How to Rob a Bank" is a movie cognizant of this exact flavor of moral tension and looks to exploit it to the fullest at every turn. A story about disgruntled and disenchanted radicals who've each been treated horribly by the American system becoming bank robbing YouTubers could've been a simple riff on the Robin Hood mythos, with the vigilantes taking from the banks and corporations and giving back to the needy (as well as themselves). And while this is an element in the film, director David Leitch and writer Mark Bianculli provide an equally compelling argument for the cause of authority, as represented by FBI Agent John West (John C. Reilly) and hacker Reagan Gardner (Zoë Kravitz).

Indeed, the pair directly examine the seductive allure of robbing banks versus its harsher reality, even name-checking the '90s Keanu Reeves classic "Point Break." This is more than just a cheeky reference, too, as both "How to Rob a Bank" and "Point Break" share the major theme of grappling with ethical behavior in a broken world.

In "How to Rob a Bank," Agent West and Gardner are on the trail of the Wolf Pack, the group of friends turned bank robbing YouTubers who've been pulling off bank jobs across the U.S. while gaining a viral following online. During a lunch break, West explains how his father was the innocent victim of allegations of insurance fraud, leading to Gardner asking if this was what inspired West to become an FBI agent. Instead, West reveals that it was "Point Break" that made him want to join the FBI, to which Gardner replies, "That means you really wanted to rob banks." West's thoughtful look in response to that comment says volumes.

This also speaks to the ways David Leitch's movie and Kathryn Bigelow's "Point Break" blur the lines of morality for those watching as much as their characters, which is by design. In both films, the forces of the law are initially portrayed as stodgy, closed-minded, and bureaucratic, while the bank robbers are alluring and even sexually attractive in their exploits. The Wolf Pack in "How to Rob a Bank" are humble, blue-collar people who adopt "Fortnite"-flavored alter ego personas during their robberies, while the Ex-Presidents in "Point Break" are punk-tinged political satirists who wear caricatured masks of past U.S. presidents while doing a job, then go off to be part of a surfer commune as themselves. Both groups initially look like idealized outlaws, and it's that quality that makes West, much like FBI Agent Johnny Utah (Keanu Reeves) in "Point Break," uncertain if perhaps they've chosen the wrong side.

Of course, it isn't long before the robbers' vigilante fantasy crashes hard into reality. But while this trajectory is fairly standard, neither of these movies lose their social commentary bite because of it.

As mentioned, Johnny Utah and John West aren't immune to the plights or charms of the robbers they're respectively chasing, with Utah nearly seduced into joining the ones in "Point Break." Yet, his and West's quests to see justice served is more about protecting the innocent. As West points out, people like him aren't seeking to stop the robbers on behalf of a corrupt system so much as they're attempting to protect the millions of other people who don't have the luxury of opting out of the system.

This is why the conclusions of both films keep their revolutionary themes intact despite the robbers getting caught. In "Point Break," Utah lets Bodhi (Patrick Swayze) surf a once-in-a-lifetime giant wave rather than taking him in, letting the man go out on his own terms. Meanwhile, in "How to Rob a Bank," one member of the Pack is killed, and West only captures the leader, Ryan (Nicholas Hoult). Nevertheless, Ryan is still successful in his quest, as the Pack's videos continue to exist online and foster a growing movement of discontent, while the rest of the Pack start a new video series: "How to Escape From Prison."

It's telling that a 1990 film ends with affection for the robber who still ends up being punished, while a 2026 movie ends with hope for a robber's escape. When it comes to cops and robbers, the ethics are murky as ever, but the revolutionary wave is beginning to grow.

"How to Rob a Bank" is currently playing in theaters.

Disneyland will always be a magical place, but there is something particularly magical during the holiday season. The lights, the fake snow (because this is Southern California), the trees, the food, and the music all make it extra special this time of year. I have been to Disneyland more times than I can count, but there is one ride I have avoided for over a decade: It's a Small World.

It's not that I don't like the ride. It's just that if I hear that earworm-inducing song, even just the first note, I will have it stuck in my head for days, maybe even weeks. However, this was my first time experiencing the ride during the holiday season, and it had me singing a different tune.

First of all, the ride has definitely had a glow-up since the last time I stepped onto the boat. From adding inclusive dolls in wheelchairs and new characters like Coco's Miguel and his alebrije dog, Dante, to adding a third and final verse to the song, there was a lot for me to see and hear. However, the holiday version takes things a whole step further.

If you have never been on this attraction, let me tell you, you are in for a treat. And yes, there is another song that may be just as hard to get out of your head as the original. The holiday version of this ride incorporates none other than "Jingle Bells." Disney knew what they were doing, and surprisingly, I am here for it.

As I took that first bend into the tunnel, with rain coming down on my head, I was greeted by a bright "Happy Holidays" sign before entering the magical, doll-filled world, complete with all the twinkling lights of the season. There are garlands hanging everywhere, toys, presents, floating Christmas trees, and signs in all different languages wishing you happy holidays and a merry Christmas.

I had a chance to chat with one of Disneyland's cast members, Alexa Garcia, about why she loves It's a Small World this time of year. She told us:

Inside, you've got the beautiful music heard in different languages, and it's just such a beautiful message during this time of the year.

I found myself connecting with the music in a way I haven't in quite some time, and I even got a little choked up. Honestly, I think having "Jingle Bells" mixed in with the iconic song throughout really helps.

And then there is the final room, which is truly a showstopper. As the boat takes its final turn, you enter a white winter wonderland with everyone singing "Deck the Halls." It is elaborate, decadent, beautiful, and above all, just really, really cute.

This ride really won me over, and I am so glad I gave it another chance. Otherwise, I would have missed out on all the holiday joy this little boat ride gave me. And with the combination of songs, you actually end up leaving without either of them stuck in your head. At least, that is what happened to me.

While I may not be in a hurry to ride It's A Small World again without its holiday makeover, I encourage everyone visiting Disneyland for the holidays to give it a chance. The holiday celebration runs through January 6, 2027. I guess I'll just have to wait until next Christmas to willingly get back on board.

#3423. Sony Wants to Give You Up to $400 for Your PS5

Companies usually want you to buy something from them. They might cut prices to make their products more enticing, or introduce perks and upgrades to make stagnant prices (or even price hikes) more appealing. But rarely do I see companies encourage customers to sell their products.

Such is the case with Sony and its PlayStation console. This week, the company began reaching out to some customers with an odd prompt: Rather than buy a new PS5 or PS5 Pro, you can sell your existing PS5 console for up to $400. There are stipulations there, of course: Your console needs to be in good working order, and, apparently, come with two controllers—even though Sony only includes one in the box. The price could also fluctuate depending on your console model, storage capacity, and included accessories. But, still, the company says it'll help you net up to $400 for your existing PS5.

It's a bizarre deal, especially when you consider who you're trading your console to. Sony isn't necessarily accepting trade-ins itself. Instead, it's partnering with BackMarket. The thing is, you can trade in your PS5 directly through BackMarket and get a better value than Sony is offering through its direct link. When I try to trade in my standard PS5 with one controller, BackMarket offers $435, $35 more than Sony's highest offer. If I add a second controller to that deal, BackMarket bumps up the total to $455.

You might also be wondering why Sony would do this. Not only is it weird for a company to encourage you to sell one of its products, but the PS5 is about to have a big moment. Grand Theft Auto VI is finally about to launch, and it'll likely be one of the biggest video game launches, if not the biggest video game launch, of all time. Why, then, would Sony encourage users to jump ship?

While Sony doesn't say, the answer likely has to do with how expensive it is to pick up a PS5 right now. Even though the console launched back in 2020, units are few and far between, jacking the price up to unreasonable levels. Sony raised international prices due to tariffs last year, but the current shortage is more probably tied to the ongoing memory crisis that's putting a strain on all tech, including game consoles. A new PS5 on Amazon will easily cost you over $800. If you want to find a PS5 Pro, don't be surprised to find it well over $1,000. Sony likely wants players who aren't using their consoles to sell them, so that active players (who will also buy games like GTA VI) will pick them up. It's not just Sony, either: Microsoft has been offering similar deals to inactive Xbox gamers this year.

If Sony reached out to you directly, you can take advantage of the deal without issue—just click the link in the email. But if you never received such an offer, you still have options. For one, that BackMarket deal is live for anyone. That links takes you to the deal for the standard PS5, but you can also head to this link to enter the info for your specific PS5 model. GameStop, of course, will happily take your PS5 off your hands, but it doesn't seem as generous as BackMarket. Right now, it seems you can get up to $275 in store credit, or $192.50 in cash for a standard PS5.

#3422. Why Batman: The Animated Series Chose Man-Bat As Its First Villain

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

"Batman: The Animated Series" is darker than most superhero cartoons before and since — literally darker. Drawn on black paper, "Batman: The Animated Series" presents Gotham City like an art deco painting mixed with an old Hollywood crime movie. But it wasn't only gangsters that went bump in the night. The very first episode, "On Leather Wings," uses one of the most out-there Batman villains: Man-Bat, aka zoologist Kirk Langstrom (Marc Singer), transformed by a potion into a half-man/half-bat creature like a winged werewolf.

Debuting in 1970's "Detective Comics" #400 by Frank Robbins and Neal Adams, Man-Bat had 20+ years of comics history behind him when "On Leather Wings" was made. But for non-comic fans, that episode would be the first time they'd seen him. According to "Batman: The Animated Series" co-creator Bruce Timm, that's exactly why he was the pilot's villain. In "Modern Masters Volume 3: Bruce Timm," he recounted:

"Man-Bat was chosen specifically [for the first episode] because he wasn't familiar to very many people outside of comic book fans. Nobody had any preconceived notions about him. It wasn't like the Joker, where you had to deal with people expecting him to be Jack Nicholson or Cesar Romero."

"On Leather Wings" was written by Mitch Brian, who had also developed the "Batman" series bible. What became "On Leather Wings" originated as an episode premise in that bible, though with the gruesome detail that Man-Bat was killing tourists, which isn't in the episode as made. Brian has said he pushed for Man-Bat to give the series a dash of the fantastical right off the bat (no pun intended) — "Batman: The Animated Series" could do not just film noir, but also Universal Horror-esque mad science and monsters.

Man-Bat as Batman's first villain also carries narrative symmetry. His moniker is a twist on Batman's own and he takes Batman's mission to "become a bat" one step further. "Man-Bat kind of works because he's literally the reverse of Batman and he's also got the obsessive interest in bats," said Bruce Timm in "Modern Masters."

Now, technically, Catwoman's debut episode "The Cat and the Claw" premiered first on September 5, 1992, one day earlier than "On Leather Wings" did. "Batman Returns," starring Michelle Pfeiffer as Catwoman, had hit theaters that past summer. (Currently, "The Cat and the Claw" is also listed as the first episode of "Batman: The Animated Series" on HBO Max.) But, functionally, "On Leather Wings" is a much better pilot episode — because that's what it was made to be.

It also demonstrated that "Batman: The Animated Series" was more than just a movie tie-in, down to the choice of villain. In "I Am The Night: The Ultimate Unauthorized History of Batman Series," author Daniel Dockery notes a villain like Man-Bat would've been "nigh impossible to pull off in live-action." Remember, this was 1992, a year before "Jurassic Park" unlocked the potential of CGI. A human-sized bat monster? And an action scene where it flies through Gotham with Batman towed behind it on a rope? Yeah, in the 1990s, a live-action "Batman" movie that even attempted any of that would look ridiculous. But in a cartoon, it was thrilling, and proved "Batman: The Animated Series" was a canvas for unique Batman stories.

Starting with "On Leather Wings" also highlights another tenet from the aforementioned "Batman" series bible: no origin story episodes, because the audience already knew Batman's origin from decades of prior "Batman" comics, movies, and cartoons.

During "On Leather Wings," the police mistake Man-Bat for Batman (Kevin Conroy) and hunt the Dark Knight instead. This premise rests on Gotham City already knowing Batman, which is only possible because the series starts in media res with Batman as an experienced crimefighter. The first time we see Batman is deliberately unspectacular; he's sitting in the Batcave, in costume, reading a newspaper article about the Man-Bat attacks.

The "Batman is framed" subplot also demonstrates that this isn't the Adam West show where Batman is literally deputized by the police and trusted by all of Gotham as a paragon of justice. Many people are already scared of Batman, so it's not a huge leap to blame him for Man-Bat's attacks. (The series' movie spin-off, "Batman: Mask of the Phantasm," even used a nigh-identical story, with Batman being mistaken for the film's eponymous villain.)

Turning Man-Bat's identity into a mystery differs from his first appearance in the comics. There, we meet Man-Bat as Langstrom first and see his gradual and tragic transformation. Mitch Brian compared Man-Bat to "The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde," and by making "On Leather Wings" a mystery, it brings Man-Bat closer to that book. It also, crucially, allows Batman to act as a detective. The twist of Man-Bat being Langstrom works because, again, he's not a villain most of the audience already knew inside-and-out.

Artist Kevin Nowlan, who had drawn a Man-Bat story in DC's "Secret Origins" #39, was initially recruited to design the villain. (See his concept art above.) Bruce Timm's finalized design includes his characters' standard broad upper chest, which fits well with Man-Bat's arms growing out into wings. In form and function, Man-Bat was the perfect pilot villain for "Batman: The Animated Series."

#3421. 26 Years Later, Charlie Brown's Final Quote Is Still a Comic Strip Classic

Unlucky in love, lucky in... absolutely nothing else

Charles Schulz's retirement took the world by surprise. Following a period of failing health, Schulz announced on Dec. 14, 1999 that he would end Peanuts. He could no longer see clearly and had been diagnosed with colon cancer. He needed to focus on his health. As a result, Peanuts came to a relatively sudden stop nine weeks later once newspapers had worked through Schulz's existing backlog.

Schulz passed away in his sleep on Feb. 12, 2000, the day before the last strip ran in newspapers. At its end, Peanuts had run for roughly 49 years and 4 months and a total of 17,897 strips. He had never taken a sabbatical or had any assistants.

The last few weeks of Peanuts' run can best be described as "business as usual." Fans had speculated for years about what might happen in the final days of Peanuts, as much of the strip was built around failure-themed running gags. Would the Great Pumpkin finally show up? Would Charlie Brown finally kick the football? Maybe the often-mentioned/never-shown red-headed girl would show up, or Charlie Brown would finally manage his team to a winning baseball game.

None of that happened. Schulz had to retire faster than he ever thought he would, so Peanuts never came to any sort of organized conclusion. It just stopped. There are a couple of strips in the final run that can be read as having some subtext on the subject, most prominently Peppermint Patty's last appearance, but Schulz didn't get the time to set anything up. All we received was the goodbye, because it was all he could give.

In his last televised interview, Schulz recounted the story of drawing the last Peanuts strip to Al Roker and mentioned he'd had an uncharacteristic fit of regret. "All of a sudden, I thought, 'You know, that poor, poor kid, he never even got to kick the football!'" Maybe Schulz might've done something with that if he'd had more time. Sadly, we'll never know.

Charlie Brown and Snoopy's last appearances in Peanuts are technically in the first two panels of the Feb. 13 strip, but that's little more than an optional introduction to Schulz's farewell message. (The first two panels in American newspapers' Sunday comics are often written/drawn as a disposable throwaway gag, in case a local paper's layout team needs to rearrange the strip on the page.)

The last full Peanuts strip ran on February 6, 2000, which is the final appearance of Sally Brown and Charlie Brown's last starring role. It's a Valentine's Day strip, and as usual for Peanuts, it's about Charlie Brown wrestling with his own lack of romantic success.

In the last installment of one of Peanuts' sadder running gags, Charlie Brown is once again waiting outside his mailbox to see if he gets any love letters. Naturally, he doesn’t.

This time, he's making sure to scrub it down. "The inside of a mailbox should always be kept clean in case you get a love letter," Charlie Brown tells Sally, right before a sudden storm chases them both inside.

Once they're both dry, Charlie Brown continues to explain how these things work to Sally, including why he's not going out in the rain to check the mail again. "When it's raining, the only letters you get are those that say, 'I never want to see you again!'"

"You seem to know a lot about love letters," Sally says.

"If I ever got one," Charlie Brown says, "I don't know what I'd do."

If this wasn't so late in Peanuts' run, it'd just be another self-effacing strip about Charlie Brown's permanent losing streak. It's also another strip that runs off of one of Peanuts' core pillars, which is about how little kids will sometimes make up their own "rules" on the fly. Charlie Brown, Love Expert, is here to tell you how it all works. He doesn't actually know, but he sounds really certain.

There is a certain extra layer of pathos with this one, though. Charlie Brown leaves the world the way he came into it, doing his best to stay positive in a setting built around his misery.

#3420. No, We Aren’t All Eating 'Too Much' Protein

If you’ll permit me a rant—I promise to make it fact-filled and interesting—I am sick of the articles that seem to pop up every few months claiming that we are all eating “too much” protein. They convey an inaccurate picture of how the body uses protein, and they demonize perfectly healthy meals that happen to be high in protein. It’s time to set the record straight.

It is true that most of us eat more than the RDA (recommended daily allowance) of protein, but that's a good thing—the RDA is meant as a minimum. It's true that protein-boosted foods are trendy, and that they're not necessarily great dietary choices in the big picture. It's also true that you can eat a healthy diet with little to no meat, but meat is not synonymous with protein. Let's look at what we actually know about the role of protein in a healthy diet, and how to tell if you're eating too much or too little.

As a refresher, protein is one of the three calorie-containing macronutrients (fats, carbs, protein) that make up most of the food we eat. Proteins are made of amino acids, and these amino acids are required for the growth, repair, and functioning of our bodies.

We can get protein from a variety of sources. Meats are particularly protein-dense; a chicken breast contains about 35 grams of protein. Other animal products, like milk and eggs, are also rich in protein. Plant-based foods tend to have less protein than animal products, but it’s not hard to meet or exceed protein requirements even on a vegan diet. Beans, grains, and soy products like tofu contain significant amounts of protein, for example.

If you’d like a cheat sheet on how much protein you’re supposed to eat based on your activity level, you can find one here. And that’s a good place to start dissecting this “too much protein” myth, because before we can declare an amount of protein to be “too much,” we need to understand how much is “enough.”

The government communicates targets for different nutrients to encourage us all to eat a healthy, balanced diet. These targets are the basis for the “% daily value” labels on the back of packaged foods, and for the nutrient makeup of school lunches. The RDA, or recommended daily allowance, is defined as “the average daily dietary intake level that is sufficient to meet the nutrient requirement of nearly all (97 to 98 percent) healthy individuals in a group.”

In other words, if 100% of us were to eat the RDA of protein, at least 97% of us would be getting enough protein—we'd be meeting the minimum to be healthy. That's right, this number is a minimum to avoid malnutrition, not a maximum, and not a recommendation for optimal health.

By the way, if you're wondering how that number is determined? For protein, it is based on nitrogen balance. Humans break down proteins, as part of our body’s daily function, and we excrete nitrogen as a result. If you eat enough protein (which contains nitrogen), the amount of nitrogen you excrete will be the same as, or more than, the amount you eat. In other words, if you aren’t breaking your own body proteins down (in excess of what you eat), then whatever you’re eating must be, in some sense, enough.

In this way of thinking, the RDA is the minimum to stay healthy. More is fine; less would mean that you may not be getting enough. For some nutrients, there is also an UL, or upper limit, telling you that more than a certain amount is too much. Upper limits are calculated for vitamins and minerals; there is no upper limit defined for protein.

Therefore, there is no official definition for “too much” protein. If somebody eats more than the RDA, they’re not eating too much; they’re just eating more than the minimum. You’re supposed to eat more than the minimum.

The RDA for protein is set at 46 grams per day for a 125-pound woman, and at 56 grams per day for a 154-pound man. (The USDA chose those as their examples.) That’s based on an RDA of 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram bodyweight, which works out to 0.36 grams per pound. So a 200-pound person would need 72 grams of protein per day.

This USDA report found that most adult men average roughly 90 to 100 grams of protein per day, although men aged 70 and up only get about 80 grams of protein per day. Women tend to average around 70 grams per day, with those aged 70 and up averaging 62 grams.

Above the RDA? Yes. Too much? I don’t see any way of arguing that. And before you say that we’re getting almost double the recommendation, let's check the math. Those RDA numbers are for 125- and 154-pound people. On the other hand, the averages for what we eat are based on actual people, not ideals. The average American man is 200 pounds, and the average American woman is 171 pounds. So, to compare the numbers:

The average woman is 171 pounds, so her RDA would be 62 grams per day. (Women, on average, eat 70 grams of protein per day.)

The average man is 200 pounds, so his RDA would be 72 grams per day. (Men, on average, eat 90 to 100 grams of protein per day.)

Again, there’s no need to stick to the minimum; going 8 grams over, or even 28 grams over, is fine. It’s probably better to go over than to just scrape by, and many of us arguably don’t get enough. Let me explain.

Let’s start with older adults. Not only does protein intake tend to decrease with age, older adults are vulnerable to issues that stem from a loss of muscle mass. People tend to lose 3-5% of their muscle mass per decade starting at age 30, but strength training and protein intake can support maintaining our muscle, and thus likely prevent or reduce that decline.

The Dietary Guidelines include a note that “About 50 percent of women and 30 percent of men 71 and older fall short of protein foods recommendations.” Meanwhile, a study found that older adults who don’t meet the recommendations are “more likely to be limited when stooping, crouching, or kneeling, standing or sitting for long periods, walking up 10 steps, preparing meals, and walking for a quarter mile.”

So even if it’s true that the average adult gets more protein than recommended, there are clearly a lot of elderly folks who don’t. These are the same people who have more issues functioning in everyday life. This may be a chicken-and-egg situation—was the functional decline a cause or an effect of the change in their diet?—but this sure does not seem to be a group of people who should be eating less protein.

There’s another large group of people who benefit from more, not less, protein: people who are pregnant or lactating. Instead of 0.36 grams of protein per pound of body weight (62 grams for a 171-pound person), the RDA for people who are pregnant or lactating is 0.5 grams/pound (so, 86 grams of protein per day).

When you’re pregnant, you also have higher caloric needs, so the increased total amount of food makes it easier to get the higher protein amount. Still, it makes more sense to spend your energy on making sure you’re getting enough protein, rather than worrying about getting too much.

You knew we were heading in this direction (I say between reps of barbell squats, wiping protein shake off my lips): People who exercise should get more protein than just the RDA.

While the fear-mongering “too much protein” articles sometimes mention that bodybuilders or elite athletes need their protein, they tend to hand-wave this away as a special concern that doesn’t apply to normal people. But I think it’s worth a closer look—and honestly, this situation applies to a lot more people than just a few athletes.

Officially, there isn’t an RDA for athletes; people who exercise can stave off malnutrition with the same 0.36 grams per pound as everyone else. But that doesn’t mean that the RDA is the best target to aim for.

The International Association of Athletics Federations, which governs track and field competitions, recommends that most athletes who are maintaining or gaining weight eat 0.59 to 0.77 grams of protein per pound of bodyweight per day. That’s 101 to 131 grams for the average 171-pound woman, and 118 to 154 grams for a 200-pound man.

A group of organizations, including the American College of Sports Medicine, largely agrees, recommending a range from 0.54 to 0.9 grams per pound for all athletes whose weight is stable or gaining. That includes people who do endurance training like distance running, as well as strength athletes whose exercise involves mainly lifting weights. Those ranges would go as high as 153 grams for our 171-pound woman, and 180 grams for our 200-pound man.

You don’t need to be an Olympian to consider yourself an “athlete” in this sense. If you’re training for a half marathon, you’re doing plenty of distance running, and should fuel accordingly. And if you’re “just” lifting weights in the gym, but taking it seriously enough that you’re training regularly and working hard, you should consider eating in these ranges as well.

Dieting to lose weight is not only a popular American pastime, it’s also arguably good for at least some people's health. If you’ve been on a diet recently, or if you’re planning to go on one, you aren’t a person who should settle for the RDA either.

Research shows that protein intake (and strength training—they go together!) is important to maintain muscle mass when we’re losing weight. After all, you’re aiming for fat loss, not trying to get your muscles to waste away. Muscle loss is especially a concern with weight-loss drugs like Ozempic, but any dieter should be aware of this issue.

For example, this study found that diets ranging from 0.48 to 0.72 grams of protein per kg of body weight (that’s 82 to 123 grams for our 171-pound woman, 96 to 144 for our 200-pound man) resulted in less weight regain after the diet, and helped people to maintain muscle mass and feel more full while they were dieting.

And if you’re losing weight and exercising? The IAAF recommends that athletes who are “undertaking high-quality weight loss” need at least 0.72 grams per pound of bodyweight, and possibly as much as 1.09 grams per pound. That would be 186 grams for a 171-pound athlete, or 218 grams for a 200-pound athlete. Most people won’t need to go that high, and it’s unclear whether athletes need to go that high. But I’m including these numbers so you see how high the ranges actually go.

Ultimately, weight loss is widely understood to be more effective and have healthier results with higher protein intakes rather than lower ones. When people focus on just eating less, without thinking about what their diet actually consists of, it’s easy to forget about protein. But the evidence suggests that you should increase protein when you’re decreasing overall calories.

The idea that protein causes weight gain is a common talking point in those articles about “too much” protein, and it’s sort of true—but it also doesn’t mean what you think it means.

When you eat more food than your body needs, your body can store it as fat. That’s true no matter what the excess is made of—protein, carbs, fat, or even alcohol. The protein you eat gets used for many different things in your body. You can build it into muscle tissue, use it for growth and repair of different kinds of cells, and so on. You can also use it for energy—basically, burning it for the calories.

So if you were eating a perfectly balanced diet, and then decided to add an extra 100 grams of protein per day, then sure, a lot of that protein would be used for energy, and since we’d have excess energy, it would get stored as fat.

But if you ate more protein, but that protein replaced other foods in your diet, then there would be no excess calories to store. Nobody is saying you should chug a couple of protein shakes on top of your regular diet. They’re saying (I’m saying) that you should plan your meals and snacks to include more protein.

For example, if your regular lunch is a turkey-and-cheese sandwich with a side of chips, you could improve the protein content of your diet by adding more turkey to the sandwich and replacing the chips with an apple. Same total calories, but more protein. As long as your total calories for the day aren’t in excess of your needs, the “extra” protein won’t get stored as fat.

In general, high protein diets don’t have any serious health consequences. There’s a major exception, though: in some medical conditions, you may be told to limit your protein intake to protect your health.

For example, people with chronic kidney disease are often advised to use the RDA (0.36 grams per pound of body weight) as a maximum rather than a minimum. Your kidneys play a role in processing protein for excretion, so a lowered protein intake reduces the amount of work that a damaged kidney has to do. That said, once a person with chronic kidney disease begins dialysis, they may be advised to increase their protein intake for better health now that their body has help to handle the higher levels.

People with certain other disorders, like phenylketonuria and homocystinuria, may also be advised to eat a low-protein diet. Obviously, if you have one of these conditions, you should be getting your dietary advice from your medical team (ask for a referral to a dietitian!) rather than from general articles on the internet.

Besides those known medical issues, the occasional findings about eating “too much” protein tend to fit into the “X is good for you/X is bad for you” ricochet news cycle. They’re not holistic assessments of protein in general on health in general, but rather specific research questions that are still being figured out.

For example, this 2017 study found that a high-protein (and high-fiber) diet seemed to slightly worsen one measure of insulin resistance, but it also improved metabolic health and body composition. The researchers concluded that the subjects’ body chemistry was probably just responding appropriately to the changed nutrient content of their diet. A few years later, a study of high-BMI women with insulin resistance saw improvements to their insulin resistance on a high-protein diet.

Or to take another example, a study in 2024 found a link between high-protein diets and atherosclerosis. But if you look at what the researchers were actually studying, they were looking at how leucine (one amino acid found in protein) affects the mTOR biochemical pathway in certain types of white blood cells. By the way, that mTOR pathway is involved in a lot more body processes than atherosclerosis, and does a lot of good things too.

So are these results interesting, and worth further study? Definitely. Worth changing protein recommendations? Only if this effect turns out (1) to actually lead to worse health outcomes, and (2) to outweigh the known benefits of higher protein. The body of evidence doesn’t yet support lowering protein recommendations, nor adding an upper limit.

So if protein is good for us, and most of us can’t really get “too much,” why are so many people arguing that we’re overdoing it? I think part of the reason is just misunderstanding (the writers don’t tend to have a background in nutrition and especially not in sports nutrition), but more often, I think they’re talking about a different issue entirely.

Often the “too much protein” stuff is just a way of talking about the environmental effects of meat consumption or dairy farming. People making this argument are trying to pry the double cheeseburgers out of our hands and reassure us that we’ll be okay. I don’t think an attack on protein is an appropriate way to make that point, since plant-based proteins exist and are a fine alternative. But I understand where they’re coming from.

Ultimately, if you’re trying to make the argument that we’re eating “too much” protein for our health, you really can’t do that without some evidence that we’re eating so much protein that it’s harming our health on a widespread level. And that evidence just doesn’t exist.

#3419. Mads Mikkelsen Delivered His Best Performance In This Unforgettable 2012 Movie

Few European actors have found the blend of native and international success that Mads Mikkelsen has. Born in Denmark, he became a star in his home country during the 1990s and 2000s, his career kicking off with Nicolas Winding Refn's 1996 crime thriller "Pusher." He's since become a favorite of Hollywood productions, too, starting with his role as the Bond villain Le Chiffre in "Casino Royale."

Since then, Mikkelsen has remained a go-to Hollywood bad guy, appearing in blockbusters like Marvel Studios' "Doctor Strange." He's also one of the privileged few to have played arguably the most famous screen villain ever, Hannibal Lecter. More than a few would argue Mikkelsen's Lecter in the 2013 TV series "Hannibal" is even better than Anthony Hopkins in "The Silence of the Lambs."

Mikkelsen's razor-sharp cheekbones, intense stare, and European accent instantly code him as "villain" in Hollywood language. When "Rogue One: A Star Wars Story" cast him as Galen Erso, a sympathetic scientist conscripted into building the Death Star, it read as casting against type to American audiences. But look at Mikkelsen's Danish resume and you'll find he's a much more diverse actor than the box that Hollywood has stuck him inside. Amusingly, one of those movies — Thomas Vinterberg's "The Hunt" — stars Mikkelsen as a good man mistakenly persecuted as a villain.

Lucas (Mikkelsen) is a Danish kindergarten teacher. One of his students, his best friend Theo's (Thomas Bo Larsen) daughter Klara (Annika Wedderkopp), has a puppy love crush on him. Obviously, he gently turns her down. Klara then vengefully suggests to the school principal that Lucas exposed himself to or molested her. (In reality, as the movie shows, her crude older brother shoved an iPad displaying porn in her face.) The ugly rumor grows out of control, and Lucas' reputation pays the price.

In "The Hunt," the town rushes to the worst possible conclusion about Lucas. All but a few loved ones like his son, Marcus (Lasse Fogelstrøm), believe the worst from hearsay. But they don't actually know it for a fact (indeed, what ultimately helps clear Lucas is the facts pointing in his favor). The movie is never ambiguous, though; we know from the very beginning that Lucas is innocent and this is all just a terrible tragedy of miscommunication. "The Hunt" also avoids reactionary narratives about scorned women peddling false rape allegations because Klara is a young child. She simply doesn't grasp the consequences of what she did, as is the case with the other preschoolers who echo her claims.

Compare a similar recent film, "Fjord," inspired by a real-life story about a Norwegian evangelical couple whose children were taken from them after suspicions of abuse. Like in "The Hunt," the allegations are implied to stem from leading questions and miscommunication from the kids. But "Fjord" counterintuitively stacks the deck in the parents' favor while trying to present objectivity, perhaps because it knows many left-leaning audiences are inclined to side against the conservative couple and takes perverse enjoyment in testing those sympathies.

A film like "The Hunt" could choose not to reveal Lucas' innocence either way or cast doubt, inviting you to sympathize with a possible monster as an endurance test. But the reality of "The Hunt," seeing an innocent man be branded with a scarlet letter, is also agonizing to watch in its own way. It's a modern iteration on the parable of the feathers in the wind, and how once spoken, even untruthful gossip can't be erased.

As Lucas, Mikkelsen sheds any of the power or menace he projects as a villain in those aforementioned Hollywood movies. "The Hunt" is also a Danish-language film, and Mikkelsen's comfort with his native tongue also makes for an even more seamless performance.

To this day, I've never forgotten the catharsis of a scene where Lucas stands up for himself. After being assaulted in a grocery store, he walks in again, headbutts the hostile clerk, and demands his groceries back. The first time I watched "The Hunt," I rewound the movie to see the scene a second time.

That relatively late-in-the-movie scene is a well-earned respite from Lucas' victimhood. Even in a story like this, too much passivity from a protagonist turns into a chore. Lucas similarly takes matters into his own hands at the movie's emotional climax. Again, Klara's father Theo is Lucas' best friend; while Theo takes Klara's side, he claims to know Lucas so well he can tell when he's lying or truthful by just looking into his eyes. Lucas goes to Christmas Mass, putting himself dead center in the community that has exiled him, and looks at Theo across the pews.

The power of this lynchpin scene is in Mikkelsen's silent, icy stare (Lucas pointedly ditches his glasses during this scene). But it's not the aloof stare of Le Chiffre or the predatory one of Hannibal Lecter. In his sad eyes and slight frown, Lucas is begging Theo to read the truth on his face. When that's not enough, he storms over to Theo, sobbing, and refuses to let him look away from his eyes.

Mads Mikkelsen is an extraordinary actor, and yet the greatest proof of that is him playing a normal man in "The Hunt."

Wicker might not get any Oscar recognition (although that would be a pleasant surprise), but I'd argue it's one of the best theater-going experiences of any film released on the 2026 movie schedule. Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård’s unconventional rom-com turned out to be much more than a smutty romance about a perfect man built of wicker. Audiences were won over not only by Skarsgård’s wicker abs, but also his character’s pure heart, leaving many hungry for more, Skarsgård included. And I laughed out loud when I heard the “sequel” he’s been pitching.

Alexander Skarsgård has never been one to take himself too seriously, especially while doing press tours. I can’t say I blame him, doing the same interviews over and over would get pretty old otherwise. However, his effortless deadpan and jesting tendencies make it difficult to sometimes tell if he’s being serious or not, like with this recent pitch to Entertainment Weekly about a Wicker follow-up:

It’s called Corduroy. We tried to find financing for it, but, for some reason, it’s been hard, but we’re pitching it around Hollywood this week.

At this point, I can’t tell if this is a serious pitch or not, but the idea is genuinely hilarious. Skarsgård added that this corduroy character would be “delicate and soft,” as well as an “attentive lover.” I’ve got to be honest, that doesn’t sound as sexy as a sturdily built wicker man, but I get the sense this concept is in very early stages of development. Forget splinters, we’d be wondering about carpet burn.

Seriously, I’m going to need someone to ask the A-lister about this again, because I really need some clarification. Skarsgård is known to joke with the media, even tot he point of teasing a “smear” campaign against his father, Stellan Skarsgård (Sentimental Value) during awards season. However, I wouldn’t put it past him to actually try and get this wild sequel made.

I’m just not fully sold on “Corduroy” for another reason. If your mind went to the same place as mine upon hearing this pitch, you understand why. Yes, I’m talking about the children’s story “Corduroy,” in which a corduroy teddy bear comes to life in a department store. Given Wicker’s salacious content and marketing, it feels really weird to relate the two, and therefore I fear it might be difficult to get that sequel pitch off the ground. However, the Legend of Tarzan actor has been persistent in the idea of a Wicker sequel, and I’m curious to see what that might look like.

This isn’t the first time the Northman actor has pitched a sequel to his latest movie. During the press tour, Skarsgård expressed interest in continuing the Wicker Husband’s story, following questions about what happens at the end of Wicker when the unconventional family of three leaves their village behind.

Clearly, Skarsgård enjoyed playing the wicker sex symbol that has taken the internet by storm, but that’s not surprising. If 2025’s kinky Pillion taught us anything, it’s that Skarsgård isn’t afraid to get a lil freaky (in the best ways) and Wicker seems to have opened a whole new realm of possibilities in his mind.

However, between the wicker husband’s kind heart and the fairytale-like setting that allows this somewhat raunchy, yet overall heartwarming love story to take place, I’m just not sure the same effect would work with a “corduroy husband” or any other textile husband for that matter. I’ll be quite surprised if something along these lines pops up on the 2027 movie schedule, but you can bet I’ll still buy a ticket. In the meantime, check out Wicker in theaters now.

#3417. 'The Body' Ending Explained: Is Grace Possessed? Netflix Showrunners Talk Season 2

Also, how White Chicks influenced a key scene

The Body, Netflix’s new campy-horror TV series, came out this week. But based on a quick social media browse, it might as well have come out months ago. The high school thriller inspired passionate fan debates among viewers and dozens of fan cams dedicated to favorite characters long before a single episode aired. Now that The Body has finally arrived, however, fans are having an entirely different debate that hinges on its wild cliffhanger ending.

In search of answers, we turned to co-showrunners Quinn Shephard and Gina Gammell, who admit they don't even know where the series is headed next and that they enjoy the conversation the finale has inspired.

"We are amiable and gullible and don't have an answer either," Gammell tells Polygon.

Below, we break down some of The Body's biggest season 1 mysteries with Shephard and Gammell, and discuss where the story might be headed next.

The following contains spoilers for The Body season 1 ending.

Broadly, The Body follows a high school dance team who may or may not have sacrificed a girl’s soul to qualify for their Regionals competition. Through its eight episodes, the show explores the shifting dynamics and allegiances between its three main characters: Anya (Kristina Bogic), Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros), and Elise (Sara Boustany).

Season 1 ends with Anya confessing the sins that had been eating at her all through the season, including both her sexuality and the fact that she feels responsible for the series’ inciting incident, where Grace (Sofia Wylie) fell into a coma after taking some ecstasy at a Halloween party. Anya reveals that, when Grace started feeling sick, she decided to drive her to the hospital, only for Grace to seemingly die in the back seat. In a spur-of-the-moment decision, Anya returns Grace’s body to her bedroom and tucks her in, hoping to cover it all up without having to deal with the consequences.

Following Anya’s confession, Grace wakes up, stunning everyone, and says, “I’m God.” It’s the season’s final line of dialogue and one heck of a cliffhanger.

“It was the place we were always aiming towards,” Shephard says.

Shephard and Gammell agree that what they enjoy the most about the season finale is the fact that it can inspire passionate debates.

"We want people to feel similarly at the end to the way you feel at all of the biggest turns of the show, which is a continued curiosity about what is really going on, and a certain autonomy to influence that in your own watching," Shephard says. "A certain ability to be like, 'No, I know for sure that she's possessed.' And then someone else is like, 'No, in the last episode, they said that she could hear stuff in the coma.' I think those are our favorite conversations to witness.”

The question of what’s real and what’s imagined lies at the core of the series, which is constantly pitting religion against reality. The many supernatural appearances and occurrences that take place could be part of a mass delusion, or they could be a miracle.

Gammell says that the theories that people share with them “entirely convince us each time. It doesn't matter. Depending on who we're speaking to, we're like, 'You're right. It is the devil.' And someone else is like, 'No, no, she has a drug interaction.' We're like, 'You're right. That is correct too.'"

If the show gets renewed for season 2, one thing is clear:

"Grace will be awake," Gammell says. She and Shephard are excited to write new dialogue for Wylie beyond "I'm God.”

Whatever comes next, Shephard and Gammell seem to want their show to continue to straddle the line between science and religion. At least for now, they want no clear-cut answers.

“We’re both people who believe in science and ghosts,” Shephard says. “So I think that we fall in the middle.”

Much of The Body works because it’s at its best when navigating tones that seem opposite, at least on paper. Shephard began writing the show’s pilot as a drama; it was only after some time had passed and she and Gammell began working together that they landed on the campy tone that makes the series so memorable.

“I think the satire and the comedy of the show was very much born from our working collaboration on it, and Gina finding the stories of things that upset me as a teenager quite funny,” Shephard says.

An example of this is a scene that depicts our three lead characters in the car together, with tensions at an all-time high. Shephard reveals that after she had written it and finalized it, she got an idea for the scene’s tone from watching White Chicks.

“I sent a still to my DP and said, ‘I think this is how the scene should look: them in the convertible: White Chicks,’” Shephard recalls.

If you’ve seen The Body, you know exactly what scene Shephard is talking about. While the actors play it like a serious drama, the tone makes it one of the show’s funniest moments. The result is a marriage of two seemingly opposing sensibilities.

#3416. Five Race-Day Smartwatch Hacks Every Marathon Runner Should Know

I love my Garmin Forerunner 970, but the fact is, most runners don't need all the features it has to offer. In fact, for most road races, you can get by with whatever smartwatch you already own—as long as you know how to use it. If you've got a marathon or half-marathon coming up, these five tricks will only take a few minutes to set up, and they can save you from one of many of the small-but-avoidable disasters that can derail a good race.

Nothing spikes pre-race anxiety like standing in a corral of hundreds of people watching your watch fail to latch onto a signal. Tall buildings, crowded starts, and a sea of other devices make the first minute of GPS unreliable, which can leave your opening mileage pace wildly off.

The fix is simple: start the GPS search early. Step outside, into the open, as soon as you've dropped your bag, and select your run activity at least 10 to 15 minutes before the starting gun. If your watch supports multi-band or dual-frequency GPS, turn it on in the activity settings, since it's noticeably better in dense downtown starts. Then, don't press start until the gun goes off (or you cross the line, if you want chip-accurate pacing).

Bonus tip: If you're in a start corral with a long wait, you can lock the signal and then pause the activity screen. Just remember to hit start when you actually take off.

Multiple data screens are great for training, but overwhelming during a race. Too many numbers invite overthinking, and seeing the "wrong" number at mile two can lead you into a very stressful mile ten.

My recommendation is to build a dedicated race screen with three to four fields at most:

Lap pace or average lap pace (not instant pace, which jumps around constantly with GPS)

Distance or lap distance, so you know where you are relative to the mile markers

Heart rate, especially in the early miles when adrenaline tempts you to go out too fast

Elapsed time, for splits against your goal

Keep it clean and stripped down, and avoid the temptation to add cadence, power, vertical oscillation, and everything else. You can always review those stats during your cool-down.

A text from your boss at mile 14 is nobody's idea of a good time. Before race day, switch your watch to Do Not Disturb or Airplane mode, or turn on a dedicated activity mode that blocks notifications. This also saves battery, which matters if your marathon is going to take you four-plus hours.

After blocking the outside world, you can set race-specific alerts, like a high heart-rate alert to keep you honest in the first half. I also know runners who set a recurring time or distance alert for fueling—say, every 30 to 40 minutes, or every 5 miles—so remembering to down a gel or a sports drink doesn't depend on your fading brain.

Here's one thing I learn the hard way, every time: Your watch will almost always say you've run farther than the race course says you have. Race courses are measured along the shortest possible route, but along the way, you'll weave around people, take wide turns, and generally add extra distance. I've run marathons where my watch reads closer to 26.6 miles (nearly an extra half mile), so my "on pace" watch is actually behind my chip time.

The hack: Ignore the watch's auto-lap and press the lap button manually at each mile marker (or at every kilometer marker, if that's what the course uses). This gives you pace data aligned to the official course, not the satellite's best guess. It also gives you a quick mental check against your plan. If you've set up your watch for it, display average lap pace, then glance at it a few hundred meters after each marker to see how you're tracking. And don't panic if your watch beeps for a mile before you pass the marker—trust the course and your lap presses, and do your best to ignore the mismatched distance adding up.

Rain, sweat, high-fives, and a hasty cup grab at an aid station can all trigger accidental taps on a touchscreen watch. Few things are worse than discovering at mile 18 that you accidentally paused, ended, or switched screens on your activity. So before the race, turn on your watch's screen lock, so a stray touch doesn't do anything.

If your watch has a configurable wake gesture, consider turning it off to save battery, and set the backlight to a short timeout. While we're talking watch-wearing protocol, remember to wear it snugly, one finger-width above your wrist bone, for a better heart-rate reading as you sweat. Finally, if your watch has one, use the post-race auto-save reminder. (Otherwise, do your best to hit stop after you cross the finish line.)

Again, you don't need the most premium running-specific watch ahead of race day. If you have time, test these hacks on a long run, so that you're not wasting any precious mental energy during the big day.

#3415. Is The Rings Of Power Connected To Peter Jackson's Lord Of The Rings Trilogy?

The canon of the "Lord of the Rings" movie and TV franchise has become a little complicated in recent years. Sauron's war finally arrives in "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3, and with the show's return, it's worth asking: Is this series canonical to Peter Jackson's "Lord of the Rings" films? We finally have a firm answer, and it's ... sort of (if we read between the lines).

In a recent interview with Screen Rant, "The Rings of Power" co-showrunner Patrick McKay addressed the canon question head-on without giving a simple "yes" or "no" answer. Still he made it pretty clear where things stand, explaining, "There is room in Middle-earth for everybody, and we're fans of those films, and we hope it's great." (He was referring to the already controversial upcoming film "The Hunt for Gollum" with that last bit.)

In terms of the "Lord of the Rings" timeline, "The Rings of Power" is set thousands of years before the "Lord of the Rings" movies. So, in theory, they could work together. Speaking further though, McKay established that the show exists alongside the many interpretations of J.R.R. Tolkien's Middle-earth books over the years and not necessarily as part of any other adaptation (including Jackson's):

"So many talented artists in so many mediums over 75 years have interpreted this material, painted or drawn it, or put it in a song or made it into a film or an animated film. I think to sit on a shelf with all those other works, we are only too delighted for that to be our fate."

He added that the movies and the show are "in conversation with one another." Put simply, then, "The Rings of Power" is not strictly canon within the universe of Jackson's films.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" brings the fabled Second Age of Middle-earth's history to life on-screen for the first time. Therefore, it's centuries removed from both the events of J.R.R. Tolkien's "The Hobbit" and "The Lord of the Rings" books and Peter Jackson's film adaptations alike.

Even so, it initially looked like Jackson was going to be involved with "The Rings of Power," only for Amazon to ghost him while developing the Prime Video series. Why? In essence, it was apparently a contractual matter. In a statement issued in 2022, Amazon claimed, "In pursuing the rights for our show, we were obligated to keep the series distinct and separate from the films." So, basically, "The Rings of Power" can't, for legal reasons, be officially canonical to Jackson's movies. Of course, Patrick McKay couldn't just come out and say that, so he found a more diplomatic way to go about it.

Jackson, obviously, is the man that turned "The Lord of the Rings" into the one fantasy franchise to rule them all, as his adaptations of J.R.R. Tolkien's books became massive, beloved hits that have endured for decades. Still, while it makes sense that Amazon would, in theory, want him to work on "The Rings of Power," it seems securing the rights for the show meant sacrifices had to be made.

Nevertheless, Jackson is producing (but not directing) "The Hunt for Gollum," with Gollum actor Andy Serkis helming the movie himself. Warner Bros. is also developing another "LOTR" movie co-written by superfan Stephen Colbert, so this franchise has a future on the big screen as well.

"The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" is streaming now on Prime Video.
