At the very start of Dancing with the Stars' 35th season, I thought Harry Shum Jr. was the ultimate frontrunner. However, I quickly came to love Ezra Frech. His story is remarkable and empowering. Plus, he’s so naturally talented, and he's partnered with one of my favorite pros, Daniella Karagach. So, as the weeks have passed on the 2026 TV schedule, I’ve wanted him to win. However, as each episode has gone by and that appreciation for Frech has stayed consistent, my love for Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov just keeps growing stronger and stronger.

While I always thought Amber was one to watch, she’s proven time and time again that she and her partner are helping set the gold standard for this season. Then, the figure skater went on the Zach Sang Show to talk about her experience on DWTS, and she said something about winning that really made her the frontrunner in my mind. When asked what it’d mean to get Pasha his first mirrorball, the Olympian said:

That would mean the world, because, I’ve said this before, is that I came into this competition, of course, who doesn’t want to win. But it wasn’t like, ‘I need this because I’ve worked my entire life for it.’ Like, I’ve been dancing for two months. Yes, it has been a very intense, very passionate two months of working, but it has been his whole life that he has been dancing. And he’s been on the show for, I believe, nine seasons. And every single year, he has put his everything into every single celeb he’s had.

Pasha has been on the show for eight seasons, and with each year, I love him and his wife, Daniella, even more. Seriously, season after season, I find myself more invested in the pros than the stars. That’s because they’re there year after year, and I get to know them all quite well through the show and social media. So, while I adore them all, and my love for Daniella is very strong, I have wanted Pasha to get his flowers really, really badly.

In his eight seasons, the highest place he’s ever gotten is third, and he deserves a win. Amber is the perfect person to help him do it. As she explained, he wanted to have an athlete as a partner, and she has “the stamina and the physical capabilities” to do tougher dances. She also complimented her partner’s ability to teach, and ended up saying:

There’s no reason that we shouldn’t be able to make this happen besides me limiting myself.

Her drive to do this for her partner is so endearing, and it’s now a big reason why I want her to win. Along with that, the Olympian went on to detail how much work the pros have to do for this show. While it looks hard for the stars, the pros have to do twice as much, and she wants Pasha to get recognized for it, explaining:

He has been putting everything into this, and I really want for everyone to see him succeed. Because it is technically, you know, every year it’s the celeb, but it’s also about the pros. Like, he is putting – imagine how much work I’m putting into it; he’s doing twice the amount. He has to choreograph; he has to do so many visual selections. Like, there’s so much that the pro does for every single show that people don’t see. So, yes, it’s about the celebrity and who wins, but it is also about the pro.

Of course, all the pros have to do this, and I'm sure their stars would praise them the same way Amber praised Pasha. However, her passion is infectious, and that, paired with their fun and high-quality dances, makes them my No. 1 couple.

Plus, of the vets still on the show who have been there for over seven seasons, Mark Ballas, Jenna Johnson, and Daniella have won before; Pasha has not.

So, yes, while I’ll be happy if Ezra and Daniella win, because they are amazing, right now, I’m rooting harder for Amber and Pasha. They are killing it week after week, and Amber’s drive to win for her pro and get him his first mirrorball is making me even more motivated to text “Amber” to 21523 as many times as I possibly can.

Now, to see who takes home the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy, make sure to tune in to the last few weeks of Dancing with the Stars on Tuesdays at 8 p.m. ET either on ABC or with a Disney+ subscription.

#3413. 15 Best Hard Sci-Fi Movies Of All Time, Ranked

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

While science fiction includes everything from space opera to cyberpunk, one sub-genre that we have a special place for is hard sci-fi. These movies place a stronger emphasis on scientific accuracy and a more grounded premise than their more fantastical counterparts. Many of the best sci-fi movies ever are set within the realm of hard sci-fi, heightening the sense of realism to their stories. We're taking a closer look at this fan-favorite sub-genre and our personal favorite movies within it.

While there are varying opinions about what qualifies as hard sci-fi, each of the movies we're including here certainly have a strong scientific grounding. Even some of the best sci-fi movies of 2026 are clear hard sci-fi projects, breathing new life into the sub-genre. With those qualities in mind, these are the best 15 hard sci-fi movies of all time ranked, each offering their own cinematic verisimilitude to the genre.

After "2001: A Space Odyssey," there was "Marooned," with Gregory Peck's space thriller based on the novel of the same name by Martin Caidin. Peck stars as NASA Director Charles Keith who finds himself working on a desperate rescue mission to save three astronauts stranded in orbit. As the incident becomes more public, Keith is forced to use an experimental spacecraft for the rescue, despite it being untested. Meanwhile, the stranded astronauts grow desperate as they begin to run out of oxygen before help arrives.

"Marooned" was released before the Apollo 13 incident, which similarly saw American astronauts seemingly stranded in space. While things like the movie's experimental spacecraft take it to sci-fi territory, the whole thing feels scientifically plausible. At the same time, the movie also keeps a tight focus on the human stakes, including the response back home and the families affected by the incident. Overlooked by audiences today, nearly 60 years later, "Marooned" sets the template for so many subsequent space disaster movies on this list.

A big factor in a lot of hard sci-fi movies is its production budget, because it's far cheaper to make a grounded sci-fi movie than an outlandishly audacious one. That certainly informs the 2004 indie movie "Primer," written, directed, produced, edited, and starring Shane Carruth, who also composed the score. Carruth plays Aaron, an engineer whose colleague Abe (David Sullivan) develops an amateur time machine in their garage. As the duo explore the possibilities of their invention, they progressively experience the dire consequences of time travel.

While "Primer" may look and feel like a lofi time travel movie at first glance, it refreshingly explores its conflict from a well-thought approach. Things like the process' physical toll on the body from its wider ripple effects are smartly explored throughout the story. The production's DIY nature actually suits the narrative well, given the amateur nature of the movie's central plot device. If you haven't seen "Primer" before, the movie is a must-watch for sci-fi movie fans and a tightly constructed one at that.

1997's "Gattaca" is another sci-fi flick that feels eerily plausible for modern society to follow within the next several years. The story is set in a world where eugenics has become widespread to avoid the birth of babies with debilitating genetic conditions. This leads to society discriminating against those who carry genetic defects, including protagonist Vincent Freeman (Ethan Hawke). Posing as a genetically engineered individual, Vincent's ruse comes under scrutiny in the wake of a corporate executive's murder.

Admittedly, "Gattaca" is the most visually stylish movie on this list, but its concept and the level of technology depicted hold a real world weight to them. The science behind the story's genetic engineering and eugenics feels particularly well-developed as the cornerstone of this dystopian society. The movie goes into meticulous detail how Vincent is able to maintain his deception and how this genetic technology has impacted civilization. A dystopian noir look at the perils of artificial perfection, "Gattaca" is a moody flick that makes the most of its premise.

Filmmaker James Cameron's most underrated movie is the 1989 underwater thriller "The Abyss," with its core themes carried over into "Avatar: The Way of Water." The movie has American and Soviet teams racing to salvage a sunken American submarine from the bottom of the ocean. Leading the American expedition is an oil drilling crew headed by Bud Brigman (Ed Harris), only to find otherworldly entities are involved. As the full scope of this mission becomes apparent, Bud tries to stop hostilities from escalating between humanity and this underwater species.

More than just standing as another Cameron project that heavily involves the water, "The Abyss" also showcases his sharp attention to detail. Cameron takes care to demonstrate the real-world dangers of deep-sea exploration, including the high pressure and chilling temperatures of the watery depths. These elements fuel the tension as much as the strange creatures that Bud encounters, along with Cameron's recurring message that unchecked human aggression is the true enemy. Claustrophobically staged and under-appreciated for years, "The Abyss" is Cameron's unsung classic and as grounded his sci-fi work gets.

The first novel that author Michael Crichton published under his own name was 1969's "The Andromeda Strain," which was adapted for the silver screen in 1971. More intelligently assembled than the standard disaster movie fare of its time, the movie opens with a satellite crashing near a small town in New Mexico. After most of the community dies suddenly under mysterious causes, it's discovered that the satellite brought back a highly lethal extraterrestrial microorganism. The movie follows a team of scientists trying to contain the situation before it can wipe out all life on the planet.

Crichton's work tends to succeed the more firmly that they're rooted in reality before expanding into the fantastical. "The Andromeda Strain" is a prime example of this, still packing a punch over 50 years since its debut. That strong scientific approach to the premise underscores the gravity that this threat is terrifyingly plausible. Still one of the best Michael Crichton movie adaptations, "The Andromeda Strain" offers a grounded sci-fi approach to annihilation by contagion.

While the 1972 adaptation of "Solaris" by Soviet filmmaker Andrei Tarkovsky is one of the best space horror movies ever made, it does veer tonally away from Stanisław Lem's novel. By contrast, Steven Soderbergh's 2002 adaptation is more of a drama and an isolated character study, though some existential thriller elements remain. The movie's protagonist is Chris Kelvin (George Clooney), a clinical psychologist who visits a remote space station only to find most of its crew is dead. As Kelvin investigates the situation, he is shocked to be reunited with his late wife Rheya (Natascha McElhone). who is seemingly alive and well.

While it's a close call, Soderbergh's "Solaris" is a sci-fi remake that's better than the original, mostly because of change in tone and Clooney's vulnerable performance. This elevates the movie's ambiguous existential contemplation, while Soderbergh wisely keeps the sci-fi elements relatively stripped down. At its core, the story is a meditation on grief and guilt while Soderbergh builds his story in a relatively grounded outer space setting. Soderbergh's "Solaris" is both his most understated and boldest project, using the mysteries of the cosmos to explore its emotional themes.

The debut feature directorial project by British filmmaker Duncan Jones is the 2009 indie flick "Moon." The movie is largely a one-man show for Sam Rockwell, who plays Samuel Bell, a technician working alone in a lunar mining facility. As Bell nears the end of his three-year assignment, he begins to hallucinate, while his health steadily worsens. This culminates in Bell coming face-to-face with a doppelganger of himself, as he realizes the disturbing truth about his existence.

With its pragmatically minimalist art design and Rockwell being the only actor on-screen for the majority of the movie, "Moon" keeps its storytelling simple but effective. The idea that the Moon could be mined heavily for helium-3 is rooted in fact, while the technology is never particularly outlandish. Like Soderbergh's "Solaris," Jones keeps its narrative focus tightly on his protagonist which is where its real strength lies. An intimately scaled sci-fi thriller, "Moon" remains Duncan's best work to date, using its grounded backdrop to atmospheric effect.

Among the sci-fi movies that nobody talks about anymore is "Silent Running," which was released in 1972. The movie takes place in a future where Earth is no longer capable of supporting trees, forcing humanity to take its forestry off-world. The story is set in a spaceship serving as a large biome for trees, tended to meticulously by botanist Freeman Lowell (Bruce Dern). When the crew is ordered to destroy the biomes by their corporate overseers, Lowell goes through murderous lengths to defend his carefully curated forests.

Of all the movies on this list, "Silent Running" is the one with the most pointed sociopolitical commentary. From its takedown of corporate greed to its eco-friendly themes, the movie feels like both a product of its time and as prescient as ever. Dern is rarely better than in his performance as Lowell, with his character standing as a portrait of single-minded obsession and carrying much of the movie. Unabashedly direct in its messaging, "Silent Running" deserves wider recognition than it receives from the public these days.

Not every hard sci-fi movie needs to unfold in outer space or revolve around high concept narratives. The 2013 romantic drama "Her" is perfectly set within a more intimate scope, given its premise. Taking place in a near-future Los Angeles, loner Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) struggles at forming a meaningful romantic connection with others. Instead, Theodore grows closer to his digital assistant Samantha (Scarlett Johansson) as she gains sentience, with a loving relationship growing between them.

"Her" is the perfect love story for the Information Age, underscoring that technological advances don't necessarily separate us from connecting with others. The movie's premise feels entirely plausible while also being prescient in the decade prior to the widespread proliferation of artificial intelligence. The tightened focus works well, with filmmaker Spike Jonze keeping the "Her" set intimate for Joaquin Phoenix, as he stays awkwardly vulnerable for much of the story. Understated in its tone and scope but still packing an emotional wallop, "Her" is Jonze's humanist masterpiece in an increasingly digital era.

Among the most celebrated hard sci-fi authors of the 20th century was astronomer and science educator Carl Sagan. The 1997 movie "Contact" adapted Sagan's 1985 novel of the same name, detailing humanity's first contact with extraterrestrial life. After astronomer Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster) detects signs of intelligent otherworldly life, the world is galvanized by the discovery. Though Arroway wants to make contact with these mysterious figures through an experimental device, complications quickly arise.

While there is certainly extraterrestrial interaction to be had, "Contact" is more about the reaction and fallout to confirmation of otherworldly life. Jodie Foster brings that thoroughly human response to the subject matter, while her character guides audiences through the story. "Contact" could've been a much stranger movie, treating Sagan and partner Ann Druyan's tale with tone-deaf disregard for scientific accuracy and characterization, but cooler heads won out. One of the best sci-fi movies of the '90s, hard with its science or not, "Contact" is an understated genre gem.

Upon its debut in 2026, "Project Hail Mary" was quickly crowned as one of the best sci-fi movies ever and deservedly so. Based on the best-selling novel by Andy Weir, the movie has our sun plagued by a strange substance threatening to dim it to catastrophic levels within decades. Molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) is forced to join an interstellar expedition searching for a way to restore the sun's output. This leads Grace to team up with a rock-based extraterrestrial on his own mission to save his planet from the threat of the same substance.

"Project Hail Mary" improves upon Andy Weir's book in key ways, streamlining the story and quietly discarding its more superfluous sci-fi elements. But even with its interstellar partnership, the adaptation retains the source material's penchant for scientifically informed storytelling. That grounds the more cosmic elements as Grace finally enacts his last-ditch effort to save his world from chilly annihilation. Keeping hard sci-fi alive and well into the 2020s, "Project Hail Mary" is a bonafide crowd-pleaser.

Still one of Christopher Nolan's most ambitious movies over a decade after its release, "Interstellar" is the filmmaker's most high-flying tale to date. Like "Project Hail Mary" after it, the movie revolves around humanity at the brink of extinction, forced to undertake a desperate mission for its salvation. In the case of Nolan's story, Earth is rocked by severe dust storms affecting its agriculture, with astronaut Coop (Matthew McConaughey) leading an expedition for a habitable planet. This is juxtaposed by Coop's adult daughter Murph (Jessica Chastain) trying to find a way to create a spacecraft capable of launching into deep space through Earth's gravity.

While there are, of course, creative liberties taken through its premise, "Interstellar" boasts a high level of scientific accuracy. This includes the astrophysics propelling the story like the singularity that serves as the key to its spacefaring scope. Everything from planets undergoing significant time dilation to the gravity equation back on Earth all feel feasible, even with all the cinematic splendor. Christopher Nolan always offers a well-thought approach to even the most fantastical subject matter, and "Interstellar" captures those qualities beautifully.

Another British filmmaker who's excelled at smart sci-fi storytelling in the 21st century is Alex Garland. Arguably the hardest sci-fi story Garland has told thus far, and certainly one of the most effective, is the psychological thriller "Ex Machina." The story follows programmer Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) who stays at the remote home of eccentric tech CEO Nathan Bateman (Oscar Isaac). Caleb is tasked with checking the sentience of Bateman's latest creation, a self-aware android known as Ava (Alicia Vikander) only for things to violently go off the rails.

There is an underlying paranoia with existential overtones that permeate throughout "Ex Machina," carrying its narrative forward. Compared to more overtly cyberpunk stories like "Blade Runner," Garland's 2014 flick takes a much more grounded view on androids and the proliferation of artificial intelligence. This is underscored by its special effects, with the "Ex Machina" VFX avoiding green screen use, preferring practical effects and sets for its execution. A cautionary tale about billionaire vanity projects taking on a hostile life of their own, "Ex Machina" is Garland's most prescient work.

Another adaptation of an Andy Weir novel to mention here is 2015's "The Martian," directed and produced by Ridley Scott. The movie is set in a near-future where humanity has established a research station on Mars as part of an international coalition. After the station's team evacuates from the planet during a severe dust storm, astronaut Mark Watney (Matt Damon) is accidentally left behind. Until a rescue mission can be carried out, Watney has to rely on the tools that he has available and his own wits to survive alone on Mars.

Andy Weir gave the 2015 adaptation of "The Martian" his seal of approval, and we do too. The movie is Scott's most buoyantly light, yet it doesn't compromise the scientific know-how behind Watney's prolonged ordeal. Matt Damon has to perform much the movie alone, expertly conveying his character's intellectual reasoning without coming off as overly dry or talking down to the audience. One of the smartest sci-fi blockbusters of the 2010s, "The Martian" treats its premise well while celebrating intelligence to save the day.

One of the most prolific hard sci-fi authors was Arthur C. Clarke, who teamed up with filmmaker Stanley Kubrick for "2001: A Space Odyssey." The 1968 movie traces humanity's evolution through a strange extraterrestrial monolith that first appeared on Earth during prehistoric times. When a monolith found on the Moon transits a signal to Jupiter, an expedition is mounted to investigate further. This voyage is nearly derailed by the malevolent artificial intelligence HAL 9000 (Douglas Rain) running the team's spaceship.

Given Kubrick's exhaustive attention to detail and Clarke's scientific acumen, "2001: A Space Odyssey" is as hard as the genre gets on film. For as many confusing moments that the movie has, it keeps the audience riveted with its solid grounding. What makes the movie work is its juxtaposition of realistic sci-fi and existential pondering, balancing hard science with cosmic introspection. The best Stanley Kubrick movie, "2001: A Space Odyssey" brings out the best in its filmmaker and co-writer to bring this spacefaring tale to life.

The Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 robot vacuum and mop is down to $799.99 from $1,299.99 in an early Black Friday deal, saving you $500 and bringing it to its lowest price to date. Much of its appeal comes from a slim 3.1-inch profile that lets it reach under beds, sofas, and other low furniture where taller robot vacuums often can’t fit. It manages this with a feature Roborock calls RetractSense, which checks the clearance as the robot approaches a tight gap and lowers the laser navigation tower into the body, leaving a camera with a 100-degree field of view to guide it underneath.

Beyond its low profile, the Qrevo Edge 2 pairs 25,000Pa of suction with a split DuoDivide main brush that guides hair toward the suction opening, so long strands and pet fur are less likely to end up wound around the roller. The rest of the fine-tuning happens in the Roborock app, where you can set cleaning schedules, adjust suction power and water flow, and choose how the robot handles carpets.

PSA: Don't get disconnected after winning the token

The Pirate Shop Access token is arguably the best reward Fortnite has ever had. With it, players can claim every reward in the shop for free for two whole weeks. And it can be activated twice! It's extremely rare, but gamers have been grinding hard to get it, as it's too valuable to ignore. The token has caused a frenzy in the Fortnite community and increased the number of hours played by millions.

Fortnite player and Reddit user Michoh44 was lucky enough to find it, but something even more unlikely happened: They were disconnected after getting the token and lost it. Their thread includes a clip where we can see them playing normally, and suddenly, there's a treasure reward pop-up, revealing the Pirate Shop Access token, presumably after a team member opened the lucky chest. A new season of the HBO series The Gilded Age is currently heating up on the 2026 TV schedule with all the social climbing, relationship drama, and elaborate costumes that it’s become known for. I’ve been watching it since the beginning, when audiences were first introduced to Enid Turner, an ambitious woman serving as Bertha Russell’s lady’s maid.

Back then, the woman only known as Turner learned quickly that if you’re going to cross Bertha (Carrie Coon), you’d better have enough standing to back it up. Turner did not and became a villain to the Russell family. If you had told me then that same character would evolve into my favorite in Season 4 of the HBO series, I never would have believed you. That would also just mean that I didn’t have the same faith in Enid as she had in herself.

Played with so many layers by Kelley Curran, Enid instantly became a character that I loved to hate but always felt like there was more under the surface. Sure, she attempted to seduce Bertha Husband, George Russell (Morgan Spector), which was a no-no for his wife, ultimately leading to her downfall within the household. The fact that she knew she was better than that kept her clawing her way up the social ladder as she returned, season after season, eventually becoming the character I now can’t help but root for.

In Season 2 of The Gilded Age, Enid seemed to have finally caught a break, marrying Joshua Winterton for financial security and a more prominent place in society. Being significantly older and in ill health led to his death, but it also left his fortune in Enid’s hands, and she was very savvy when it came to using it to the fullest extent of the social-climbing ladder.

Yet somehow, that wasn’t the end of Enid’s story. It has reached even higher with the delicious fun in Season 4. Now married to the not-very-secretly gay Oscar Van Rhijn (Blake Ritson), the duo has formed a partnership with a shared goal of social domination. Together, they plot and plan with devilish schemes that I’ve found myself rooting for with delight.

As a character, Enid is a magnificent sleight-of-hand magician, creating illusions and deceptions as she rises in social ranks. She is the definition of fake it until you make it, going toe-to-toe with her one-time rival at an upcoming lavish dinner that you must stay tuned for in Episode 5, airing on November 29.

While Marian and Larry can’t seem to get on the same page in Season 4, Enid and Oscar might not have romance between them, but being similar in age and mentality means they can understand and support each other in ways neither has had before. It allows her moments to shine with the confidence needed to not only take on Bertha but finally gain the upper hand.

The Gilded Age cast is truly stacked with talent, but what Kelley Curran has been able to do over four seasons, turning a hated villain into a powerful figure that viewers can root for, has been fascinating, fun, and entirely surprising to watch. It’s early in the season for this HBO show that got the world talking, and there’s quite a bit of Enid’s journey still to go, but you can watch all the drama on Sunday nights or with an HBO Max subscription.

#3409. James Gunn Addresses Rumors Of Skydance Changes To Superman Sequel Man Of Tomorrow

News that James Gunn and Peter Safran would be "stepping down" as DC Studios co-heads shocked the industry. At this stage, there's been no official word on what might become of Gunn's DC Universe, but there has been all sorts of conjecture and rumors making the rounds. One of these rumors suggests that the upcoming "Superman" sequel, "Man of Tomorrow," will be significantly reworked ahead of its 2027 release. Now, Gunn has taken to social media to quash the rumor — though at this point it's hard to know who to believe.

Following the Warner Bros./Paramount merger, DC Studios now belongs to Skydance, and it seems the new ownership has big changes in store. Reports have claimed that Skydance CEO David Ellison will dismantle Gunn's DC Universe following his departure. Meanwhile, Nexus Point News published an article in which it cited sources claiming "Man of Tomorrow" is being trimmed down ahead of its July 2027 release. According to the outlet, planned cameos are being cut and reshoots being planned. If Ellison is, indeed, planning to raze Gunn's cinematic universe, that would make sense. According to Gunn himself, however, it's all nonsense. The director wrote a post on Threads stating:

"There are a lot of untrue rumors going around, but one of them is that Skydance has seen 'Man of Tomorrow' and that all sorts of sweeping changes are being made. No one from Skydance has even seen the movie — the only people that have are Peter Safran and a very small trusted group of friends and family. So any stories around this narrative are false."

On one hand, it's reassuring to hear that James Gunn will be able to finish his movie without Skydance making changes. On the other, he didn't actually state unequivocally that the new owners wouldn't be altering "Man of Tomorrow," only that nobody from Skydance has seen the movie yet. But given what we're hearing about how David Ellison plans to reboot the DC Universe, and the fact he's appointed a new DC Studios head in Jeremy Latcham, it would make sense for "Man of Tomorrow" to be reworked.

Gunn previously confirmed that Xolo Maridueña's Blue Beetle would return in "Man of Tomorrow." Nexus Point News' report claims that this is one of the cameos on the chopping block following Skydance's Warner takeover. If true, it would frankly make a lot of sense. Ellison clearly has plans for DC moving forward, and he won't want audiences confused by cameos that suggest the return of erstwhile heroes to a universe he plans to dismantle.

Page Six has reported that Gunn is only staying to finish "Man of Tomorrow" because Directors Guild of America rules mean he "could not be removed" from the project. If accurate, this suggests Ellison would have given Gunn the boot from his own movie if he could — adding more credence to the idea that Skydance wants to make changes to "Man of Tomorrow" and the DC Universe as a whole.  According to the director himself, this is all untrue. But everything we've seen and heard suggests otherwise.

A Puck report has claimed that James Gunn and Peter Safran's DC Studios exit was driven in part by cost-cutting. Given all the financial promises David Ellison had to make in order to close the Warner/Paramount merger, and the fact Gunn and Safran were making a tidy little profit for themselves via a deal that gave them significant autonomy as DC Studios co-heads, that makes sense. As such, if Skydance is committed to putting out "Man of Tomorrow," it will want to do all it can make sure it's profitable while also trying not to misguide audiences with cameos and setups for a DC Universe future that simply isn't going to arrive.

It's unclear whether the same rules that supposedly prevented Skydance from removing Gunn from "Man of Tomorrow" will also prevent them from meddling too much in the final product. But it seems almost certain that Ellison will want to have some say in the movie. With Jeremy Latcham now set to oversee DC Studios, clearly the Skydance CEO has a different vision in mind for the brand moving forward. The fact that nobody from Skydance has seen "Man of Tomorrow," therefore, doesn't necessarily mean they don't have major changes planned.

Bearing in mind Gunn and Safran were previously told they would be staying on at Skydance before Ellison suddenly dropped the axe, it's hard to say who knows what over at DC Studios. For now, Gunn clearly believes he'll be able to put out the "Superman" sequel he wants to make, but who's to say what might happen over the coming months. "Man of Tomorrow" is set for a July 9, 2027 release, and a lot can happen between now and then.

#3407. Keanu Reeves And Denzel Washington's Forgotten '90s Shakespeare Movie Is Worth Revisiting

Kenneth Branagh's 1993 film adaptation of William Shakespeare's "Much Ado About Nothing" is, without hyperbole, one of the best films of its decade. And what a cast! Denzel Washington plays Don Pedro, a soldier returning home from the war, bringing with him the handsome young Claudio, played by Robert Sean Leonard, and Don Pedro's grumpy, villainous half-brother Don John, played by Keanu Reeves.

Additionally, Branagh plays the sharp-witted Benedick, and stands romantically opposite Emma Thompson, playing the even sharper-witted Beatrice. The actors were married at the time, and their scenes together play like gangbusters. Claudio falls in love with the pretty young Hero, played by Kate Beckinsale. Michael Keaton turns in one of his funniest performances as Dogberry, a slovenly cop. Also keep an eye out for Imelda Staunton, Richard Briers, and the amazing Brian Blessed.

Branagh understood that Shakespeare's text was so aggressively light and frothy that he needed to make a film that matched its tone and spirit. As such, "Much Ado" is bright, brisk, pastoral, and gorgeous. Despite a plot involving staged infidelity, faked deaths, and bitter reactions, the movie is overall an injection of liquid sunshine. The bulk of the film is laughter, romantic shenanigans, playfully flirtatious barbs, and relaxing summer night parties in the Sicilian countryside. And, naturally, as a comedy, everything works out in the end. I want to live in this movie.

There have been other recent, passable film renditions of "Much Ado" in recent years, including Joss Whedon's 2013 version, which bore the filmmaker's unique voice, and the 2023 romantic blockbuster "Anyone But You" with Sydney Sweeney and Glen Powell, but neither can match the glories of Branagh's version. It remains the high-water mark for filmed versions of this play.

"Much Ado About Nothing" takes place in Messina, and opens with a glorious homecoming from Don Pedro and his men. This is a joyous occasion, and everyone in Messina is happy to begin a period of merry-making. It also marks the reunion of bitter exes Beatrice and Benedick, who seemingly hate each other, but who verbally spar so well, it's quite clear they're romantically perfect for each other. Each of their friends schemes to force Beatrice and Benedick back into each other's arms, largely by being "overheard" in choice situations.

Upon homecoming, Claudio instantly falls for the pretty young Hero, but he hasn't the wherewithal to charm her. Luckily, at a masked ball, Don Pedro stands in for Claudio, successfully charming Hero in his stead. A marriage is immediately arranged because this is Shakespeare, and comedies have to end with marriages. Meanwhile, side characters are hooking up left and right. "Much Ado" is a marvelously horny movie, and every actor looks the best they have ever looked.

Of course Don John is lurking in the shadows to foul everything up. He sees all the happiness at play and wishes to squelch it for reasons of generic villainy. He arranges for Claudio to witness a couple undressing in a window, convincing Claudio that he is witnessing Hero cheating on him already. Claudio, being a bit of a golden retriever, believes him and becomes bitter, rejecting Hero at the least opportune moment. And while there are some hard feelings of anguish, Branagh has already communicated through his film's bright white coloration, brisk music (by Patrick Doyle), and warm photography (by Roger Lanser), that everything is going to be fine.

The only real issue one might take with Branagh's "Much Ado About Nothing" is — and I hate to say it — Keanu Reeves' performance. Reeves is a capable actor in the right kind of taciturn roles, and he is one of the best human beings we have on planet Earth, but he clearly struggles with Shakespeare's language. After "Much Ado" was released, a notable parody of Reeves' performance was featured on the TV series "The Critic," wherein Reeves was mockingly placed in a film version of "The Merchant of Venice," intoning, "Hath not a dude eyes?"

But Reeves' performance aside, "Much Ado" is pretty damn perfect. The film currently has a 90% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, based on 48 reviews. Roger Ebert gave the film three stars out of four, writing:

"Sunshine and laughter, and merrymakers on a hillside sprinkled with flowers. In the opening scene of 'Much Ado About Nothing,' Kenneth Branagh insists on the tone the movie will take: These are healthy, joyful young people whose high spirits will survive anything, even the dark double-crosses of Shakespeare's plot."

For a while there, Kenneth Branagh was on a hot streak. His 1989 debut feature "Henry V," also based on Shakespeare, was a critical darling, and his 1991 past-lives noir "Dead Again" is way better than it has any right to be. The '90s were very good for Branagh overall, as he also made "Peter's Friends" (1992), "Mary Shelley's Frankenstein" in 1994 (which is better than you remember and accurate to Shelley's novel), "In the Bleak Midwinter" (1995), and one of the very best movie versions of "Hamlet" in 1996. "Much Ado" was just a bright, soft, white feather in his feather-festooned cap.

#3406. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.

#3405. Zelda: Ocarina of Time Is Actually the Perfect Way to Introduce Kids to Nintendo

Walk into The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time’s Kokiri Forest, and it feels like you’re walking into a picture book. Especially in the remake, everything is moss-green and dappled with light. Fairies flit about. Kokiri children are rhythmically attending to their tasks. Everyone is friendly, everything is beautiful, and the world both feels safe and makes sense. Then you walk into the Great Deku Tree and spiders start falling from the ceiling. My daughter screamed. I jumped, too, and I knew they were coming.

Since Zelda: Ocarina of Time returned Nov. 5 with its splashy Switch 2 remake, parents on Reddit have argued over how scary (read: appropriate for kids) it is. Some players say the new graphics make the spiders and the ReDeads worse. Others played at age eight and turned out fine. A few parents are playing with their kids, but skipping whole dungeons in an effort to save their children some nightmares. All fair strategies, and they raise the question: Can a game with a screaming zombie in an underground mausoleum be a kid's first Nintendo game? Parents of kids as young as 4 and 5 are asking, despite the game’s official E10+ rating.

I’ve played the three child-era dungeons with my 4-year-old. Fear is quite present in this game. But so are the tools for fighting it. Which makes Ocarina of Time — The Legend of Zelda’s fairy tale — the perfect way to introduce kids to Nintendo.

The ReDead’s paralyzing scream, Dead Hand reaching up through the floor of the Well, the long walk through the Shadow Temple: Parents who grew up with the N64 Ocarina of Time tend to have the same laundry list of nightmares. Most of these live in the later dungeons, though, and there’s a fair chance that nearly three decades of remembering these seminal gaming experiences have amplified the dread.

Parents of kids playing for the first time in 2026 report smaller, easier-to-navigate fears: 4-year-olds who panicked at the first boss and lit up at the second, spiders that terrified them until they learned to hit back.

Good fairy tales have always been a little scary. G.K. Chesterton wrote that a baby has known the dragon "intimately ever since he had an imagination," and that what the fairy tale supplies is "a St. George to kill the dragon." Here, we have a tiny Link — a peer to my child — facing something scary and fighting back, with appropriate tools to deal with the fun-sized dangers at hand. The child-era half of the game is there for a reason: It's not not scary, but kids are largely good with it.

Eiji Aonuma describes Hyrule as a world with a bright side and a dark side. Link comes from the bright part, Aonuma told one interviewer, and Ganon from the part with "a lot of scary things." The remake's tools could make something "very, very scary" if the team tried, he said, but the game is "supposed to be for all kinds of players."

Art director Aya Shida wanted a Hyrule convincing enough to believe in without being literal about it. Her team reached for puppet shows and practical-effects films because both make fantasy characters feel real without reproducing reality exactly. The setting "feels somewhat dark," she said, and the colorful, quirky characters who live in it give the game its "mysterious, almost dreamlike charm."

In a world built that way, the dark stays a fairy tale's dark: frightening enough to feel real, and charming enough to keep playing. You’re running away from the spiders, but running toward the opportunity to free a squawking chicken from a wooden box. (How did it get in there? My kid wants to know. So does Navi.)

After Link pulls the Master Sword from the stone and ages seven years, the game does get darker. Parents of young children have come up with strategies to match. Some are holding the Well and the Shadow Temple back, and commenters in some Reddit threads suggest waiting until kids are 8 or 9 before starting at all. Others report a 4-year-old who lit up when Link grew up and a 15-year-old who cried at the ending. (I find this deeply relatable; same on both counts.) Reading comes up constantly, with parents reading the dialogue aloud for the youngest kids and some crediting the game with teaching their kids to read.

Whether any individual child is ready for this game is, of course, an individual decision, one that every parent will make based on their knowledge of their unique kid. But, for me, experiencing the remake along with my child made the sense of wonder Child Link feels as he steps out into this world palpable — and it gave me a new appreciation for the honestly very kid-friendly framing of the first half. The Great Deku Tree hands Link a mission with stakes he can understand and provides tools he can wield. By the time he meets bigger perils, he’s ready.

That’s all I can hope for my kid when she, too, is ready. We’re still in the first half on our playthrough. She cheers “fight, mommy, fight!” when a Skulltula descends, thinks Jabu-Jabu’s Belly is gross — correct — and has fallen for Young Princess Ruto. She laughed at me when I did a belly-flop into Kokiri Forest’s lake the first time I tried the dedicated jump button. She immediately clocked that the Keaton Mask looks like her beloved Pikachu, which is going to make following this game up with Kirby and the Forgotten Land, Super Mario Bros. Wonder, and Pokémon: Let’s Go! so, so easy. I’ve gone on to play the Forest Temple without her, and, yes, it’s scarier, but it’s also longer and has more backtracking than she’d have patience for. That temple and the grown-up half of the game will be there when she’s ready for it. I can’t wait to watch her grow into it, even if I’ll miss the days when only the child world had her full attention.

#3404. Batman: The Animated Series' First Pilot Was An Episode Of DC's Super Friends

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

It can't be overstated what an evolutionary leap "Batman: The Animated Series" was compared to previous "Batman" cartoons. Compared to the cheap animation seen in Filmation's "The New Adventures of Batman" or Hanna-Barbera's "Super Friends" franchise, the Fleischer Studios-inspired aesthetic of "Batman: The Animated Series" looks even better. "Batman: The Animated Series" also never underrated the intelligence of its young audience, both in its dialogue and its willingness to let scenes run on atmosphere, not words.

It wasn't an overnight flip. There had been attempts to launch a new "Batman" cartoon for several years. It was the massive success of Tim Burton's "Batman" movie in 1989 that helped that finally let "Batman: The Animated Series" release them. Before that, future "Babylon 5" creator J. Michael Straczynski pitched "Batman and the New Robin," co-starring Batman and Jason Todd.

In the 1980s, Alan Burnett — future producer and story editor on "Batman: The Animated Series" who was then working on "Super Friends" — wrote a pilot for a "Batman" series. Burnett, a "Batman" comic fan since childhood, wanted a cartoon that would honor their darker spirit. But, per behind-the-scenes book "I Am The Night" by Daniel Dockery, "Hanna-Barbera and ABC weren't ready to commit to a dark Batman series."

We can glimpse Burnett's vision and not just through "Batman: The Animated Series." His pilot became an episode of "The Super Powers Team: Galactic Guardians" titled "The Fear." While chasing Scarecrow (Andre Stojka), Batman (Adam West) stumbles into Crime Alley, where his parents were murdered. Overcome with fear, he flees. Scarecrow plots to exploit Batman's fear to defeat him, forcing Batman to face his past and overcome his terror. Darker than most "Super Friends" episodes, "The Fear" serves as a "Batman: The Animated Series" beta test.

"The Fear" was the first depiction of Batman's origin outside the comics and it feels extra special that Adam West got to act it out. The episode understands the weight of this; it initially plays Batman's fear of Crime Alley as a mystery. Bruce has to explain to Robin (Casey Kasem) and Wonder Woman (BJ Ward) how his parents were killed and his vow to avenge them.

These flashbacks, telling us how Bruce Wayne became who he is, are another sign of the episode's origins as a "Batman" series pilot. Compare how "Batman: The Animated Series" didn't shy away from Bruce's past while also assuming that the audience already knew it. Yet despite the ambition of "The Fear," it's still a "Super Friends" episode written for young children.

A revealing comparison is "The Fear" and "Nothing to Fear," the first Scarecrow episode of "Batman: The Animated Series." (Ironically, Alan Burnett wasn't involved with "Nothing to Fear." The episode was scripted by Henry Gilroy and produced under the show's first story editor, Sean Catherine Derek.) In both episodes, Batman is plagued by fears related to his parents; in "Nothing to Fear," he's scared that his father would be disappointed in him. Batman (Kevin Conroy) ultimately shakes off that doubt with a now immortal line: "I am vengeance! I am the night! I am Batman!"

"Nothing to Fear" shows some growing pains. Series co-creator Bruce Timm wasn't wholly satisfied with the episode, and tellingly, Scarecrow (Henry Polic II) would be redesigned, twice, later in the series. Bruce's self-doubts in "Nothing to Fear" are also set when an old colleague of his father's admonishes him for despoiling the Wayne family name.

The original "Batman" series bible described Bruce Wayne's public persona as careless, self-centered playboy "who spends all of his time frivolously squandering the Wayne fortune." This is, of course, a purposefully cultivated persona to ensure no one suspects he could be a hero like Batman. But "Batman: The Animated Series" instead generally depicted Bruce as a friendly guy outside the mask. "Nothing To Fear" is one of the show's earliest episodes, so this might be a holdover from that earlier characterization.

Still, when "Nothing to Fear" begins with a sweeping establishing shot of Gotham (drawn on black paper as was standard on "Batman"), it instantly has more atmosphere than "The Fear" did. It also makes Batman's Scarecrow-induced hallucinations more frightening. When Batman is surrounded by fire, his father's face literally forms from the flames. After Scarecrow is dosed with his own poison, he imagines Batman as a monster.

Speaking of, the Scarecrow isn't spreading panic for its own sake like in "The Fear." In "Nothing to Fear," he's driven by revenge. Once a psychology professor named Jonathan Crane, he used his students as test subjects for his fear drugs. Now, he wants to burn down the university that fired him. Brief flashbacks to Crane's childhood and academic career explain he's always delighted in scaring people. Later "Batman: The Animated Series" episodes would continue digging much deeper, and more sympathetically, into their villains' pathologies.

Instead of the Super Friends flying off into the sunrise with a captured Scarecrow, "Nothing to Fear" has a melancholic ending. Bruce stands at his parents' grave, leaves a flower, and as he walks away his shadow morphs into Batman's. The tragedy of his childhood will continue to follow Batman as long as he lives.

#3402. An Incredible Hulk Issue Saved Marvel's X-Men Comic From Cancelation

Can you imagine the X-Men without Wolverine? Well, as strange as it seems now that he's the face of the franchise, Logan only joined the X-Men in 1975, over a decade after the team's comic debut.

In those early years, "X-Men" struggled. Stan Lee and Jack Kirby's hearts weren't in it, and the character chemistry between the original team wasn't there. There weren't many strong villains, either. Magneto was well over a decade from his reinvention as a traumatized Holocaust survivor. In fact, most of the defining qualities and characters of "X-Men" came not during that original stretch but during writer Chris Claremont's enormous 16-year-run (1975-1991). Things would get worse for the X-Men before they got better.

"X-Men" sales weren't too impressive in the 1960s. The book didn't just face cancellation, it was effectively canceled in 1970. After "X-Men" #66, the comic only reprinted previous "X-Men" stories for five years. Roy Thomas, the former Marvel editor in chief who wrote the last leg of the original "X-Men" run that ended at #66, said that Marvel's publisher Martin Goodman was attempting to get some value out of the book without the cost of producing new stories.

The X-Men still showed up as guest stars in other series, like Steve Englehart's Watergate scandal-inspired arc of "Captain America," "Secret Empire," so they hadn't been completely forgotten. Then, in 1975, the Marvel powers that be decided to give the X-Men another shot. Writer Len Wein got the job of writing the relaunch, "Giant-Size X-Men" #1, and used a character he'd debuted in a 1974 "Incredible Hulk" issue as part of the team.

In Wein and artist Herb Trimpe's "Incredible Hulk" #180-181, the Hulk stumbles across the Canadian border. There, he fights a short, ornery mutant with adamantium claws: Weapon X, aka the Wolverine.

The exact creation of Wolverine remains a disputed piece of comics history. The general historical consensus is that Roy Thomas came up with the notion for a Canadian superhero and possibly the name "Wolverine," while Len Wein and artist John Romita Sr. (then Marvel's art director) designed Wolverine as we know him. In recent years, Thomas has tried (and succeeded, at least officially) to claim a co-creator credit on Wolverine, which has angered many in the professional comics community, along with Wein's widow, Christine Valada.

Regardless, Wein is the one who wrote Logan's debut appearance in those "Incredible Hulk" issues — sparking the enduring Hulk and Wolverine rivalry — and then added him to the X-Men, where he went from team jerk to breakout character. It's worth noting that the Hulk himself survived a brush with cancellation. (His first ongoing series lasted only six issues.) Incidentally, the Hulk had also guest-starred in "X-Men" #66, the last one before its pseudo-cancellation. Perhaps the Hulk left some of his incredible invincibility behind in "X-Men" during that appearance. In any case, the Hulk was present for both the X-Men's end and the beginning of their resurrection.

"X-Men" began publishing new stories again with issue #94, starring the "Second Genesis" team introduced in "Giant-Size X-Men." Wein soon departed, leaving the team in Chris Claremont's hands alongside artist Dave Cockrum, and together, they made comics history. But while Wolverine's popularity grew, he didn't immediately become the book's star.

In fact, it was Colossus who was intended to be the new lead. That's why, per Claremont, Colossus has the traditional muscular, square-jawed superhero build. According to Cockrum's successorJohn Byrne, Claremont, and Cockrum even considered dropping Wolverine. Byrne, a Canadian like Logan, pushed to keep him, and that paid off.

The first X-Man who Chris Claremont made a star was Jean Grey, who'd been the token girl and little else in the original run. Claremont has a thing for powerful women (see: how he wrote Storm). So, he remade Jean into the team's powerhouse and changed her moniker from "Marvel Girl" to "The Phoenix."

Jean's transformation culminates in "The Dark Phoenix Saga," which is also when Logan solidified his place as the book's star. In "X-Men" #132, the X-Men are captured one-by-one by the Hellfire Club, with Wolverine being dropped into a sewer and written off as dead. The very last page of the comic shows Wolverine, claws brandished, rising out of the water to rescue his friends, then #133 features him tearing through the Hellfire Club.

Yes, Logan was an "obnoxious loudmouth," as Dave Cockrum put it, but his bad attitude actually made him cooler. So did his mysterious past, which only grew in mystery as the years went on. Plus, let's face it, there's no superpower more badass or metal (literally) than adamantium claws.

Through the 1980s, the X-Men became Marvel's premier team. Wolverine, in turn, became the X-Man who got solo stories written/drawn by prestige talent, like Claremont and Frank Miller's 1982 "Wolverine" mini-series or Barry Windsor-Smith's horror-infused origin story "Weapon X." The "X-Men" movies and cartoons have always made Wolverine a star from the beginning, too.

The "X-Men" comics faced marginalization during the 2010s due to Marvel Studios not owning the "X-Men" movie rights. Now that this has changed, Marvel is preparing the X-Men to lead the next Marvel Cinematic Universe saga. Based on its casting choices, it's not messing around.

#3401. 10 Shows Like 'Cyberpunk: Edgerunners' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a new season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).

Though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely new places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi. Which is to say, if you're looking for more heady sci-fi series, these 10 are a good place to start.

An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves). The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Different settings, but both shows offer up ragtag crews with highly dubious fates. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

This one's set in 22nd-century Japan, with a slick Blade Runner-esque aesthetic and a setup reminiscent of Minority Report. Here, technology exists to measure intentions, so crimes can be stopped before they’ve occurred, at which point the “criminals” are placed into psychological treatment (à la A Clockwork Orange)—or subject to summary execution because their threat potential is too high. That ability to predict behavior bleeds over into every aspect of life: careers and even relationships are determined in large part by the same systems that sniff out criminal intent. Obviously, this is all perfectly fine, and there’s no potential for abuse or miscalculation whatsoever...though there are a couple of warning signs. The first involves a new Enforcer who becomes a potential murderer himself when he miscalculates the extent of a criminal’s potential to do wrong, and, even more significantly, the existence of a criminal mastermind who is somehow invisible to the tech, even as his criminal actions grow more and more elaborate. Stream Psycho-Pass on Prime Video and Crunchyroll.

Created by Tim Miller and with director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. Its format dictates that no two episodes are going to have the same premise, but it shares with Cyberpunk an edgy sensibility and stories set in an apocalyptic future, albeit with a dark sense of humor—its four seasons offer up a mix of tech, sex, violence, and gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

One of several completely standalone spinoffs of the wildly influential 1995 film (itself based on the beloved manga series), Stand Alone Complex requires no prior knowledge. The style is largely the draw, as the series luxuriates in its fictional Nihama City setting, a world unto itself in a future Japan in which cybernetic people hack directly into the internet. Our sympathies are more with the authorities—in this case, Public Security Section 9, a cybercrime and antiterrorism police unit—than the cyber criminals, but the show approaches some of the same themes as Edgerunners with legit punk style. Stream Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex on Tubi and The Criterion Channel.

In this adaptation of the Richard K. Morgan cyberpunk classic of the same name, Joel Kinnaman and Anthony Mackie (yes, both of them) star as Takeshi "Tak" Kovacs. In this future megacity setting, human consciousness can be transferred between bodies. The tech is widely available, but only the wealthy can afford the backups and protections that make it a form of virtual immortality. Kovacs is a former soldier turned mercenary, revived from a backup after 200 years by Laurens Bancroft (James Purefoy), one of the wealthiest men alive. His motives for bringing the man back are shrouded in mystery, but he's giving Tak a chance to solve a very cold case: his own murder. Stream Altered Carbon on Netflix.

Another popular (and Emmy-winning) game adaptation, Arcane is based on League of Legends, a top-down actioner involving online opponents shooting lasers across a map. It doesn't sound like fodder for a show this impressive, but here we are. The League of Legends lore forms the backdrop for the show, but the pull is in the narrative involving two sisters caught up in the growing conflict between a utopian city and its oppressed underclass, without whom it couldn’t exist. The painted animation style is truly something special—not a stylistic match for Cyberpunk, but the two shows both go far above and beyond to create striking visual worlds. Stream Arcane on Netflix.

Vash the Stampede is a hunted outcast with a dark history that slowly comes to light over the course of the series. He’s got a reputation as a human wrecking ball, bringing destruction wherever he goes, and seemingly just for fun—but in reality he’s far more respectful of life than his pursuers. Still, cities evacuate at the mere possibility of his arrival, and a huge bounty sits on his head (no matter that the bounty hunters do far more damage than Vash). He and his friends—actually a couple of insurance agents—find themselves in a series of misadventures on the planet Gunsmoke, building to a final showdown that caps the series with finality. Visually, it’s probably one of the defining ‘90s shōnen-style action series, with elegantly choreographed gunfights that never get old. Tonally similar, Trigun also shares with Cyberpunk 2 the work of legendary composer Tsuneo Imahori, his music being crucial to both shows. Stream Trigun on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Another from animation studio Trigger, Darling in the Franxx leans heavily into the mecha sub-genre, set in a post-apocalypse where children are bred and indoctrinated into piloting the title's massive Franxx to defend the remnants of humanity. Adults are pretty much immortal, so the kids simply don't have any other utility. Two of these teens begin to develop romantic feelings for each other, potentially complicating their usefulness to society and leading to an explosive, bittersweet finale. Stream Darling in the Franxx on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

What starts out as a relatively straightforward action show about space bounty hunters (the title's “Killjoys”) develops surprising depth over the course of its five seasons. As officially sanctioned Killjoys, the trio at the show’s heart (Hannah John-Kamen, Aaron Ashmore, and Luke Macfarlane) are bound to remain politically neutral at any cost. Initially, that’s a way to get them right into the heat of a fight, but as they develop ties of friendship and family in an exploited community, they come to understand the high cost of unchecked wealth and greed, and the ways in which neutrality always benefits the oppressors. The show’s creators make exceptionally good use of a limited budget and offer up some impressive queer rep along the way, a rarity in pop sci-fi. Stream Killjoys on Tubi or buy it from Prime Video and Apple TV.

Another great cyberpunk metropolis: here it's Kansai, an increasingly lawless city run by elite criminals known as Akudama. An ordinary girl, quite inadvertently, becomes caught up in a major planned heist and is forced to fake credentials as a master swindler in order to stay alive. Like Cyberpunk, the show tackles anti-authoritarian themes among a diverse crew of outsiders. Stream Akudama Drive on Cunrchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

#3400. 5 Times Patrick Stewart's Jean-Luc Picard Proved He Was Star Trek's Greatest Captain

The late, great Patrick Stewart brought Captain Picard to life. The captain of the USS Enterprise-D on "Star Trek: The Next Generation" was, on the page, a resolute and principled character, meant to resemble Horatio Hornblower, a note that show creator Gene Roddenberry gave to Stewart during the show's development. Stewart, however — a classically trained actor – drew on several classical and personal sources to properly create Picard, including Hornblower, Shakespeare's King Henry IV, and one Regimental Sergeant Major Alfred Stewart, Patrick's stern and glowering father.

The character emerged not just as stern and authoritative, but also possessed of deeply held values and very, very high standards. Picard feels like the college professor you hope to never disappoint. He's not fatherly, but he can be kind. He knows how to make good decisions quickly, but is always careful to listen to input from his crew. He trusts the experts around him, and rarely suffers a crisis of confidence. He may be aloof, but that aids his command style; Picard attracts respect through his almost unshakable competence. If you are in any position of authority — from a government official to an assistant manager at a Sephora — you can look to Captain Picard for inspiration.

All of the above qualities make Picard a great captain of a giant space-faring vehicle. There were, however, several times when the already stalwart captain went above and beyond and proved that his command skills were not merely excellent, but exemplary. Picard would go to bat for his crew, stand up for his principles, and even push himself beyond his comfort zone to ensure he was being the best commander he knew how to be.

The five following examples prove that Picard is greatest captain in "Star Trek."

The episode "Disaster" is essentially the disaster movie "The Poseidon Adventure" in space. The USS Enterprise is hit by a quantum filament and rendered adrift. The crew becomes trapped in various areas of the ship, and communication is not operational. Without communication, each group of characters has to deal with a miniature crisis, e.g., a baby is being born in Ten Forward, and radioactive barrels are leaking in the cargo bay.

When the disaster strikes, Captain Picard is in the middle of hosting a walking tour for three children, Jay (John Christian Graas), Marissa (Erika Flores), and Patterson (Max Supera), who won the tour as a prize in a recent science fair. Picard is very uncomfortable with children and has no idea how to be a warm and understanding tour guide. The disaster traps Picard and the three kids in a turbolift, and leaves the captain with a broken ankle. This appears to be one of Picard's worst nightmares.

What seems like a sitcom scenario, though, eventually proves itself to be an opportunity for him to continue plying his skills as a command officer. He begins to intuit that the children require a gentler approach than hardened Starfleet officers, and turns their survival into a mission they can all go on together. He assigns imaginary ranks to the kids, and manages to keep them all calm, even as they have to exit the turbolift and climb a shaft ladder to escape. He doesn't become fatherly, but manages to parlay his captaining into that of an attentive elementary school teacher. And he does this while having to face his own discomfort with youngsters. It's an inspiring piece of leadership.

"Q Who" was the first episode of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" to feature the Borg, a species of soulless, tech-absorbing cyborgs who forcibly and unthinkingly add ship parts and people into their machine collective. The Enterprise encounters the Borg after the trickster god Q (John de Lancie) hurls it many, many lightyears in an instant. Q was inspired to bring the Enterprise to the Borg after Picard, in a perhaps-haughty fashion, declared that humans were quite capable of facing any threat the cosmos had to offer, and didn't require any of Q's magical help in their galactic trekking. Q wanted to show them a threat they couldn't handle.

The Borg proved to be a formidable threat. After one invader drone is killed by a phaser, another immediately appears, now immune. The Borg can adapt to any attack. They are also capable of self-repair, and possess weapons and technologies the Enterprise cannot repel. The Borg neatly slice a cylindrical piece out of the Enterprise's saucer section.

Picard tries to remain calm throughout this experience, but the Borg are very much unlike anything he has previously encountered. Eventually, Q reappears to Picard to point out that the Borg will pursue the Enterprise relentlessly, behaving like a machine and incapable of being negotiated with. Q asks once again if he truly needs help. Picard, previously so confident, admits that he is scared, and finally confesses that, yes, he needs Q's help. Q smugly rescues the Enterprise, returning it to its previous location. It's one of Q's best moments in the franchise.

Picard is a stalwart leader, but it takes true leadership skills to admit when one requires help. The ship was Picard's first priority, and his pride took a back seat. In showing his fear, in this case, Picard became a better commander.

On "Star Trek," the Prime Directive dictates that no Starfleet officer may interfere with the natural evolution of any world. The Directive was put into place to ensure that Starfleet never takes on a colonialist mindset, merrily enforcing their own values on another world. The Prime Directive also dictates that any society that hasn't yet invented faster-than-light space travel should not be contacted under any circumstances.

That second part was violated by accident in the episode "Who Watches the Watchers." A low-tech agrarian species called the Mintakans, hovering in its own Bronze Age, was being studied by a hidden Federation lookout when an accident caused its camouflage to drop, revealing everything. A Mintakan named Liko (Ray Wise) is electrocuted by the uncovered outpost, and he is taken on board the Enterprise to be treated. Liko seems to remain conscious, and, in a haze, glimpses Picard giving orders. When Liko returns to his people, he declares that "The Picard" is a deity. A new religion threatens to begin.

Of course, accidentally inspiring a religious movement is the worst kind of cultural contamination, and Picard is horrified to learn that a mere accident may unwittingly alter the evolution of the Mintakans. In order to prove that he is not a deity, Picard resolves to introduce himself to a panicked Liko, who is armed with a bow and arrow. Picard aims to prove his mortality to Liko, and if he needs to be shot with an arrow to prove that, so be it. Picard was willing to sacrifice his life in order to preserve the culture and ensure that a religion would not be founded. That is a deep devotion to Starfleet principles and an impressive adherence to cultural non-contamination.

The episode "The Drumhead" contains what might be Captain Picard's greatest speech, and /Film's Nina Starner has written about how educational the episode is.

The plot of "The Drumhead" surrounds an explosion in the Enterprise's dilithium chamber, and the ensuing investigation that follows. The explosion appears to be an act of sabotage, perhaps instigated by a visiting Klingon named J'Dan (Henry Woronicz), and may also be connected to a Starfleet medical technician Simon Tarses (Spencer Garrett). The matter is being investigated by a special prosecutor named Norah Satie (Jean Simmons), who is notorious for her hard-line tactics, and who is living up to the legacy of her legal expert father.

As the episode grinds on, Satie begins seeing enemies everywhere. It's revealed that J'Dan was collaborating with the Romulans, and that Tarses once lied on his Starfleet Academy application about his species; he is secretly half-Romulan himself. Neither of these things, however, prove who caused the sabotage, and Satie begins probing deeper, questioning Tarses' loyalty. She is very eager to rout out Starfleet's enemies, and is able to find cracks in every argument. Picard tries to stop her investigation, but that only makes Picard her enemy as well. It's not long before Picard is also on trial.

Picard can only point out that Satie has gone mad with intolerance and quotes her father: "With the first link," he says, "the chain is forged. The first speech censured, the first thought forbidden, the first freedom denied, chains us all irrevocably." The entire affair reminds Picard that humans are not as enlightened as they thought, and are still prone to prejudice and paranoia. It takes confidence, insight, and moral tenacity to reach that conclusion. There is still hard work to be done.

The episode "The Measure of a Man" is one of the five most essential episodes of "Star Trek: The Next Generation," displaying the careful consideration of life, right, and humanity that the franchise has become known for. In the episode, the android Data (Brent Spiner) draws the attention of a cyberneticist named Maddox (Brian Brophy) who wishes to dismantle Data to better learn how he ticks. Data refuses, of course, which causes Maddox to declare Data to be the property of Starfleet, and not an autonomous being with a consciousness and free will of his own.

Picard had worked directly with Data closely for about two years at that point, and had come to know Data as a person. A hearing is instigated to figure out if Data is actually conscious, and Picard takes on the role of his defender. Picard argues that Data is allowed to determine his own fate, while Maddox, via William Riker (Jonathan Frakes), argues that Data is little more than a glorified machine. In a conversation Picard has with Guinan (Whoopi Goldberg), she points out that there will always be people like Maddox, who long for a class of "disposable people" who can be forced to labor for free. The captain immediately recognizes that she's talking about slavery.

Picard realizes that the soul of Starfleet is at stake, and uses all of his mental acuity and emotional outrage to stand up for Data. A captain willing to go to bat for his crew is a great captain indeed, but Picard has to go so far as to argue for Data's very humanity. He is very willing to defend people he cares for, and also what is right.
