#3399. 32 Years Later, Star Trek's Most Important Movie Is Officially Free on Streaming

There are few things Star Trek fans love more than a good crossover. Bringing together characters from different eras of the franchise is practically guaranteed to generate excitement, particularly when those characters happen to be two of Starfleet's most legendary captains. But what happens when the movie designed to unite them doesn't quite live up to expectations?

Released in 1994 and now streaming free on Pluto TV, Star Trek: Generations brought Captain James T. Kirk (William Shatner) and Captain Jean-Luc Picard (Patrick Stewart) together on the big screen for the first and only time. The result was a movie that divided fans, delivered one of the franchise's most controversial deaths, and destroyed one of television's most beloved starships. Yet more than three decades later, Generations deserves another look, particularly for what it has to say about growing older, accepting loss, and knowing when it's time to move on.

The film opens with Kirk, Montgomery Scott (James Doohan), and Pavel Chekov (Walter Koenig) attending the maiden voyage of the Enterprise-B. Kirk is retired, although it's obvious he hasn't entirely adjusted to life outside the captain's chair.

When Kirk discovers that the ship's helmsman is Demora Sulu (Jacqueline Kim), daughter of his former crewmate Hikaru Sulu (George Takei), he's surprised his old friend found time to start a family. Scotty reminds him of something Kirk himself has always said: If something is important, you make the time.

It's a seemingly insignificant exchange that establishes one of the movie's central themes. Kirk has spent his life exploring the galaxy, but what has he missed along the way? He's saved countless lives and made history, yet he's struggling to find purpose without the Enterprise.

Decades later, Picard faces his own reckoning with mortality after learning that his brother Robert and nephew René have died in a fire. The tragedy leaves him confronting the possibility that his family line will end with him, along with the realization that the life he chose came at the expense of another he might have had.

Both captains eventually find themselves inside the Nexus, a mysterious energy ribbon that offers its inhabitants a seemingly perfect existence. For Picard, that means experiencing the family life he never had. Kirk finds himself back in a peaceful home, with the opportunity to reconnect with a woman from his past. Perhaps Edith Keeler?

The temptation is understandable. Who wouldn't want the chance to revisit a happier moment or correct a regret? But Generations makes the case that a meaningful life isn't necessarily a perfect one. Sometimes it's the choices we make, and the sacrifices that come with them, that give our lives purpose.

None of this means Generations is without problems. Far from it. The movie's villain, Dr. Tolian Soran (Malcolm McDowell), wants to return to the Nexus so badly he's willing to destroy entire star systems to make it happen. While McDowell brings considerable menace to the role, Soran never quite becomes the memorable antagonist the story needs.

Then there's Kirk's death, which remains one of the most debated moments in Star Trek history. After surviving Klingons, Romulans, Khan, and countless other threats, the legendary captain meets his end beneath a collapsing bridge. For a character who spent decades boldly going where no one had gone before, it's not exactly the grand farewell many fans imagined. And yet there's plenty here to appreciate.

Stewart delivers some of his finest work as Picard struggles with grief, particularly during a quiet conversation with Counselor Deanna Troi (Marina Sirtis). The destruction of the Enterprise-D is also genuinely shocking, especially for viewers who spent seven seasons watching the ship become almost as much a character as the people aboard it.

There's also the introduction of Data's (Brent Spiner) emotion chip, which provides some welcome humor, even if the movie occasionally leans a little too heavily into the android's newfound feelings.

Most importantly, Shatner and Stewart make the film's long-awaited meeting worthwhile. Their scenes together aren't built around elaborate action sequences or clever one-liners. Instead, they feature two captains reflecting on what it means to make a difference. It's a quieter approach than some viewers might have expected, but one that feels appropriate for these characters.

Beyond its story, Generations occupies a unique place in Star Trek history. It was the franchise's first theatrical film built around the cast of Star Trek: The Next Generation, arriving just months after the television series concluded its seven-season run.

For years, Kirk and his crew had been the faces of Star Trek on the big screen. Now it was Picard's turn. The movie makes that transition literal. Kirk begins the film as a celebrated former captain watching a new Enterprise depart without him. By the conclusion, he's helping Picard save millions of lives and making one final sacrifice before leaving the future in another captain's hands.

The destruction of the Enterprise-D reinforces that transition. The ship that carried Picard and his crew through seven seasons of television adventures is gone, clearing the way for a new chapter. The Next Generation cast would return in three more films, beginning with 1996's Star Trek: First Contact.

There's something fitting about a movie so concerned with the passage of time serving as the bridge between two eras of Star Trek. The franchise was changing, just as its characters were learning to accept change in their own lives.

Generations may not be the best Star Trek movie, but beneath the spectacle, questionable decisions, and collapsing bridges is a thoughtful story about two men who devoted their lives to making a difference. When Kirk gets one last opportunity to do exactly that, he doesn't hesitate. For all the movie's imperfections, it's hard to imagine a more appropriate final choice for the captain of the Enterprise.

Star Trek Generations is free to streaming Pluto TV. You can also watch it on Paramount Plus.

#3398. Ridley Scott's Blade Runner Used Extra Footage From A Stanley Kubrick Movie

In the American theatrical version of Ridley Scott's 1982 sci-fi film "Blade Runner," the film had a happy ending for Rick and Rachael.

This was an alteration made to "Blade Runner" after Scott's original cut was not well-received by test audiences. Scott's intended ending involved a weirdly symbolic image of a character examining a piece of origami folded into a unicorn, and Rick Deckard (Harrison Ford) walking into an elevator with the replicant Rachael (Sean Young). The ending was ambiguous and downbeat, in the spirit of film noir.

Scott recalled the experience in a 2015 interview with The Hollywood Reporter, saying that an unnamed investor wanted him to tack on a happy ending where Rick and Rachel drive off into the woods together. In the happy ending, Rick talks in voiceover about how Rachel is a special kind of replicant who can live indefinitely. Harrison Ford is on record about how much he hates that voiceover.

There have been many cuts of "Blade Runner" over the years, and Scott has been very frank about how much he dislikes the "happy ending" that was mandated to him.

Despite the frustration, though, Scott followed orders from his investors. To make that happy ending, Scott consulted with fellow director Stanley Kubrick and managed to get some of Kubrick's footage that was shot for the opening credits of his 1980 horror film "The Shining." The "happy ending" of "Blade Runner" featured a high shot of a lovely wilderness as Rick and Rachael drive off into the woods together. That was actually reused "Shining" footage, granted to Scott with Kubrick's blessing.

Stanley Kubrick had previously cold-called Ridley Scott after Kubrick watched "Alien" for the first time, wondering how the heck Scott had pulled off one of that film's most memorable moments. That call began their relationship as colleagues.

Scott remembered the whole experience borrowing "The Shining" footage, explaining:

"I had finished Blade Runner, and it was a disaster. My investors were giving me a really hard time, saying 'You can't end the film with picking up a piece of origami, looking at the girl, walk in the elevator, nod, and bingo that's it.' I said, 'It's called a film noir.' And they said, 'What's a film noir?' That was a big problem. And he said, 'We have to test this with an uplifting ending, where they will go off into the wilderness together.' I said, 'Well if they go off into a beautiful wilderness, why do they live in this dystopian environment?'"

Scott then said he asked Stanley Kubrick for a little of that lovely woodsy footage he shot for "The Shining" and inserted it into "Blade Runner." He continued:

"By then I had talked to Stanley a few times. I said, 'I know you shot the hell out of 'The Shining,' can I have some of the stuff?' So at the end of the film in 'Blade Runner,' that's Stanley Kubrick's footage."

Of course, the cut of "Blade Runner" that used footage from "The Shining" was eventually abandoned in favor of the more popular Director's Cut. To orient you on all the jiggery-pokery that went down with "Blade Runner," /Film has assembled a guide to the film's multiple endings. It's ... a lot.

And then, after all that, Kubrick was said to have hated "Blade Runner" regardless.

Sarah Maitland, who spent a spell collaborating with Kubrick on his never-completed version of "A.I. Artificial Intelligence," spoke with Far Out Magazine in 2025, and recalled a time when Kubrick talked about "Blade Runner," and how the movie was kind of pointless. Half the movie, Kubrick said, was devoted to solving whether or not Rachael was a replicant, and Kubrick felt that if no one could tell the difference, then why bother with anything? "[I]f they can't tell," Maitland recalled Kubrick saying, "why do they think it matters? There is nothing in that film that suggests for one second why it should matter."

Kubrick was a pal for lending Scott that "Shining" footage, but nothing he did made "Blade Runner" a better movie.

#3397. Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means.  Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

Recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

#3396. Miles Teller Opens Up About ‘Paper Tiger,’ Adam Driver, and Losing His Home Before Filming James Gray’s Movie

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Neon will release “Paper Tiger” in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

An actor who started at 22, Miles Teller earned rave reviews out of the gate for his debut performance in “Rabbit Hole,” when he was signed swiftly by CAA, followed by “Whiplash” and “The Spectacular Now.” He has worked steadily ever since, with everything from auteur fare like “Whiplash” and studio franchises such as “Divergent” and “The Fantastic Four” to his name. Holding his own opposite Tom Cruise in the blockbuster “Top Gun: Maverick” pushed him into the limelight, but he was still playing Rooster, the son of radar intercept officer Nick “Goose” Bradshaw (Anthony Edwards). Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

His latest role in James Gray’s “Paper Tiger,” which earned raves at Cannes, sees Teller play a real grown-up, Irwin Pearl, a Queens engineer and family man opposite Scarlett Johansson as his wife Hester, and Adam Driver as Gary, his older brother, a former cop. No longer the onscreen son of a leading man, Teller is now firmly in father roles. Irwin is slowly building a solid business when his brother offers a quicker route to success. Alas, the naive Irwin goes for the idea and, during an unscheduled night reconnaissance, blunders with the Russian mafia, seeing things he should not see.

I sat down with Teller at the Carlton Hotel in Cannes after the movie wowed in its world premiere. He was seeing it for the first time. We do not count fake standing ovations at IndieWire, but I was there and can vouch that it played well. The dynamic between Driver and Teller is powerful, with Johansson holding her own in the middle. Even though the movie did not land a Cannes prize, it will play the fall festivals and enter awards contention.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

Anne Thompson: You’ve played the Cannes game before.

Miles Teller: I’m one of those actors [where] it’s pretty hard to watch yourself. I always have a hard time. I was here with Nic [Winding] Refn for this limited series that we did [“Too Old to Die Young”]; that was my first time at Cannes. I’ve done Cannes with “Maverick.” It’s truly an overload of the senses.

You’ve never given this kind of performance before.

Hopefully, your taste evolves as you get older. It struck me that on my first film, “Rabbit Hole,” I was playing the wide-eyed teenager, and we filmed the majority of that movie in a house in Queens. And now I’m playing the part of the parent.

That was your breakout. You revealed some strong emotions related to your own car accident. I’m so sorry you lost your home in the Palisades Fire.

When I met James for this movie, our house had just burned down. And I had just lost my grandfather. We were renting a place in Santa Barbara, and then I got the call saying James wanted to meet me for this. That infused this story and performance with a lot of love as well, because of that feeling of home that Keleigh [Sperry] and I had lost. I’d lost it with my grandfather, but then also just the physical place where you can have people come gather, where you have memories attached. We did not have that, so that probably came through.

Do you believe that you have to grow up a bit before you can find your way in Hollywood?

If you want to have a long career, the audience, hopefully, that you attract in your early 20s, as they get older, and they start having kids or not having kids, but just getting more life experience under the belt, you want to reflect that in your choices as well. And James makes movies for adults, he deals with characters. I’ve loved every one of his films, and I’ve always felt like he gets incredible performances, so I was excited to play a man at this point.

Every actor is going to get to a place where you know it’s tough because you do something that has some success to it, and then people want you to keep doing that same thing, whether that’s from the studio side or you keep getting scripts that are that same kind of thing.

When I started out with “Rabbit Hole,” and then I wanted to audition for comedy, they’re like, “he’s not funny.” And then you do comedies, and you want to be going back to drama, and they’re like, “Willard from ‘Footloose,’ what are you talking about?”

I remember “Bleed for This.” [He gets up to close the shutters to block the noise for my audio, and pours me some water.] That was a point where I was 27, and I said, “OK, I want to step up and play, not the funny friend. Playing Vinny Patz, as a five-time world champion boxer, very much a man’s man, absolutely, that was something. But it always comes down to a director, oftentimes taking what I feel is a chance on me, casting me in a role that I haven’t necessarily shown those abilities before, but believing that I could do that.

You had to carry the TV series “The Offer,” in which you play Al Ruddy, who produced “The Godfather,” running interference between Francis Ford Coppola, Robert Evans at Paramount, and the mafia. That must have been tough.

I was intimidated by portraying Al, to be honest with you, not just his bravado and accomplishments, but it felt like I was playing somebody who had more life experience than I had at that point, and there was a certain maturity to that. I enjoyed that Al, being a man of action, if he takes a step back, he’s taking two steps forward. Typically, there’s five or six different producers doing all these things: that was all Al.

In “Paper Tiger,” there’s one scene between you and Adam Driver where you get into a fight. Your face was shaking with anger.

I know. I saw that. Yeah, there was a twitch going on there. At least in my own life, your family can get to you in a way that nobody else can. Those feelings are so deeply rooted and established from childhood, so I guess in that moment, and neither one is fully aware of the ramifications of the Russians, this deal going bad, and how it’s affecting that person in their life. In that particular scene you’re letting out. It’s not just about what they’re talking about right there. It’s an entire lifetime of misgivings — he’s going to let him have it. When that’s happened to me in my personal life, you feel so bad afterwards. It’s a horrible feeling when you’re not talking to a sibling or your parents, and often it’s hard to make amends.

How did James Gray base this film on his own father’s experience?

With his father, that was the biggest regret. He took it to his deathbed, the fact that he brought this [danger] into his home, and his family became collateral damage for his business ambition. [In the movie] the venture that he went into, to go into business with his brother, he makes a mistake that was very naive. I think it’s easy to forgive this mistake. When I read this script, I had a ton of empathy for this family in this situation, and then also what Hester is going through.

Did you have any models for your character in this movie? Your own father was an engineer.

No, he was a project controls manager, but worked nuclear. The men that I grew up around, my father and my grandfather, were strong men, but very sensitive, and were dependable, reliable. My grandfather was married to my grandmother for 60-something years. I never saw her open a door for herself. I never saw her carry her own bag. He was a Marine, but he also was well-versed in world history, and he was a sweet man who was never afraid to show that side of him, but he also would stand up for himself, or his wife, or his kids, whatever it is. He took a lot of pride in that.

I found it refreshing, even comforting, to watch a movie about a kind, loving family man who’s good at his job, who’s competent. He’s a good dad. You haven’t shown that side to such a degree.

I felt immensely for this father and husband. It was clear he loves his kids, and he’s trying to lead by example, and to show them that success in life is not based on the car you drive. He wants to show them that you can build something on your own merit, and if you work hard and treat people right, that you can earn it.

Those values are no longer as respected as they once were. So, if you were to look back at your career, you did some studio work, like the “Divergent” series. Have you made a course correction? That comes with maturity, too, when an actor recognizes what they want to do rather than doing what people tell them to.

Early on, I didn’t want to feel like I was repeating what I had just done. I didn’t want people to be able to expect what I was going to do next. I always want to defend young actors in their careers, because people say, “Oh, why did you make that choice? Why did they make that choice?” You’re just hoping to get a role, and it’s less than 10 percent of people in SAG who pay their bills off acting alone. We all want to work on the best material with the best directors and the best actors. There’s an ebb and flow. I used to be more critical of work other people were doing, because you get thrown into this rat race when you’re first starting out.

Who were you competing with? Who was in your class?

It was me, and Michael B. [Jordan] and [Robert] Pattinson and Shia [LaBeouf] and [Zac] Efron was big, “The Hunger Games” stuff was blowing up. As I’ve gotten older, I appreciate and have respect for longevity, if you can hang around. I always wanted to contribute. When I was going to the Lee Strasberg Institute at NYU, and looked on the wall, there’s all these incredible actors that went through there. I hold acting and actors in such high regard, whether it’s theater or film or TV.

You seem to be delivering performances at such a level that you keep getting more work. The work itself is selling you. You had to counteract some bad press. Did that hurt you in terms of getting roles?

That was so mishandled. The reason why I have not done profiles is because I said, “Wow, if I’m not doing this interview on camera, this person can misquote things or put things out of order or say things that didn’t happen.” It felt like such a violation of what actually transpired. I told my team, “Guys, I don’t think I’m doing this again, because I’m reading this and this doesn’t sound like me to me. This is not life, so why would I ever want to be a part of something where they can just put that in?” So it’s unfortunate that being a good person, that doesn’t sell. People want to click on the negativity. If you go to bed and put your head on your pillow and how you treat people truly, that’s what matters. That [2015] interview was like 12 years ago.

Some people still remember. Well, casting directors know who you are and what you can do.

The actors, the directors, the crew, the producers, you can’t hide who you are when you’re on set.

Legal questions surround the Michael Jackson estate and his lawyer, John Branca, who you play in “Michael,” which has grossed $707 million worldwide. What’s going on with the sequel?

They had to rework the third act of the last movie. As far as the sequel goes, I know they’re working on it. I haven’t had any direct discussions, other than the team is excited to complete that story.

#3395. Slow Horses Star Jack Lowden Was In Dwayne Johnson's Most Underrated Movie

We just saw Jack Lowden wrap up another successful season of "Slow Horses," in which his character, River Cartwright, reunited with a former love. It was one of the most surprisingly tender installments of the best spy show on TV, with "Slow Horses" Season 6 immediately improving on Season 5 by embracing a darker overall tone (while still maintaining the series' signature sardonic wit). Those who particularly enjoyed this latest season might be intrigued to know that Lowden previously starred in a film that similarly combined a heartfelt emotional core with a dry wit: "Fighting with My Family."

To be clear, this 2019 biographical sports dramedy is nothing like "Slow Horses" in terms of its genre and tone. But it does mix naturalistic drama, action, humor, and heart in a similar fashion to the spy series. That's not too surprising considering the film was written and directed by Stephen Merchant and "Slow Horses" was overseen for its first five seasons by Will Smith, both of whom came up in the British comedy scene of the early 2000s. Merchant is, of course, best known for co-creating "The Office" with Ricky Gervais, while Smith was a writer for, and starred in, the BBC sitcom "The Thick of It."

Another thing tying these two projects together (aside from both being set in England) is Lowden, who delivers one of his most underrated performances in "Fighting with My Family." It also has The Rock in it, if that sort of thing appeals. In fact, the film is also one of Dwayne Johnson's most underrated movies, even if he isn't actually in it all that much.

"Fighting with My Family" is based on the 2012 documentary "The Wrestlers: Fighting with My Family." The film saw director Max Fisher spend a year following the Knight family of Norfolk, who run the World Association of Wrestling from their suburban home. The doc particularly focused on the Knights' daughter, Saraya-Jade Bevis, as she tried out for the WWE. That story, it seems, caught the attention of Dwayne Johnson, who teamed up with Stephen Merchant to give Bevis' story the big screen treatment.

In 2019, Merchant spoke to /Film about "Fighting with My Family," recalling how he'd acted with Johnson in 2010's "Tooth Fairy" and had "got along well" with the wrestler turned actor. The pair evidently stayed in touch, which ultimately led to their collaboration on "Fighting with My Family," which Johnson executive produced and appeared in. "I have no particular interest in wrestling and didn't know anything about it," admitted Merchant. "[Johnson] happened to see a documentary while in Britain filming 'Fast & Furious 6.'" This was the genesis of "Fighting with My Family." After Johnson became acquainted with Bevis via WWE, he reached out to Merchant to write and direct. The comedian accepted.

The film he wrote similarly follows the career of English wrestler Saraya Knight/Paige, played by Florence Pugh, as she works towards a career in WWE. Jack Lowden plays her brother, Zak Knight/Zak Zodiac, who has similar dreams of making it to the big leagues. Only Saraya earns a spot in the WWE's training program, however, and she is forced to leave her family behind to pursue her dreams.

As /Film's Ethan Anderton wrote in his review, "Fighting with My Family" gives WWE fans the movie they deserve. But this is more than a wrestling movie. It's also a heartfelt comedy drama that boasts great performances from both Florence Pugh and Jack Lowden. "Slow Horses" fans should get a kick out of seeing Lowden as Zak Knight. Whereas River Cartwright is the upper-middle class son of a former MI5 head, Zak is a determined youngster who grew up in a council house. It's interesting to see how the Scottish actor renders the latter in comparison to his other best-known role.

Lena Headey and Nick Frost play Zak and Saraya's parents Ricky and Julia Knight, and both of them have a great time in their roles. Then there is, of course, The Rock, who shows up a couple times throughout the movie and is, well, The Rock. Beyond his cameos, though, Dwayne Johnson was invested in the story and did a great job shepherding the project to fruition — as evidenced by the critical response.

"Fighting with My Family" earned a 93% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes and a $41.5 million take at the global box office on an $11 million budget. All in all, then, it was a success, even if it didn't become a major hit with a massive cultural impact. Now, Lowden is said to be one of five finalists to become the new James Bond, so if you want to acquaint yourself with the actor's filmography ahead of what might be the biggest moment of his career, "Fighting with My Family" is a great place to start. The film is available to watch for free on Tubi.

#3393. League of Legends: New Dawn Revealed, Major Overhaul Set for 2027

The evolution of the long-running MOBA will get a full reveal in January

Between matches at the 2026 League of Legends World Championship, Riot Games teased fans with a long-anticipated announcement: The next era of League of Legends is upon us.

Revealed in an array of cinematics and gameplay, the “all-encompassing, large-scale update” coming to the 17-year-old game in 2027 is titled New Dawn. If the cheers that bellowed through the Barclays Center in Brooklyn are any indication, diehard fans of the franchise are ready.

Riot left most details of this major overhaul to the imagination. The cinematic trailer for New Dawn revealed stunning renders of several fan-favorite champions, including Blitzcrank, Lux, Leona, Sett, Poppy, Volibear, Riven, Jhin, and Ahri. Snippets of gameplay saw Master Yi and Morgana in action. But what is at the heart of the update? The studio says it will have more to reveal in January.

What the announcement did reveal is that League will get a brand-new game client in 2027; Riot last overhauled the architecture in 2016. The sizzle reel also promised a refreshed version of the Summoner’s Rift map, a defining feature of the long-running MOBA. For now, fans can only speculate what Riot’s description of “evolved gameplay, and new ways to experience players’ favorite champions” really means.

Whatever the case, there’s a clear ambition on Riot’s part to grow the game not only for longtime players but a potentially new audience that may only know League from Arcane or the Riftbound TCG. At a pre-Finals press event, League executive producer Paul Bellezza made it very clear that Riot sees the game as “multi-generational” and would love for it to run “100 years.” Doing that requires strategy. At a time when major live-service franchises are also gunning for expanded and renewed attention (see: World of Warcraft: Forever), it’s only natural that Riot would follow suit with League.

But the company isn’t ready to share their real game plan just yet. Instead, it bundled announcements of a new vision for gameplay with a reminder that League remains a major esports endeavor. Next year’s calendar will see some bigger changes too: The 2027 season kicks off in China with an expanded First Stand tournament, followed by the Mid-Season Invitational in Valencia, Spain. Worlds 2027 will span Japan and South Korea, with Nagoya hosting Japan’s first-ever World Championship matches before the tournament concludes in Seoul. Riot is also considering replacing the traditional Worlds Play-In Stage with the Demacia Cup, potentially opening the door for more teams to compete.

#3392. Bove, il McDonald's portato da Cataldi e il legame con la Fiorentina

Nell’intervista per la presentazione del docufilm, ricorda anche il risveglio dopo il malore e il sostegno di Cobolli.

Danilo Cataldi andava a trovare Edoardo Bove in ospedale e gli portava di nascosto del McDonald’s durante il ricovero seguito al malore del 1° dicembre 2024, avvenuto in Fiorentina-Inter. Bove lo ha raccontato in un’intervista a Sky Sport 24 per la presentazione di In «Un Battito», il docufilm dedicato a quanto gli è accaduto e al percorso successivo al trauma. Ha parlato anche della Fiorentina, della convivenza con il defibrillatore e del sostegno dell’amico tennista Flavio Cobolli.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

L’ex Roma ha ripercorso ciò che ricorda di quel giorno, a partire dal risveglio: «Avevo vent'anni quando mi sono trovato ad affrontare qualcosa che ha stravolto la mia vita. Mi sono ritrovato in una situazione completamente nuova e ho dovuto imparare a capire come proseguire. In un certo senso, potermi fermare e ragionare su quello che stava succedendo è stata una fortuna. Del 1° dicembre 2024 ricordo soprattutto il momento del risveglio e la gioia nel vedere le reazioni dei miei familiari».

Bove ha spiegato di non avere ricordi del malore e di convivere tranquillamente con il defibrillatore. Ha affrontato anche le paure legate al ritorno in campo, scegliendo il supporto di una mental coach e di uno psicoterapeuta: «Non ricordo quello che è successo durante il malore, perché non ho vissuto direttamente quei momenti. Convivo tranquillamente con il defibrillatore e mi auguro che non mi riservi altre sorprese. Non ha modificato la mia personalità né mi ha impedito di affrontare il percorso. Sapevo che, una volta tornato a giocare, avrei potuto avere delle paure: per questo ho deciso di affidarmi a una mental coach e a uno psicoterapeuta, per riuscire a superare il trauma. Adesso sono più tranquillo e vivo il calcio con una consapevolezza nuova. Ho compreso che non può rappresentare l'unico centro della mia vita: esistono tante altre cose importanti che, forse, prima consideravo scontate».

La Fiorentina è rimasta vicina a Bove nei mesi successivi al malore. Il calciatore ha ricordato il rapporto con la squadra e la possibilità di continuare a seguirla anche senza scendere in campo: «Per me è stata una seconda famiglia. Mi è rimasta vicino nel periodo più difficile che abbia mai attraversato e sarò sempre grato a tutte le persone che mi hanno dato una mano. Mi hanno consentito di continuare a seguire la squadra anche quando non avevo la possibilità di scendere in campo. I compagni non mi hanno mai fatto sentire messo da parte e, pur essendo lontano dal terreno di gioco, hanno continuato a farmi sentire parte del gruppo. Sono riconoscente alla società e a tutto lo staff: è un rapporto che conserverò per sempre».

#3391. Jensen Huang’s Biopic Feels Inevitable — The Right One Might Be Impossible

Hollywood loves a visionary, especially one whose biggest gamble eventually made him a billionaire. But the trouble with making a biopic about a tech mogul actively shaping the future? That kind of story often refuses to sit still long enough to be told before ending in calamity.

When it comes to Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, any filmmaker hoping to get ahead of the microchip company’s uncertain next chapter may already be too late. Or is it still… too early?

On Thursday, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned as CEO and board member, effective immediately. And no reason was given for the departure: a rather extraordinary development for someone who helped build the company into one of the most powerful and lucrative forces in artificial intelligence. For Hollywood, it’s the kind of twist that practically demands a screenplay. Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

Huang’s rise from teenage Denny’s employee to the face of the AI boom always had the makings of a prestige drama. Now there’s a corporate disaster — involving an alleged Chinese espionage operation and reports of multiple extramarital affairs — at the end of it. Hot dog! Still, it’s anyone’s guess whether that fiery conclusion can seem genuinely relevant by the time film and TV creatives get around to adapting it.

The entertainment industry has spent much of 2026 demonstrating how difficult it is to dramatize Silicon Valley while the real people involved keep making headlines. Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning,” for example, opened to just $5.5 million in North America. That’s a disappointing debut for the follow-up to David Fincher’s “The Social Network,” which won three Oscars including best adapted screenplay.

Revisiting Facebook through the perspectives of whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) and Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), Sorkin attempted to turn Mark Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) and his social media platform’s disastrous effects on politics and public discourse into a satisfying sequel.

Of course, audiences had already spent years living with the very real consequences of Zuckerberg’s company’s actions. And in his “D+” review for IndieWire, Ryan Lattanzio described Sorkin’s approach as “less old-fashioned than completely out of date,” criticizing a falsely triumphant finale that failed to reconcile how little had actually changed in the world after the investigation’s revelations came to light.

While Sorkin was late to the party, Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” has had the good fortune of arriving right as things have been starting to get worse. Dramatizing OpenAI’s chaotic 2023 firing and rehiring of Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield), the dark comedy finds absurdity in the gap between Big Tech’s grandiose promises and the frequently clownish folks making them.

In his “B-” review for IndieWire, David Ehrlich praised the coming film for recognizing how “deeply fucking stupid the road to superintelligence has turned out to be.” He also questioned its tendency to simplify an ongoing story into something more resolved than it is. (Suffice to say, any film that tries to predict the cultural conversation also risks declaring history finished too soon.)

“Artificial” has benefited from some remarkable timing, too. Amazon MGM dropped the project after entering into a partnership with OpenAI — with sources telling the Los Angeles Times that the script’s critical perspective on artificial intelligence specifically contributed to the decision. Neon eventually acquired it, and a well-received New York Film Festival premiere helped build some serious awards-season momentum for routine Oscar contender Guadagnino.

Then came the U.S. midterms, during which voters across the country backed restrictions on data-center development. That makes the questions about who controls AI and who actually pays for its consequences feel spectacularly urgent, effectively turning a simple boardroom fight into a existential consideration of society with significantly heavier stakes.

Of course, tech biopics don’t necessarily have to predict the future to be powerful.

Consider Hulu’s “The Dropout,” which won Amanda Seyfried an Emmy for playing Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. Four years later, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s boundary-breaking documentary “You Can See Everything” once again made Holmes a viral sensation — even bringing Seyfried into contact with the woman she portrayed.

As IndieWire TV critic Ben Travers recently argued, “The Dropout” remains effective precisely because it didn’t pretend to know everything about Holmes in 2022. Fielder and Oppenheim’s contribution often gets so close to its subject that Holmes’ motives become difficult to pin down, while the series maintains enough separation to keep her actions and victims in focus.

“Sometimes a healthy distance provides greater clarity,” Travers wrote.

That’s a useful lesson for anyone hoping to next adapt the life of a Silicon Valley billionaire before history has finished passing judgment on them. And in Huang’s case, there’s already plenty of material to work with — before pretending to know how his former employer’s whole saga ends.

Having cofounded Nvidia in 1993, Huang nearly lost the company after betting on a method of rendering video-game graphics that Microsoft effectively rendered obsolete. With Nvidia running out of money, he then scrapped its original technology and made a last-ditch gamble on a new chip that ultimately helped save the business.

Huang eventually helped develop the graphics-processing infrastructure that would make his company’s hardware essential to the AI boom. Fast-forward to a public apology to his wife and throw in a leather jacket? Hollywood could probably have a trailer ready by Christmas.

But that would also be the easiest, and potentially least interesting, version of Huang’s story, right? Nvidia’s success was built on the backs of countless engineers, researchers, and developers aside from Huang. The fallout within the AI giant will impact everyone.

A truly great movie about Huang and Nvidia would need to understand the company’s founding and survival, follow the enormous risks Huang took with that future, and then seriously interrogate what happens when a single corporation becomes indispensable to the technology rapidly reshaping nearly all of modern life. Those are three(!) very different artistic ambitions. Considering the entertainment industry’s own increasingly lucrative partnerships with AI companies, and Amazon’s offloading of “Artificial,” there’s reason to wonder just how much scrutiny Hollywood would be willing to apply to the innovators they are in business with.

Which brings us back to the question of when to make a Jensen Huang biopic.

The tech industry is moving faster than filmmakers can reasonably hope to keep up with, but the bigger problem may be that news around the Silicon Valley story most worth telling is changing just as quickly. A film about the man who helped build the future we’re facing might have been an easy sell a few years ago. These days, the more pressing issue is what kind of world Huang actually put in motion — and whether Hollywood can afford to doubt it in public.

#3390. Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Company Is Stepping In

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough."

Enough Phone really does seem small. The company says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it plans to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current plan is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade."

Now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is currently in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company currently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the company's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

#3388. ’12 12 12′ Review: Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan’s Ticking-Clock Heist Thriller Runs on Broken Time

Every episode of “12 12 12” opens with the same explanation of its title: Citing the fictitious law enforcement manual, “Principles of Crime, FBI Research Center, 4th Edition,” Anthony Mackie explains, “A high asset robbery, professionally conceived, is 12 months in planning, 12 hours in execution. A bank robber who’s not caught within 12 days is not caught at all.” Then the screen splits horizontally to reveal images from the 12 months of preparation, the 12 hours of execution, and the 12 days when thief extraordinaire Paul Galvin (Jamie Dornan) does his best to elude Mackie’s obsessed FBI agent Jack Strickland. And then, we’re off to the races. Related Stories ‘The Good Daughter’ Review: Rose Byrne Sizzles in Peacock’s Brutal Trauma-Drama About Crime-Solving Sisters ‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations

The heist genre, in theory, seems ripe for this kind of temporal manipulation. A game of wits between cops and criminals typically involves plenty of twists, many of which pull the rug out by flashing back to show where, when, and how it was placed so stealthily underfoot. Also working in “12 12 12’s” favor is the genre’s familiarity: There will be “getting the team together” montages, there will be unexpected hiccups in the days and hours during the robbery, there will be chest-thumping meetings between our confident cop and the equally confident con artist. Throw in the complex heist itself and the tense escape soon after, and there appear to be enough recognizable pieces that jumbling them up shouldn’t prove too confusing.

And “12 12 12” isn’t confusing. It is, however, convoluted. Taking a serpentine route through well-trodden territory does more to undermine our enjoyment of an otherwise well-mounted chase than it does to liven things up. Heists are inherently exciting. They’re exciting in conception (when master thieves can wow us with their slick plans), they’re exciting to see carried out (when the shit hits the fan and even the most astute architects have to think on their feet), and they’re exciting to get away with (when safety is within reach, but it could be snatched away at any moment). Anticipation, suspense, and anxiety work to form a natural arc, and disrupting that arc over and over, every hour for eight hours, in service of a few extra twists — and to extend what’s obviously a movie-length story across eight hours — simply isn’t worth it.

On that note, let me get this minor but essential point out of the way now, quickly and clearly: Jamie Dornan needs more weird roles, not more conventional ones. We saw what he can do in “Barb and Star Go to Vista Del Mar” (a modern comedy classic). Let the man cook — or sing or dance or all three at once! He can do it! Honestly, I believe he can do anything. (Remember the bee movie?! No, not that bee movie — the other one.)

Anyway, here his character’s only unique attribute is his brilliant… planning. He’s got a mind for details, and he uses it to map out every possible contingency before embarking on his elaborate heists. Caught in a bind with his dumbass brother (Jack Kesy, doing his best Travis Kelce impression), Bobby lays it out in aptly blunt terms: “Paul, you’re the fucking plan guy, so plan me a plan.”

But the only plans Paul wants to make these days are for his family: He’s happy working on fishing boats off the coast of France and coming home to his wife, Severine (Agathe Rousselle), in their little apartment above a bar. He’s bonded with his father-in-law, Serge (José Garcia), who’s the Marxist papa Paul never had, and he’s got a kid on the way.

Unfortunately, Bobby can’t stop being Bobby and winds up indebted to the wrong people; people who don’t just want their money back, but who want more money to make up for the inconvenience. And since Bobby already owes more money than either brother could ever pay back, Paul has to take on one last job to free his brother — and himself — from their lives of crime.

Too bad that puts him back on Jack’s radar or, I should say, squarely on Jack’s radar, since Jack is nursing a (secret) grudge against Paul from years earlier. Ever since, he’s been obsessed with catching the one criminal who’s eluded his grasp. He wants revenge, he wants “respect,” he wants to win — “12 12 12” throws out a number of motivations for Jack early on that clearly don’t paint the full picture. They’re placeholder reasons until the show deems it time to dig into what’s really driving him to move to Zurich, hole up in a shitty police station, and wait for Paul to try to steal something.

Mackie, who’s reunited with his “Falcon and the Winter Soldier” director Kari Skogland, gives great determined face, and Dornan is the softest, sweetest guy on the FBI’s most-wanted list. Thankfully, co-creators Dudi Appleton and Jim Keeble don’t ask their lead characters to betray their core identities amid all the twists and turns, shading Jack as more of an antagonist (all-consumed and, thus, single-minded to a fault) and Paul as more of the protagonist. (He doesn’t want to steal, but now that he must, he’s going to do it the right way.) That helps keep our rooting interests in line, which goes a long way toward a satisfying emotional payoff, even when the momentum ebbs and flows with every flash-forward, -back, and -sideways.

With slick locations and clever-enough problem-solving, “12 12 12” should satisfy die-hard heist fans (but not “Die Hard’s” heist fans). It just takes a circuitous route to scratching that itch, and that’s almost as aggravating as not scratching it at all.

“12 12 12” premieres Friday, November 13 on Apple TV with two episodes. New episodes will be released weekly through the finale (Episode 8) on December 25.

#3387. Florence Pugh’s Steinbeck Adaptation Officially Passes Massive Netflix Milestone

East of Eden has reaped a bountiful harvest for Netflix. Not only has the new adaptation of the classic John Steinbeck novel been a critical success, but it's still garnering new viewers. The seven-episode miniseries, which stars Florence Pugh, has just passed a major milestone.

Based on Steinbeck's bestselling 1952 novel, East of Eden is a generational saga that centers around Cathy Ames (Pugh) and Adam Trask (Christopher Abbott). The two meet in the late 19th century when Cathy is found half-dead by half-brothers Adam and Charles (Mike Faist). Trying to overcome their respective dark pasts, Cathy and Adam marry and travel west to California. However, Cathy can't defy her true nature, and abandons Adam with their twin sons, Caleb and Aron, shortly after their births. When the two grow to manhood, they must reckon with the ghosts of their past.

After being released on October 1, East of Eden has now spent six consecutive weeks on Netflix's top ten list. It's an impressive feat for a miniseries based on a novel that's already been adapted into an Oscar-winning film, back in 1955. In fact, there's a familial connection between the two adaptations: Zoe Kazan, who created, co-wrote, co-showran, and produced the miniseries, is the granddaughter of Elia Kazan, who directed the film. It currently holds an 88% Fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes; Collider's Terese Lacson gave it a rave review, calling it "a daring new perspective on the familiar story."

Kazan and co-showrunner Jeb Stuart are moving on from East of Eden to take on a task that's almost as daunting: Larry McMurtry's classic revisionist Western Lonesome Dove. The Pulitzer Prize-winning 1985 novel was already adapted into a much-beloved miniseries in 1989 with Tommy Lee Jones and Robert Duvall. Stuart spoke with Collider about taking on McMurtry's magnum opus, and what the new Netflix adaptation will do that the original didn't: "I have great respect for the original miniseries, and obviously the novel is like East of Eden. It's a big, bold American novel that's...also something you could use as a doorstop, it's 900 pages. Because it is 900 pages, there's a lot they didn't get into that four-episode miniseries that was, you know, Robert Duvall's masterpiece."

East of Eden is now streaming on Netflix. Stay tuned to Collider for future updates.

#3386. Three Ways to Avoid CAPTCHA Prompts When Using a VPN

VPNs make it harder to track your online activity across websites, but it also makes them suspicious about your origins. When you borrow an IP address that hundreds of other people are also using for any number of reasons, you’re much more likely to get repeat verification requests from online firewalls.

CAPTCHAs are simple puzzles that websites use to filter out bots and spam. They’re supposed to be easy for people but hard for robots, such as simple object recognition tasks or audio-visual challenges. However, they can still disrupt your browsing experience if they happen too frequently.

Most modern CAPTCHA providers, like Google's reCAPTCHA v3 or Cloudflare Turnstile, start working long before they give you a puzzle to solve. It usually starts with a risk score that studies your IP address, browser and device signals, or recent online activity.

If the CAPTCHA provider can’t confidently identify your request as human based on those signals, it requests that you complete a puzzle before deciding if the request should be blocked. That means when you get repeat CAPTCHA requests, there’s something affecting your browser’s risk score. For example, popular VPN servers spread the same IP address across any number of users, which can easily make a website mistake you for a bot farm. If you change your IP address frequently by switching servers often, that might look suspicious too.

Luckily, there are ways to deal with frequent CAPTCHA requests using tools and services available with your browser and VPN. Cloudflare has already cut its CAPTCHA requests by 91% using its Managed Challenge platform. Apple has also been shipping token-based verification on devices since iOS 16 and macOS Ventura. In June 2026, Cloudflare even announced a joint effort called the Private Access Control Tokens (PACT) standard with Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Shopify.

While there’s no direct off switch for CAPTCHAs, you can use different fixes to improve your browser’s trust signals when using the internet. That way, you’re less likely to be hounded by verification requests.

The easiest fix for repeat CAPTCHAs is to stop connecting to whichever server your VPN app picks automatically. Proton recommends choosing servers with lower traffic load. In fact, its apps display load as a percentage to help you avoid the most crowded options. I'd also skip big traffic hubs like New York or London, since that's where most traffic originates from. Servers in smaller cities located nearby are often just as fast but never as populated.

You should also avoid changing IP addresses too frequently, which can look suspicious on its own. Pick a server that seems to behave well, then continue using it for at least one session. Also remember you’re more likely to get premium server options if you’re on a paid VPN plan. Major platforms like ExpressVPN, Surfshark, Proton, and Nord are particularly likely to have a larger server collection to pick from.

Costs nothing more than your current subscription

Hopping between servers often can backfire

Private Access Tokens (PAT) let you verify the authenticity of your request using your device rather than an IP address. Apple calls it Automatic Verification, where an Apple server validates your device and Apple Account to assign you an anonymous token.

To enable Automatic Verification on an iPhone or iPad, go to Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification. On a Mac, open System Settings > [your name] > Sign-In & Security > Automatic Verification.

Unfortunately, there’s no equivalent feature for Windows, Android, and Linux users. That said, Cloudflare offers the Silk extension for Chrome, Firefox, and Edge that serves a similar function. A quick look at the ratings will tell you it’s not as effective, but Cloudflare’s upcoming cross-browser standard called PACT seems promising once it is released.

Doesn’t share personal details with websites

Chrome and Firefox extensions can be unreliable

If you pay a bit extra for a dedicated IP add-on, VPN providers can assign you a unique IP address that isn’t shared with anyone else. For example, NordVPN offers dedicated IPs in 30 countries for $2-5 a month and Surfshark charges $3.75 a month for it.

There are also dedicated providers like Private Internet Access, which charges $3.99 per month for a zero-trust setup so not even their employees know which IP address is assigned to you. On the other hand, Proton VPN offers dedicated IPs only to business plan users, so you’ll need to be on the Workspace Standard, Premium, or Enterprise plans to get one.

That said, there is a trade-off here too. NordVPN itself admits that a dedicated IP makes it easier to link online activity back to a single user. Also, many websites can still tell that the IP address originated from a VPN data center rather than a consumer’s device.

Get unique IP addresses with pristine reputation

Works across desktop, mobile, and even smart TVs

Also functions as an allowlisted address for work

Add-ons cost more on top of the VPN subscription

Offers less anonymity than shared VPN servers

#3385. Why Doctor Strange Abandons The Avengers To Join Doctor Doom Explained

There's a sensible reason why Doctor Strange betrays the Avengers and becomes Doctor Doom's right-hand man during the collapse of the Marvel multiverse. Every major Avengers antagonist has led an army and a group of devoted lieutenants. In The Avengers, Loki weaponizes the Chitauri to invade the Earth, assisted by the brainwashed Hawkeye and Erik Selvig. In Avengers: Age of Ultron, Ultron builds an endless hive-mind swarm of Ultron Sentries designed to evolve alongside him and enlists Wanda and Pietro Maximoff before the twins defect. When Thanos finally makes his move in Infinity War and Endgame, he brings the Black Order and hordes of Outriders and Chitauri with him.

One of the biggest questions surrounding Avengers: Doomsday is the identity of Doctor Doom's acolytes, who seem to draw inspiration from the Black Swans and Black Priests of Jonathan Hickman’s Time Runs Out storyline. While there's a possibility they're Doombots or alternate Victor von Doom variants, close inspection of their masks and cloaks suggests that Doom is secretly leading corrupted or brainwashed variants of MCU magic users. Doctor Strange, Wanda Maximoff, Clea, and Sylvie are the most likely heroes-turned-villains hiding behind the hoods, potentially manipulated into believing that Doom's authoritarian rule is the only way to save a collapsing multiverse from total destruction.

Marvel Studios inevitably makes significant changes to every major comic book storyline it adapts into live-action, and the plot of Time Runs Out and Secret Wars is no exception. Just like the exact location of the Infinity Stones ahead of Avengers: Infinity War and the Avengers' method to undo Thanos' Snap ahead of Avengers: Endgame, the mystery behind Doctor Doom's followers might be one of Avengers: Doomsday's biggest points of speculation and one of its biggest twists as well.

As the Marvel multiverse collapses in Jonathan Hickman’s Secret Wars saga, Doctor Strange realizes that neither the Illuminati nor the Avengers can prevent the end of all existence. Throughout the preceding Time Runs Out storyline, Strange watches brilliant minds like Reed Richards and Tony Stark exhaust every scientific and ethical option while incursions erase entire realities. Having already abandoned conventional superhero morality by embracing dark blood magic to save his world, Strange ultimately discovers that the omnipotent Beyonders are orchestrating the multiverse's destruction.

Doctor Strange uncovers Victor von Doom’s secret identity as Rabum Alal, the Great Destroyer who spent years killing Molecule Men across parallel worlds before gathering the survivors into a massive bomb to use against the Beyonders. Doom embraced the unthinkable role of cosmic executioner to buy creation a fighting chance. So, joining forces with Doom and Molecule Man for a last stand against the Beyonders before the final universes collide, Strange witnesses Owen Reece channel the Ivory Kings' godlike energy into Victor.

Following Doctor Doom's creation of Battleworld, Doctor Strange cements his choice to support Doom and accepts the role of Sheriff Strange, willingly partnering with Doom so that at least a sliver of humanity survives. Strange knows deep down that Victor is a tyrant whose rule will eventually crumble under his own pride, but he also understands that without Doom’s iron grip, nothing would exist at all. Although Strange's support of God Emperor Doom is a betrayal of his heroic principles, he has no option but to help a ruthless monarch hold the pieces together until a better world can be reborn.

As Sheriff of Battleworld, Doctor Strange becomes the supreme enforcer and right-hand magistrate of the realm, bearing the exhausting burden of keeping Victor von Doom’s patchwork reality from tearing itself apart. Based in Battleworld's Isle of Agamotto, Strange leads the Thor Corps and mediates violent border disputes between rival barons like Sinister, Apocalypse, and Maestro. Whenever rebellions erupt or forbidden memories of the old multiverse resurface, Sheriff Strange arrives to restore stability. Besides, Strange also hides the sealed life raft of surviving Earth-616 heroes he discovered years after Battleworld's creation, keeping the mysterious vessel locked away to prevent it from affecting the peace while he outwardly enforces Doom's every decree.

After eight years of enforcing Battleworld’s laws, Sheriff Strange turns against God Emperor Doom during the explosive climax of Jonathan Hickman and Esad Ribić’s Secret Wars #4. Strange had secretly kept the mysterious Earth-616 life raft hidden inside his Isle of Agamotto sanctum for five years after discovering it, unsure of what lay inside. When a separate raft belonging to the sinister Cabal led by Thanos and the Maker breaches Battleworld, Strange finally has the Earth-616 vessel opened, awakening Reed Richards, Spider-Man, Black Panther, Captain Marvel, Star-Lord, Cyclops, and the Mighty Thor to join him in the fray.

The Battleworld conflict draws God Emperor Doom himself down to the battlefield, where the omnipotent ruler kills Cyclops and confronts Sheriff Strange. Then, Strange performs a powerful teleportation spell that scatters Reed Richards, Black Panther, and the rest of the surviving heroes safely across Battleworld’s various domains where they can ignite a coordinated rebellion. Shockingly, after Strange mocks Doom's lingering fear of Richards, God Emperor Doom obliterates Strange on the spot with a single blast, making Strange a martyr whose final spell ensures the downfall of Doom's empire.

The MCU captured the spirit of Doctor Strange’s pragmatic compromise in Avengers: Infinity War, when he voluntarily handed the Time Stone over to Thanos on Titan. Although Strange's decision is now seen as the wise first step in his successful plan to overturn Thanos' Snap and bring half of the universe back to life, it used to seem like an uncharacteristic move from one of the MCU's brightest minds. Just like his Secret Wars counterpart, Benedict Cumberbatch's MCU Strange recognized that outright victory at that moment was impossible and that temporary defeat was the sole pathway to survival.

Since the MCU has already shown Strange willingly hand victory to a tyrant once, Avengers: Doomsday will likely adapt Sheriff Strange with a clever twist so the beat doesn't feel repetitive. Instead of having Earth-616 Strange consciously strike another secret bargain with Doctor Doom, the MCU's adaptation of Time Runs Out and Secret Wars could introduce a brainwashed Strange who may have lost an off-screen battle against Doom following the events of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness. This scenario is more likely, considering the rest of Doctor Doom's acolytes are also likely to be fellow Avengers.

How do you think Avengers: Doomsday will adapt Doctor Strange's allegiance to Doctor Doom?
