#3383. In Shana Feste’s Films, Gender-Flipping Cinema’s ‘Tradition of Celebrating Damaged Men’ Is Its Own Reward

Shana Feste knows her filmography might be a bit tough to pin down. Some directors like to stick to a certain genre. Not Feste. Some only like to work with certain stars. Not Feste. Others enter a franchise and never look back. Not Feste.

But over the course of nearly two decades behind the camera, Feste has carved out a particular sweet spot, regardless of the genre or the cast or the wider world her stories fit inside: She likes complicated women. Not unlikable women, but messy women, contradictory women, women who get things done their own way. It’s a signature unto itself.

“My filmmaking, my history, people have not really known what to do with me. I’m making a comedy, I’m making a horror film, I’m making a genre thriller,” Feste told IndieWire during a recent interview. “But I do find that they’re all starting to build into each other, especially the trajectory from ‘Country Strong’ to ‘Run Sweetheart Run’ to ‘Heartland.’ I’ve always been drawn to women who don’t behave correctly. I’ve always been interested in women who don’t grieve correctly, who mother incorrectly, who love incorrectly. I just want women to have the freedom to behave in this contradictory, destructive, funny, selfish way and be given the same freedom that male characters are given.” Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

Another shared characteristic between Feste’s complicated women: They may be messy or unexpected, but they tend to get shit done. In her new film “Heartland,” getting shit done is at the center of the story, as the Nashville-set drama follows Jessica Chastain as Misty Jones, a former country-singing superstar who left the business after her designation as the, ahem, “cunt of country” became too much to bear. She’s thrust back into that world after her niece, rising star Charlie Heart (Carter Faith), goes missing. Misty, being Misty, takes it upon herself to get to the bottom of an increasingly dark and twisted mystery, no matter what it takes.

“I am a mom of three, 51, and I’m like, ‘Let’s write about some women who get shit done,’” she said. “I find a lot of those women exist. I’m living in the South now that I see those women every day and am inspired by them. We have this long-established cinematic tradition of celebrating damaged men. But when women behave similarly, they could be labeled as hysterical or dramatic or that word, unlikable. I want to prove that wrong.”

For the (complicated, messy, extremely capable) character of Misty, Feste said, she initially tapped into her longtime love of film noir. She always gravitated toward the Humphrey Bogart types, she said, but wondered what might happen if they gave those sorts of roles to women. That also fed into the dark underbelly of the Nashville scene that the film interrogates, a perfectly noir-ish idea.

“It could have been any city, but specifically this dark underbelly had to do with the music world,” Feste said. “Sadly, it was a common experience for a lot of artists that I spoke with. It was an experience that I’ve experienced in our industry, and it was all too relevant. When we were making the movie, a lot of conversation around Diddy was happening. He had just been arrested, and things were coming into light. We thought, oh wow, this is such a topical moment. And I’m like, it’s always topical, sadly. Whether we’re Epstein, Diddy, Weinstein, this is always going to be in the world, sadly.”

But Feste is also someone who loves this world and wants to celebrate what’s good and true about it. “Country Strong” was about making it — and maybe even making it again — even at great personal cost. “Heartland” just ratchets that sensibility up.

“I wanted to lean into the secrets and the dark corners and the underbelly, but I also will always celebrate the artistry and the storytelling of country music,” she said. “Misty says one line that really speaks so much to me about what the film is: ‘You don’t deserve country music.’ It takes a lot to deserve country music in my eyes. Country music is like the apex of storytelling. So to point out someone who doesn’t deserve country music, I mean, that’s a big insult for me.”

Feste started writing “Heartland” around four years ago, mostly because she was really missing the world of country music that framed her 2010 music drama “Country Strong.” “My father died about eight years ago, and I found myself listening to a lot of country music when he died,” she said. “In the years after he died, going back to the music that he loved, that he used to play for me in the car when we were driving on road trips, I realized that when you’re a writer, you don’t know quite why you write something until years later. And I realized, oh, I’m really missing my father.”

She was also eager to reteam with her “Country Strong” collaborators Jenno Topping and Randall Poster, two people who Feste said have believed in her the most over the course of her career. (Topping and Poster both produced “Heartland,” with Poster also serving as music supervisor, as he did on “Country Strong.”) “When I’m having my darkest days about, I don’t know, me and what I create and my career, knowing that they believe in me has always been such a huge lift,” Feste said. “So having them help me tell this story was just monumental. It was being with someone that you knew had your back the entire time.”

If “Heartland” sees Misty feeling ill at ease in the very spaces that used to celebrate her talent, Feste had the opposite experience. Six films into her directing career, she said “Heartland” let her approach her work in an entirely new way. And it felt good.

“What was really valuable with this experience is that I felt completely comfortable saying, ‘I don’t know,’ and I don’t know if I’ve ever felt that way,” she said. “Certainly not with my first few films, feeling like as a woman, I had to know every answer from every head of department immediately. It was only working with this group of filmmakers, Jenno and Randy and [production designer] Naomi [Shohan], some of my heads of production, that I knew that they saw my vulnerability not as a weakness, but as a strength. I was able to say, ‘I don’t know, what do you think?’ That’s where a very new form of collaboration happened that I haven’t experienced in my career, and with Jessica as well.”

Casting Chastain was an easy call for Feste. She wanted someone who could sing and who was admired in this space, but Chastain’s way of working and approach to on-set life gave Feste more to work with than she could have dreamed.

“I always want my films, especially when we’re shooting a movie that takes place in Nashville, to feel authentic, and I knew Jessica already had a huge buy-in from this audience. The South, they love her from ‘George & Tammy,’” Feste said. “And Jessica can sing, and that is another qualifier. Whenever I’m making any kind of movie with music, I want the actors to be able to sing their own material. But I think most of all, Jessica is one of the biggest champions of other women that I’ve ever met.”

It was freeing for Feste to say “I don’t know,” but Chastain also made it clear that she was there to support Feste’s vision and leadership.

“There were certain times on set where it would get a little loud or kind of disorderly, and people would be talking and having opinions, and no matter what, she’d be like, ‘Shana, sorry, I couldn’t hear you,’ and it was like this just gentle reminder, ‘This is who is leading the ship right now for me,’” the filmmaker recalled. “It was done in the classiest, most polite way.”

That approach turned the collaboration into more of a partnership. When Chastain had an idea, Feste was eager to listen. Even a decade ago, she said, that might not have been so easy for her.

“If I had been the director that I was 10 years ago, it would’ve scared me to death, because Jessica is not afraid to come into a scene and say, ‘OK, wait, that might not be serving us. Let’s throw that idea out of the window. What if we did this?,’” Feste said. “As a director, I’m planning, and every shot is in my head, and I’ve done the work, and I’ve done the homework, and I’m the A student. And to be able to relinquish control and admit when my idea wasn’t the best idea and she’s coming in with a stronger idea because she is Jessica Chastain? She has done the work. She has made this character so rich. This wasn’t a scary experience. It was actually going to elevate the scene and make it work even better.”

It was always the plan for Feste’s stars to also sing their songs to add to the film’s deeper authenticity. “When I’m watching movies that feature performing artists, and there’s so much hype, and they’re playing this celebrated musical performer, and then they come on, and we hear them sing and we’re like, have they been re-voiced? It’s just kind of mediocre? You just kind of lose your authenticity. You lose the ownership of the movie,” she said.

Casting Jennifer Nettles was something of a no-brainer for Feste, and so was actually directing the country superstar. “I didn’t know how to direct someone how to move on stage. That is something that’s not in my repertoire of directing. I can direct someone talking about their divorce in a bedroom, but how to command a stage and move your body? That is something that she learned over 20 years of experience being a superstar,” she said. “Most of the time I said, ‘Just speak to the audience like you are at the Opry, like you’ve done a thousand times. Make it your own.’ She did so much heavy lifting for me.”

So too did Carter Faith. In early discussions about the five characters in the film who are musical artists, Feste said she and Poster were constantly trying to figure out who they would sound like in the real world. Was Misty an Emmylou Harris? A Miranda Lambert? And who was young rising star Charlie Heart? Was she a Taylor Swift type? Poster had an easy answer: She sounds like this actual rising star, Carter Faith. And when it became clear that Faith was able to and interested in auditioning for the role? Serendipity.

“She was like a breath of fresh air,” Feste said. “I remember asking her, ‘Carter, what do you think you have in common with Charlie?’ And she said, ‘Well, we both have boy names.’ My heart exploded. It was the most non-Hollywood endearing response. Then I heard her story of how she was eating red beans and rice, crashing on couches, calling all of these places on Lower Broadway just to get an audition to be the performer at 10:00 AM on a Monday morning. She is someone who really moved to Nashville the day she graduated from high school to make it. She was Charlie. So much of her experience was exactly what the character was going through. So it was only the question of, are you brave enough to access all that trauma of how you got here? And she was absolutely, she said yes, and she trusted me, and it makes me emotional thinking about it because that’s an incredible trust to have.”

Faith also wrote the lyrics to the song that plays at the end of the film, which Feste sees as “dialogue that I could never write.” All the songs in the film and on its soundtrack, including the ones Feste simply imagined as titles first, like “Texas Land,” or that her stars like John Hawkes wrote or that Poster commissioned, add to the film’s incredible authentic feeling and sound. “Working with musical performances in film, it is so additive because it just takes the storytelling to another level. It’s beyond the dialogue. It’s beyond physical blocking. It tells story in this just purely emotional, raw, beautiful way,” she said.

Next up: In true Feste fashion, she’s working on or thinking about a variety of other projects next, including the next chapter of the “Dirty Diana” story, which she first cooked up during lockdown, a TV series about a Southern family, and her “dream project,” which is about Texas bank robbers. Mostly, she said, “I really want to continue working in this space. I want to continue telling stories about messy, complicated, vulnerable Southern women. I think that’s my bread and butter.”

Beyond the discount, the PartyBox 330 has plenty to offer if you're looking for a speaker that can handle everything from backyard barbecues to larger gatherings—sitting between the smaller Club 120 and the larger PartyBox 520 in JBL's lineup, it delivers deep, punchy bass and enough volume to entertain a crowd, while its roughly 20-hour battery life means you can keep the music going all day without having to find an outlet. #3381. John Wick Meets Reacher In This Must-Read Thriller That Keanu Reeves Is Adapting Next

Cher Thompson is a Senior Staff Writer at Screen Rant, where she covers everything from explosive reality TV moments to cast interviews about the twists and turns of scripted dramas. With a background in creative writing, marketing, and teaching, Cher knows how to spot both the storytelling genius and the guilty pleasures in pop culture. Her work blends wit with insight, making readers feel like they’re chatting with a friend who just happens to know way too much about TV.

After starring in the John Wick film franchise and witnessing the success of the Jack Reacher adaptations, Keanu Reeves' next major movie project will blend the two seamlessly using an exciting new title as its foundation. The best action thrillers in recent memory have managed to combine a strong story from the central character, creating compelling stakes that feel bigger than simple survival. With most of the protagonists in the action thriller genre coming from a place of expertise, being highly trained operatives or experienced investigators, the appeal of their stories comes from the creative ways they resolve massive conflict.

With many action thrillers having adapted their worlds from novels or written work, some of the most memorable franchises have come from source material that established the world and tone of the story, like the Reacher franchise. Others, like John Wick, have come from original spaces, but were inspired by real stories that were then inflated into fictional settings with higher, more intense stakes. Reeves, the star of the John Wick films, is moving into a space with his next project that feels more aligned with the Reacher franchise, despite still being on the big screen in his new film.

Inspired by an upcoming novel by Oliver Lowe, Reeves will star in Kill Current. The novel, which is set to release in May 2027, is the first of a series focusing on Jon Hendricks, a cynical former CIA operative who returns to the field after a mysterious murder brings him to the center of the crime. With Reeves set to star and produce, the upcoming adaptation of Kill Current is giving audiences the chance to jump in on the ground floor.

The first of a new series focused on CIA agent Jon Hendricks, Kill Current sees the former operative having retired from active duty, but returning to the field when his former trainee, Rivers Elliot, disappears. Hendricks looks to find Rivers, but the investigation quickly spirals out of control when a piece of technology that isn't meant to be sustainably used for at least another decade becomes a part of the case. With international travel and a larger geopolitical conflict at hand, things twist and turn for Hendricks throughout the novel, leading him to conclusions he never could've imagined on his own.

With the novel being compared most consistently to the Reacher franchise, Kill Current has echoes of the Lee Child series in its larger story, and has also been compared to John le Carré's work, as well. While Hendricks isn't a carbon copy of Jack Reacher, he definitely has many of the same qualities as the wandering hero, but the technological focus of the series provides a different element to the story. With a planned series in the works, Kill Current is just the opening of what will likely be a far longer story, which could be great for the adaptation side of the franchise.

As someone who's known to take his work seriously, knowing that Reeves is behind the adaptation of Kill Current is an exciting step in the right direction. While it was only announced in September 2026, Kill Current's adaptation has already been pushed into development, which means there's a great chance it comes to fruition. As the first major project from Reeves production company, Two Dragonflies, it's clear that Reeves' involvement in the adaptation is more than just a face for the film. Instead, being on the development side, Reeves is proving that he's bringing his past experiences to the universe in order to create a franchise.

For readers looking for a new thriller series to dive into on the ground floor, Kill Current should be a viable option, especially considering that there's already movement on a film adaptation. With Reeves working on the adaptation in a more extensive way and the novel itself receiving praise as the first a hopefully successful series, Kill Current is prepared to be the next action thriller to reach Reacher and John Wick levels of hype.

Kill Current is available for pre-order through this link.

#3380. The 7 Best Christmas Movies To Watch in November

'Tis the season to be jolly! Well, almost. As Mariah Carey defrosts and Thanksgiving dinner gets prepped, some Christmas lovers are still eager to haul out the holly and start celebrating. If you’re one of those in that camp and are ready to watch some Christmas movies, we have seven Christmas movies to watch this November to get you in the holiday spirit.

We have a fun batch of films that span the classics through new holiday films that debuted this year. Not every film goes full-throttle Christmas, just in case you’re not ready to trade out the changing of the leaves for some white landscapes. From hilarious holiday gatherings to an action-thriller that sparks annual debates about whether or not it’s a Christmas film, these movies are perfect to jump-start the season!

Let’s begin with the ultimate debate: is Die Hard a Christmas movie? Well, if you’re reading this entry, then you’ve got your answer! Directed by John McTiernan, the 1988 action thriller follows off-duty New York City police detective John McClane (Bruce Willis) as he visits Los Angeles on Christmas Eve to reconcile with his estranged wife. When a team of heavily armed criminals led by Hans Gruber (Alan Rickman) seizes her office building to steal millions in bearer bonds, McClane must wage a solo, barefoot guerrilla war to rescue the holiday party hostages, including his wife, Holly Gennaro-McClane (Bonnie Bedelia).

Watching Die Hard in November is the unofficial kick-off to the holiday movie season because it lets you embrace the Christmas spirit early without committing to traditional sap. The film is perfect for a November viewing because, at its core, it is still a family reconciliation movie about a dad trying to make things right with his estranged wife and kids by Christmas, complete with a Grinch-like corporate villain getting foiled. By checking it off your list in November, you beat the December content overload and stake your claim early in the eternal debate. Who doesn't need an ‘80s-soaked, action-packed shoot-em-up?

It’s very likely Elf gets added to the early Christmas rotation because it is simply pure joy. Plus, now two decades old, it’s been happily passed down to the next generation of kids and kids at heart. Directed by Jon Favreau and written by David Berenbaum, the iconic Christmas comedy tells the story of Buddy Hobbes (Will Ferrell), a human who was accidentally transported to the North Pole as a toddler and raised to adulthood among Santa's (Ed Asner) elves. After realizing he is actually human, the delightfully naive Buddy travels to New York City in full elf attire to find his biological father, Walter Hobbs (James Caan), a cynical children's book publisher on Santa's naughty list.

Elf bridges the gap between autumn cynicism and full-blown holiday magic without demanding heavy solemnity. It captures that exact late-fall-into-winter shift in Manhattan—crisp air, department store window displays going up, and the gradual creep of festive lights—mirroring the exact mood of walking outside in November. It works for both kids who love the candy-cane silliness and adults who appreciate Ferrell's physical comedy, making it an easy crowd-pleaser before holiday schedules get chaotic in December. Favreau designed the movie to combat modern cynicism, infusing it with hand-crafted, Rankin/Bass-inspired North Pole charm rather than high-pressure holiday stress.

Two years ago, Hallmark Channel jump-started a new tradition by capitalizing on a certain pop culture romance involving a mega pop star and her Kansas City Chiefs boyfriend. Well, after that success, they followed it up with a Buffalo Bills-centric Christmas love story. Now, the action is moving to Chicago in Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story. In this story, Avery Clark (Lyndsy Fonseca), an ambitious freelance reporter, returns to Chicago for Christmas and is assigned to write a human-interest piece on a lifelong Chicago Bears superfan, Darlene Donnelly (Marsha Mason), who's about to attend her 500th game. Because she knows next to nothing about football, the superfan’s handsome grandson, Matt Donnelly (Robert Buckley), a local firefighter, steps in to show her what Bears Nation really means.

As with the previous two films, Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story leans heavily into the beauty of fandom through the fanfare of Chicago Bears stadium traditions and crisp autumn-into-winter football weather before Christmas decorations completely take over. A love letter to the Windy City, the film showcases iconic Chicago spots and captures the city's energy. Centered on warm, generational family bonds, Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story lets you kick off your holiday watchlist early in the winter transition, offering comfort, community, and rom-com cheer that unites holiday fans with football lovers.

It’s hard to believe, but this Christmas will be our first without everyone’s favorite mom, Catherine O’Hara, so it’s a perfect time to kick off the holiday season with the beloved classic Home Alone. Directed by Chris Columbus and written by John Hughes, Home Alone follows eight-year-old Kevin McCallister (Macaulay Culkin), who is accidentally left behind in suburban Chicago when his family flies to Paris for a Christmas vacation. While he initially enjoys his newfound freedom, he must protect his home from a pair of bumbling burglars, Harry and Marv (Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern), known as the Wet Bandits.

Home Alone is a perfect November watch that has become a seasonal gateway tradition. The comfort film combines chaotic family dynamics with pure childhood wish-fulfillment. You get glowing Chicago neighborhood lights, snow-dusted streets, and a John Williams score that eases you into the holidays. Home Alone strips away the heavy focus on Santa or presents, focusing instead on themes of independence, overcoming fear, and finding your way back to family. Beneath the slapstick booby traps, Kevin's journey delivers pure warmth. If you love Home Alone and you’re eager for more, thankfully, there's an equally delightful sequel, Home Alone 2: Lost in New York!

If there’s ever been a film for all seasons, it’s Meet Me in St. Louis. But let’s face it, it qualifies as a Christmas movie because of the iconic rendition of “Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas.” Directed by Vincente Minnelli, the classic follows a year in the life of the upper-middle-class Smith family as they navigate romance, family bonds, and everyday dilemmas in turn-of-the-century Missouri. Divided into seasonal vignettes, the narrative builds anticipation for the upcoming 1904 World's Fair until the father, Alonzo (Leon Ames), announces a sudden corporate relocation to New York City.

Meet Me in St. Louis is the ideal transition-season film to watch in November because it literally covers an entire calendar year, moving gracefully through summer, autumn, Halloween, and Christmas, rather than diving straight into snow and Santa Claus. The iconic film starring Judy Garland treats November as an awkward purgatory before eventually building toward its famous holiday climax. It lets you slowly open the door to the Christmas season, highlighting why it draws such anticipation. The centerpiece is Garland’s Esther Smith singing the beloved Christmas classic to her heartbroken little sister, Tootie (Margaret O’Brien), as the family faces a dreaded move to New York City.

While the title The 12 Dates of Christmas may sound familiar, this is a brand-new film for 2026. The romantic holiday comedy follows Christina Walker (Lucy Hale), a successful business owner who has consistently prioritized her career over her personal life. After facing pressure from her family at the holidays, she pledges to find a partner and embarks on a plan to go on 12 blind dates in the 12 weeks leading up to Christmas Eve. Along the way, she navigates a series of hilariously disastrous setups while unexpectedly crossing paths with an old high school crush, Peter Grant (Ian Harding).

The 12 Dates of Christmas is an ideal early-November holiday watch because its core premise literally maps out a slow-burn countdown to December. Sometimes, the best Christmas movies to watch before December are the ones that are considered low-stakes guilty pleasures. This film is a light, breezy transition into festive viewing without plunging you straight into heavy-duty December tinsel overload. A big draw is the Pretty Little Liars reunion. Seeing Hale and Harding reunite on-screen gives it a cozy, familiar comfort-watch energy that matches the urge to curl up indoors as the weather turns.

With the sequel on the way, it’s the perfect time to revisit The Family Stone. Written and directed by Thomas Bezucha, the family dramedy centers on the ultra-liberal, bohemian New England Stone family whose dynamics are upended when their eldest son, Everett (Dermot Mulroney), brings his rigid, corporate girlfriend, Meredith Morton (Sarah Jessica Parker), home for Christmas. Overwhelmed by the family's hostile reception, she calls her easygoing sister, Julie (Claire Danes), for backup, which triggers a chaotic chain of events and unexpected romantic partner-swapping within the household.

The Family Stone captures the pre-holiday dread and messy human friction of going home for the holidays before the sugar-coated magic of December sets in. November marks the start of the holiday travel gauntlet, and the film leans into the immediate, sweaty-palmed anxiety of meeting a partner’s intensely tight-knit, unfiltered family for the first time. Watching it in November lets you process the emotional weight of family gatherings before you are sitting across from your relatives at the dinner table. With a star-studded ensemble including Diane Keaton, Rachel McAdams, Craig T. Nelson, and Luke Wilson, the film is a fun watch of icons having a blast together.

#3379. Samsung’s Newest Flagship Soundbar System Is $500 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Samsung’s flagship soundbars have reached the point where the yearly upgrades are more about refinement than reinvention, and that is pretty much the story with the Samsung HW-Q990H—and with Black Friday approaching, this 2026 model is already seeing a $500 discount, bringing its price down to $1,497.99 from $1,997.99. That's its lowest price to date.

Samsung kept the same 11.1.4-channel setup from the older HW-Q990F, including the soundbar, wireless subwoofer, and two rear speakers, but leaned harder into software this time around—features like the SpaceFit Sound Pro automatically adjust the sound depending on your room layout, and unlike some auto-calibration features that barely change anything, this one reportedly shifts the audio balance in noticeable ways. Sometimes it improves dialogue clarity and bass response. Other times, you may prefer tweaking things yourself with the built-in seven-band EQ.

The system also handles basically every major audio format, supports wireless Dolby Atmos with compatible Samsung TVs, and includes 4K 120Hz HDMI passthrough for people gaming on a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X. That said, while the bass is strong for a compact subwoofer, it compresses when you push the volume near maximum, so it's not perfect for huge spaces or people who want nightclub-level output. More importantly, if you already own the HW-Q990F or even the older HW-Q990D, upgrading probably will not feel dramatic enough to justify the cost. But for someone starting from TV speakers or an entry-level soundbar, this system can completely change how movies, games, and even sports feel at home.

#3378. David O. Russell’s ‘Madden’ Biopic Is Out Next Week — Does Anybody Know or Care?

Once upon a time, a new David O. Russell movie would be a must-see cinematic event. The writer/director earned three consecutive Best Picture Oscar nominations with “The Fighter,” “Silver Linings Playbook,” and “American Hustle,” all of which scored at the box office and are roundly regarded as generational classics of their era and even holiday fare. But did you know Russell has a new movie opening next week from Amazon MGM Studios? That would be “Madden,” his biopic starring a physically distended and hair-pieced Nicolas Cage as the iconic NFL commentator. When I told an IndieWire colleague about this story, they had heard of “Madden” the movie, yes, but had no idea that Russell directed it. Doesn’t bode well. Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

The film co-stars Russell perennial collaborator Christian Bale, strapped back into the hair and makeup chair for another grotesque transformation, as Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis, receding bleach-blond hairline and all, plus a wigged-out Kathryn Hahn as Madden’s wife Virginia, and poor Sienna Miller as Davis’s wife Carol. Reports have claimed the sports biopic carries a $75 million budget, making it one of the “Spanking the Monkey” director’s most expensive movies next to the critically flayed COVID release “Amsterdam,” which, not adjusted for inflation, cost a reported $80 million and earned a paltry $14 million domestically. That’s a movie that entirely vaporized from the cultural imagination — though you may recall a much-memed excerpt of a blink-and-you’ll-miss-her Taylor Swift being thrown under a car to her doom.

The “Madden” release strategy does not inspire confidence, either, suggesting a classic case of bag-and-tag on the part of Amazon MGM Studios: a day-and-date release on Prime Video globally with a perfunctory, subterranean-level theatrical bow, both on Wednesday, November 18. The critics’ screening takes place Monday, November 16, with the embargo lifting about 15 hours later. Muted marketing only further intimates Amazon wants to take the latest Russell joint gently into that good night — but why? Is it that bad? The trailer has more than 8.6 million views and counting, though that’s largely explained by the prolific fanbase behind Madden, who died in 2021, and the NFL. Less so by any fanbase of Russell’s.

To be fair, the studio has its hands full trying to position “Project Hail Mary” in the Oscar race and back into voters’ consciousness after opening theatrically six months ago. Amazon MGM’s social media heist movie “How to Rob a Bank” opens in theaters this Friday, while another awards hopeful, “I Play Rocky,” is in limited release. While “Project Hail Mary” was a box office juggernaut for the company, the tech giant has yet to master juggling multiple tentpole-scale projects theatrically at once — though they’ve had a banner year with considerable successes “Verity” and “The Sheep Detectives” spread out throughout 2026.

Co-scripted by Russell and Cambron Clark, “Madden” centers on Madden’s Super Bowl-winning partnership with Al Davis and the Raiders that led to the “NFL Madden” games. The film wrapped production well over a year ago, in late spring 2025 in Atlanta. A TMZ report from May 21 claimed several actors walked off set after Russell allegedly used a racial epithet during a scene. A reputation for volatility has followed Russell across projects, from the widely seen behind-the-scenes footage of the filmmaker chewing out his “I Heart Huckabees” star Lily Tomlin, to Amy Adams’ confessional interviews in which she revealed the filmmaker made her cry throughout the “American Hustle” shoot. George Clooney has called Russell “a miserable fuck” and swore never to work with him again after his experience making “Three Kings.”

The five-time Oscar nominee has built a career on quirky, sprawling ensembles and pushing actors toward extreme physical performances, like Christian Bale, who went gaunt (again) to win an Academy Award for “The Fighter,” then put on the pounds for “American Hustle.” Back in October, Russell and producer Todd Black appeared at the Virginia Film Festival in Charlottesville to present four clips from “Madden” — which showcased Cage in prosthetic padding that’s more January Jones in “Mad Men” Season 5 than Kazu Hiro Oscar-level effort, plus an exasperatingly accented Bale with bleached eyebrows, and the women, including Hahn and Miller, in insane wigs. Clearly, this is Russell operating at an 11, with characters, based on these clips, squawking over each other like the most strident ensemble scenes out of “Silver Linings.”

During the panel, Russell described the casting process as “trippy,” noting that Cage gained weight for the role along with the prosthetics.

“We were scared because we weren’t telling a documentary, but we were honoring John Madden and honoring Al Davis,” Black said. “We were trying to make it an entertaining story without making it a documentary. So some stuff was inspired by, some stuff was true, and a lot of stuff we made up, not wildly, but just for entertainment value.”

The producer added, “I think when you see the movie, you’ll see it really is an incredibly positive film that when you watch it at Thanksgiving time, I think you’ll watch it with your family, hopefully, and you’ll walk out feeling really happy about it and telling people it’s such an inspiring film.”

He might be onto something. With three NFL games scheduled for Thanksgiving — including the Kansas City Chiefs at the Buffalo Bills on NBC and Peacock — “Madden” could prove apt counter-programming to sports spectacle. That’s if enough people know where to watch it, or that it’s available at all.

#3377. Netflix's New 8-Part Psychological Thriller Earns Near-Perfect Rotten Tomatoes Audience Score

Growing up around performers, storytelling was always central to Emma's life. Add in a nerdy older brother who introduced her to Marvel at far too young an age, and her love for entertainment led her to pursue a Journalism degree at Indiana University, where she discovered her passion for entertainment reporting. She spent nearly one year in Los Angeles covering industry stories and fully immersing herself in the world of entertainment media.

Netflix's newest psychological thriller is off to a promising start.

Created by Quinn Shephard, The Body follows a group of Catholic school girls whose dance-team initiation goes wrong, leading to prophetic visions and mass hysteria throughout their town. The psychological thriller stars Kristina Bogic, Geena Meszaros, and Sarah Boustany, alongside High School Musical: The Musical: The Series actor Sofia Wylie, former NFL player Nnamdi Asomugha, and Louisa Krause.

According to Rotten Tomatoes, The Body has earned a 98% audience score from more than 500 ratings. The eight-episode series, which premiered on Netflix on November 11, also holds an 86% critics' score based on 22 reviews, putting its audience rating 12 percentage points above its critical score.

The strong audience reception follows an equally promising start. When The Body premiered on November 11, it debuted with a perfect 100% critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes based on six reviews. Although that rating has since dropped as more critics weighed in, the series has continued to receive positive responses, with audiences currently rating it even higher than critics.

In ScreenRant's review of The Body season 1, Dani Kessel Odom gave the psychological thriller a 6/10, calling it a "campy, entertaining hot mess." While praising its religious satire, the review criticized the show's inconsistent pacing and rushed ending.

With only a few days since its release, the Rotten Tomatoes score could still fluctuate as more reviews are submitted. Nevertheless, its near-perfect audience rating gives the Netflix thriller TV show an impressive early reception, particularly as the series combines several genres, including supernatural horror, coming-of-age drama, and psychological suspense.

The series follows a group of teenage girls who pray to the Devil, whom they call the Prince of Darkness, hoping to win their dance-team regionals. #3376. I Played Wendy's RPG, and It's Actually Worth It for the Free Food

November is a huge month for video games. Nintendo dropped its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 last week, and the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is right around the corner. But the game we've been waiting for most of all also launched this month: WendyQuest, the free RPG from Wendy's. (No, this is not a joke.)

Despite the absurdity of a hamburger chain making a full video game (complete with Wendy's-themed puns), the thing is, this game is pretty solid—even if it is a promotion at the end of the day. WendyQuest's main purpose is to offer customers coupons they can use toward purchases in real life, though it's a bit of a commitment. It took me just under an hour of gameplay before I earned my first coupon, and Wendy's says it takes roughly 15 hours to beat. All that to say, this is a pretty unique marketing campaign.

I was surprised booting up WendyQuest on my iPhone. This doesn't necessarily feel like a thrown-together product. On the flip side, the production quality is quite high. The music is solid and very much traditionally RPG; there are even three save slots, in case you plan to return to this RPG again and again.

There's even a story, albeit cheesy (no pun intended): As the game explains, the "Four Great Spirits of Flavor" created Savoria, "a food-rich paradise." All was well until Mech Corp, led by the evil Dr. MechBorg, built robots to take over Savoria. The plot is far from compelling, and the writing can be a little over the top, but hey, I'll give them credit: They thought through a full story here.

You play as Wendy, the "representation of true culinary excellence and taste as dictated by the four ancient spirits of flavor." Wendy (or The Wendy, as some call her) is tasked with saving the world, traveling between villages and picking up new characters along the way. The game world even has "real" Wendy's locations you can visit. These act like inns and shops in other RPGs, giving you a chance to heal while also buying equipment.

Like other RPGs, WendyQuest uses turn-based combat. You have to charge up your attacks, but stop before they hit 100%, or you'll miss. (It took me a while to master the timing.) I'm pretty impressed with how challenging some of these battles can be, though you are quickly given the option of an amulet that gives you a huge leg-up in combat. You don't have to take it, but it makes fights easier if you're only in it for the coupons. That, combined with the spatulas the game encourages you to buy, lets you mow down enemies. You can also utilize your companions here: "Frygor," for example, can either attack enemies with a barrage of fries, or use those fries to build a shield to protect you.

While there are tons of enemies to fight, the key baddies are the "mechs." There are five in total, and after you defeat each, you get a coupon. Spoiler alert: The first mech drops the "Fry Stone," which nets you a coupon for a free order of medium fries—though you need to buy something in tandem, as well as use the Wendy's app. While I stopped my gaming here for this article, the other four coupons are:

Free biscuit or croissant (I didn't even know Wendy's sold biscuits and croissants)

Again, it's wild that WendyQuest has a 10+ hour campaign, with over 1,000 lines of dialogue to boot. I'm not sure this is a game I'm going to see through to the end, but I'll admit, it's a fun marketing approach from Wendy's. Sure, they could have run a promotion in the Wendy's app to give people coupons, but instead, they built an entire RPG. I respect it. You can download the game for iOS, Android, or Steam.

#3375. This Beloved Sci-Fi Novel Is Finally Getting Adapted After 12 Years, but It’s All Wrong

After 12 years and at least two scrapped attempts, Red Rising by Pierce Brown is finally getting adapted for the screen. Last month, Paramount Pictures announced that it had purchased the film rights to the acclaimed science fiction series, and it had even assigned writer Justin Rhodes and director Francis Lawrence to the project. The news broke days after Paramount's parent company finalized its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, creating the conglomerate now known simply as Skydance. With that much new momentum behind it, things are looking pretty good for this project, yet many fans still feel it taking the wrong approach. Like other doorstopper novels, this story might be better suited to a series than movies, and it might actually look better if it was animated rather than live-action.

These arguments have been made for several recent adaptations, and they've become increasingly popular among fans online. In this case, Brown actually spoke up about the idea of animation directly on social media. He told fans that he is simply trying to give the story its best chance at succeeding on the big screen, intimating that there are some very complex legal issues at play behind the scenes. Brown even suggested that an animated adaptation could come later if there's demand for it.

In a discussion with fans on Instagram, Brown assured fans that he did not compromise his own wishes in this latest deal to adapt Red Rising. It sounds like the author himself has wanted a live-action movie from the start. He explained: "If the film works, everything is on the table. If the film fails, animation is still on the table. If animation worked... Goddamn you don't comprehend the legal/rights complexity it'd take to make it a film. If animation failed, it's dead."

It sounds like Brown's pursuit of a live-action adaptation was at least partially motivated by the logic of sales. It's nice to see him assuring fans that he is not opposed to the idea of animation for this story. Red Rising is set in a distant future where humanity has colonized the entire solar system. It takes place on various planets, moons, and spacecraft, all with elaborate terraforming and engineering in place. On top of that, the characters are often flying, battling with advanced weaponry, or pulling off even more outrageous stunts that are hard to picture in live-action.

A "live-action" adaptation of Red Rising will really be a mass of special effects and CGI, which is why animation is such a popular option for fans. If the most important elements of the story are going to be animated by artists anyway, why not simplify the whole thing with a more stylized look? However, Brown's comments seem to suggest that it would be extremely difficult to sell a live-action adaptation after an animated adaptation, especially if the animated adaptation was unprofitable. That means the franchise's current course is its best chance of succeeding on multiple fronts, and it leaves other doors open as well.

Just a decade and a half ago, the idea of a fantasy novel adaptation performing better as a ten-episode series than a movie would have sounded strange in Hollywood, then Game of Thrones came along. Today, many other long, epic fantasy and sci-fi novels are succeeding as series, and the medium seems to suit their stories better than movies would have. It may be that in a few years, we'll look back and talk about animated adaptations in the same way.

Animation is a natural choice for many of the best sci-fi and fantasy books, especially if the adaptations are going to rely heavily on CGI. These stories could look beautiful in the hands of talented artists and animators, while voice actors could bring the characters to life. Sadly, animation is still seen as a medium for children, or for cheap, niche projects. If Hollywood can shift its attitude towards animation the way it did with TV adaptations, we could enter a whole new golden age of sci-fi and fantasy on the screen. This practice could reign in some of the unbelievable budgets monopolizing the industry and put creative control back in the hands of a small, nimble team again.

That won't be the style for this upcoming adaptation of Red Rising, but it's good to know that the option is still there. So far there's no word on when the movie will start production or when it might hit theaters. In the meantime, there are six novels in the Red Rising saga available now in print, digital, and audiobook formats. Brown has been hard at work on the seventh and final novel, and could announce its publication date any day now.

#3373. Russell Brand Was Sentenced for Rape and Sexual Assault on Monday. By Friday, Netflix Had a Sleazy Doc Ready to Go

The term that comes to mind most is “ambulance-chasing.” Earlier this week, just one week after Russell Brand was convicted of rape and sexual assault and two days after he was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for his crimes, word spread that Netflix was prepping a documentary on the comedian-turned-criminal.

Olivia Isaacs’ documentary has been in the works for a while. Deadline’s initial story on the project even noted that it “was referenced during the trial” and that while “giving evidence at London’s Southwark Crown Court, Mark Pinheiro, a former friend of Brand, said he had been approached by a producer about the Netflix show.” Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

But that the project — “Russell Brand: Open Secret,” a slim and unfocused documentary feature that clocks in at just under 90 minutes — was being dropped on the streamer to ride the wave of interest after Brand’s conviction and sentencing felt distasteful. How essential, after all, could this be? And what could it tell us about Brand’s actual trial, sentencing, and conviction?

Turns out, not much. Isaacs’ film doesn’t get into the trial until its final five minutes (counting its end credits to boot), when it uses title cards to share the conviction news, note that all of the allegations contained in the film itself “pre-date” those that led to the conviction, and make clear that Brand’s legal team was contacted after the Monday conviction and chose not to respond. That’s perhaps the most interesting part of the film’s literally tacked-on final moments: a desire to show its work when it comes to the journalism and attendant standards behind Brand’s long-simmering takedown.

Other elements are far less successful, as Isaacs’ film leans hard on tired tropes and cloying conventions. Captions frequently mention “[unsettling music playing]” or “[dramatic music playing]” during the most benign moments. Old footage of Brand, from home video to early stand-up gigs, is played slowly, all the better to maximize the sense that something is wrong with this man. Far more effective are interviews with those who were allegedly victimized by Brand, but those are often drowned out by played-out techniques.

The film opens with a typical “rise and fall” style montage, charting Brand’s humble beginnings, meteoric rise to fame, profound injection into the cultural consciousness (he met the queen! and also Tom Cruise!), stumble into right-wing ideology, and eventual criminal convictions for horrific acts the film posits everyone knew about forever.

It is, after all, called “Russell Brand: Open Secret.”

Isaacs’ film lacks a thesis beyond the general idea that everyone knew Brand was a creep from the jump. She assembles a hodgepodge of talking heads to hammer that home, including fellow comedians, some genuinely freaked out ex-girlfriends, a handful of accusers (including one who, reticent to appear on camera, is replaced with an actress, one of the film’s most thoughtful choices), and some bizarrely starry-eyed commentators (journalist George Monbiot comes across particularly badly here, zipping from talking about his early delight in Brand and his now-held belief that Brand’s far-right switch is the most horrifying aspect of all of this, oof).

Most compelling are Times journalists Rosamund Urwin and Charlotte Wace, who worked tirelessly to investigate myriad accusations against Brand for years (Urwin first began to look into Brand in January of 2019). Even smushed up against a herky-jerky timeline and a loose sense of purpose, the way that Urwin and Wace talk about the precise nature of their work, what they can and cannot report, the women they spoke to, and the ways in which they were nearly shut down (and, in fact, many other investigations of its ilk were allegedly turned off) is both gripping and necessary.

With more time and better access, the film could have focused more on the police and legal minds that helped build the case against Brand, but in the rush to get this out in the world, that was surely not a major aim.

By its midpoint, Isaacs’ film turns its lens on the culture that helped give rise to Brand, the wild “noughties” when “ladette culture” ruled and being overtly sexy and crude was de rigueur. Women were into Brand! Being ruthlessly unfunny and breathlessly boorish was hot! Also, his dad was mean to him! Diddy and David Walliams jump scares! These are some of the insights on offer in “Open Secret,” and the only thing truly revealing about them is how huge of a mistake it was to let someone as outwardly disgusting and deeply unwitty as Brand get into a place where he could pick and choose his “damsels” or his “whores,” depending on who is talking about them.

The film speed-runs through the last few years of Brand’s life and career, as he pivots into far-right shock politics and Christianity just as the walls are starting to close in on him. Brand may have alleged that his former cadre of famous friends and stalwarts won’t “touch him with a barge pole” these days, but the film’s distinct lack of bigger talking heads stands out. That could stand some further interrogation, too, but there’s simply no time for that. (Well, there is, but not if you want to be a part of this news cycle.)

The four-day gap between Brand’s conviction and the film’s release is zippy, even for Netflix, which has gotten progressively speedier with its true crime joints. In July of 2024, it was announced that Netflix would release a multi-part Karen Read documentary, just days after her first murder trial ended in a mistrial due to a hung jury on July 1, 2024. Three episodes dropped earlier this month.

In January of 2026, the streamer announced a Lucy Letby project with “unprecedented access” after the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) announced it would bring no further criminal charges against the former nurse, who was sentenced to life imprisonment for a slew of charges of murder and attempted murder of infants in her care following a review of additional allegations. “The Truth and Tragedy of Moriah Wilson” was first publicly announced in February of 2026, almost three years after Kaitlin Armstrong was convicted of first-degree murder of the cyclist in November of 2023.

“Russell Brand: Open Secret” will surely capture lots of eyeballs as this part of the news cycle winds down, but what the film trades for immediacy, it more than loses in actual insight. Part two can’t be far behind. Let’s just hope it takes far more time to make and far more consideration to craft.

“Russell Brand: Open Secret” is now streaming on Netflix.

#3371. Battle Royale Told A More Brutal Version Of The Hunger Games 12 Years Earlier

Japanese cinema offered a rendition of The Hunger Games 12 years earlier, and it’s so much more intense. Young adult dystopian fiction has produced some of the most successful entertainment franchises of the 21st century. Few have made a bigger impression than The Hunger Games, Suzanne Collins' bestselling book series and its hugely successful film adaptations.

The Hunger Games franchise established a distinctive formula for dystopian blockbuster filmmaking, combining political commentary with high-stakes survival drama. However, the idea of forcing young people to fight one another to the death in a government-controlled competition wasn't new when Collins introduced Panem. In fact, a Japanese filmmaker had already explored a remarkably similar premise, taking it in a considerably more violent and disturbing direction.

Released more than a decade before the first Hunger Games movie, Battle Royale is one of the most provocative dystopian movies ever made. Its influence and similarities to Collins' franchise continue to invite comparisons, particularly among those who want something considerably more brutal after finishing Katniss Everdeen's story.

Directed by Kinji Fukasaku in 2000, Battle Royale adapted Koushun Takami's 1999 novel of the same name. The premise will sound immediately familiar to anyone who has watched The Hunger Games: a totalitarian government selects a group of teenagers, transports them to an isolated location, and forces them to fight until only one remains alive. However, while Katniss Everdeen enters the arena as part of a televised competition, the students in Battle Royale are victims of a government program intended to terrorize an increasingly rebellious younger generation.

Battle Royale centers on a class of 42 junior high school students who are abducted during a school trip and transported to an island. Their former teacher, Kitano, explains that they have been selected under the Battle Royale Act, a government policy that forces one school class to participate in a three-day fight to the death. Each student receives supplies and a randomly assigned weapon, while explosive collars ensure nobody can simply refuse to participate or escape.

The basic mechanics are remarkably similar to The Hunger Games, but Fukasaku's film makes the experience considerably less like a sporting event. There are no elaborate opening ceremonies, celebrity stylists, or opportunities to cultivate public affection. The teenagers are simply abandoned with instructions to kill their classmates, and the government expects them to comply.

Rather than turning violence into an elaborate national spectacle, it presents the competition as a bleak institutional punishment designed to demonstrate the consequences of challenging authority.

One of the most obvious differences between Battle Royale and The Hunger Games is their respective approaches to violence. The Hunger Games certainly contains disturbing material, particularly considering its teenage characters, but its PG-13 classification required fairly restrained bloodshed. Fukasaku, meanwhile, makes little effort to soften the brutality.

Students are shot, stabbed, beaten, and blown apart, with Battle Royale frequently emphasizing the physical consequences of each confrontation. Its violence isn't restricted to the anonymous background deaths of characters audiences barely know, either. Fukasaku gives several students individual personalities and relationships before subjecting them to sudden, shocking deaths. The contrast between their ordinary teenage lives and the savagery of the competition is precisely what makes it so uncomfortable.

The sudden deaths reinforce how little control the students have over their circumstances. Even characters who initially appear confident or capable of surviving can be killed within moments, often by people they previously considered friends. The arbitrary distribution of weapons makes matters worse, ensuring that some students begin with a significant advantage over others.

There is also a particularly nasty sense of unpredictability to the film's violence. The Hunger Games establishes a more conventional progression of alliances, confrontations, and strategic eliminations, whereas Battle Royale frequently allows paranoia and panic to dictate what happens next.

Despite their obvious similarities, Battle Royale and The Hunger Games approach their dystopian settings from different political perspectives. Both examine authoritarian governments that maintain control through fear, using young people as instruments of state power. However, The Hunger Games focuses particularly on class inequality, propaganda, and the exploitation of poverty.

Panem's Hunger Games are an annual reminder of the Capitol's victory over the rebellious districts. The wealthy citizens are encouraged to treat the deaths of teenagers as entertainment, while the impoverished districts are forced to sacrifice their children.

Battle Royale, by contrast, focuses more on generational conflict and the breakdown of trust between adults and children. Its fictional government responds to fears about juvenile delinquency by introducing a policy that effectively declares an entire generation expendable. The students are punished collectively, regardless of whether they have actually committed any wrongdoing.

Battle Royale doesn’t present a conventional heroic rebellion but rather examines what happens when a society teaches its children to distrust one another. Its characters are frequently frightened, selfish, impulsive, and emotionally overwhelmed, which makes them seem considerably closer to ordinary teenagers than the increasingly strategic competitors of Panem.

For anyone who loves The Hunger Games, Battle Royale is a perfect next watch because it offers the deadly survival premise in a much less sanitized form. Both put teenagers in situations where survival means confronting people they know, but Battle Royale’s approach makes the psychological and physical consequences much more immediate. There is no glamorous preparation for the competition, no carefully managed public image, and no expectation that the contestants will become celebrities.

The Hunger Games examines how an authoritarian government uses spectacle and propaganda to maintain power, whereas Battle Royale spotlights the destruction of trust between ordinary people. The films also make an interesting double feature because their protagonists respond to institutional cruelty in different ways.

Katniss gradually becomes a symbol of rebellion, while Shuya and Noriko are primarily concerned with surviving. As a result, Battle Royale is particularly valuable for anyone interested in dystopian narratives that don’t adhere to classic Hollywood blockbuster storytelling.

Battle Royale is particularly effective at exploring the emotional consequences of its premise without turning every character into a perfectly calculated survivalist. The friendships, romances, jealousies, and petty disagreements that define school life don't suddenly disappear when the students are given weapons. Instead, those familiar relationships become the foundation for some of the film's most upsetting moments.

Ultimately, Battle Royale deserves to be watched on its own merits rather than simply as the Japanese predecessor to The Hunger Games. Its examination of institutional cruelty, teenage alienation, and the destructive consequences of authoritarianism gives it considerably more substance than its notorious reputation for violence might suggest. Fans of The Hunger Games adventures will recognize plenty of familiar ideas, but Fukasaku's film takes them somewhere much darker.

The Hunger Games is the first of four in the action-drama movie series based on the novels by Suzanne Collins. Set in a dystopian world where people are separated into twelve districts to maintain order, this first film in the franchise focuses on Katniss Everdeen as she is forced to participate in The Hunger Games: a draconian gladiatorial survival event where there can be only one winner.

The dystopian action movie Battle Royale takes place in a future Japan, where a group of high school students fight to the death in a deserted island until only one survivor remains. Directed by Kinji Fukasaku, the 2000 film gave rise to a whole genre of similar stories such as the Hunger Games books and movies, as well as the video game Fortnite.

#3369. Will ‘Dune’ and ‘Avengers’ Drown Out Everything Else at the Box Office This Christmas?

Look, it’s only November, but we know we’re not the only people getting excited about Christmas already. In fact, we know that some studio executives have been thinking about the holiday season a lot for a while now. That’s because they know as well as anyone that they have two juggernauts to contend with: “Dune: Part Three” and “Avengers: Doomsday,” which open on Dec. 18 in true clash of the titans fashion.

There’s a question that if those movies take up so much oxygen, will there be room for anything else? The last “Dune” movie surpassed $700 million globally at the box office, and “Avengers: Doomsday” has already sold over $60 million in pre-sales. Those top two titles create enormous competition for everything opening on Christmas weekend itself. Those include the Dwayne Johnson threequel “Jumanji: Open World” from Sony, the football biopic “Mr. Irrelevant” from Paramount, Robert Eggers’ horror film “Werwulf” from Focus, and Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” from Neon. Paramount’s “The Angry Birds Movie 3” is also opening on December 23 just ahead of the rest. Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

Anyone will tell you the Christmas holiday is always crowded at the movies. And there’s usually room for multiple blockbusters to draw crowds. Despite the onslaught of new titles, U.S, distributors are confident they’ll be able to secure the screens they need to be successful. For instance, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” this year opened at the end of July to $360 million domestic, and “The Odyssey” in its third week in theaters still made $50 million. Even during the “Barbenheimer” weekend, “Sound of Freedom” in its third week managed to bring in another $19.8 million. There’s always opportunity if the demand is there.

Recent Christmases have been similarly crowded. Last year had “Avatar: Fire and Ash,” “The Housemaid,” a new “Spongebob,” and “Marty Supreme” open the weekend before Christmas, then “Anaconda” and “Song Sung Blue” over the holiday itself. 2024 had “Mufasa: The Lion King,” “Nosferatu,” “Sonic the Hedgehog 3,” “A Complete Unknown,” “Babygirl,” and “The Fire Inside” all in a short span just before Xmas.

But this Christmas does bring some unique challenges that studios are preemptively working around for their titles that are not “Dune” or “Avengers.” Both of those films have had tickets on sale for months, and both are locked in a fight for premium large format screens that distributors would be lying to say they didn’t want, even if it’s for a family film that doesn’t need it. Warner Bros. and Legendary’s “Dune: Part Three” specifically will exclusively be on IMAX screens, which has famously left “Doomsday” without them, leaving Disney to create its Infinity Vision certification to drum up excitement.

To compete, “Angry Birds 3” is still opening in 3D if on otherwise standard format screens. “Werwulf” won’t have IMAX as Focus did for “Nosferatu,” but it has pre-sold select 35mm screenings of the film that have already done quite well (they went on sale on the full moon last month). The hope, too, is that titles like “Jumanji” and “Mr. Irrelevant” appeal to crowds that are distinctive from the male, fanboy-heavy audiences for “Dunesday.”

One source IndieWire spoke with argued that even though this Christmas is top heavy, it’s arguably lighter in sheer quantity than we’ve seen in recent years. What we’re not seeing is a movie like “Marty Supreme” or “Uncut Gems” getting a run in a more mid-size or limited number of screens. Universal doesn’t have a movie opening in that window, nor does Amazon MGM. Other awards titles like “The Debut” from A24 are going earlier in the month and aren’t doing the limited, Christmas day, qualifying run before going wide in January (GKIDS’ “Look Back” may be an exception, opening December 30).

There are some potential holdovers that could generate money well into Christmas. Rival studio execs are keeping an eye on movies like Disney’s animated “Hexed” or Universal’s “Focker-in-Law,” and Focus’ “Elsinore” will also be going wider shortly before the holidays.

The hope now is that all of these films get their flowers and collectively put an exclamation point on a stellar 2026, with the box office now projected to finish far above $10 billion domestic, a number that might’ve been a pipe dream this time in 2025. That’s reason for holiday cheer, indeed.

#3368. The 8 Greatest Vampire Books Released Since 'Dracula', Ranked

The vampire is one of the most enduring monsters in fiction, shifting in step with the times. Supernatural bloodsuckers have existed in folklore for centuries, but they took their core modern form in Bram Stoker's seminal Dracula back in 1897. Since then, countless writers have built on, tweaked, or subverted those ideas over the last 129 years.

This list looks at the finest of those books released in the wake of Dracula, from the blockbuster dark fantasy of Empire of the Vampire to the small-town horror of Salem's Lot. Some of the titles below retain the traditional Gothic atmosphere, while others incorporate sci-fi, psychological horror, historical fiction, or character study.

"Too much hate will burn a man to cinders." Empire of the Vampire is a great hybrid of vampire tropes and epic fantasy, courtesy of Jay Kristoff, author of Nevernight and The Lotus War. The story takes place in a high fantasy world decades after a mysterious catastrophe known as Daysdeath obscured the sun, allowing vampires to emerge from the shadows and conquer much of human civilization. Its protagonist, Gabriel de León, is a former member of the Silver Order, an organization of warriors trained to hunt the undead.

Imprisoned by his enemies, Gabriel recounts his extraordinary life to a vampire historian, from his upbringing and military exploits to his desperate quest to recover humanity's last hope. The atmosphere is delectably Gothic the whole way through, and elevated by intricate, lovingly crafted worldbuilding. For instance, the different vampire bloodlines all have distinct powers and belief systems.

"Do you see? I am a vampire." This book was an important milestone in the development of vampires in popular fiction, even years before the blockbuster movie adaptation. In particular, it broke ground by treating its bloodsuckers as psychologically complex protagonists capable of guilt, desire, existential despair, and perhaps even growth. The plot focuses on Louis de Pointe du Lac, a vampire who tells his life story to a young journalist in modern-day San Francisco.

Louis is a compelling protagonist. He struggles with the moral implications of his existence, repeatedly questioning whether his need to consume human blood makes him fundamentally evil. Lestat, meanwhile, embraces immortality with an enthusiasm that both fascinates and horrifies his companion. On top of that, the book throws in a powerful sensual and romantic subtext, which would greatly influence the genre going forward.

"Innocence ain't all it's cracked up to be." Layered characters and genuine horror are the name of the game here. This banger from Joe Hill (the mind behind Horns and King Sorrow) follows Victoria McQueen, a young woman who discovers that she has the power to locate lost objects by riding her bicycle across a mysterious covered bridge. This unusual talent eventually brings her into conflict with Charlie Manx, a seemingly immortal predator who abducts children and transports them to a nightmarish supernatural realm.

Manx travels in a sinister Rolls-Royce Wraith, using his vehicle to drain the life from his victims while maintaining his unnatural longevity. NOS4A2 is a fresh riff on vampire mythology. Just like traditional vampires, Manx grows decrepit and weak when he goes too long without feeding, but he consumes souls directly rather than drinking blood, and behaves more like a serial killer from a thriller than one of the alluring yet dangerous vampires of yore.

"Dusk is the time when men whisper of matters about which they remain silent in the full light of the sun." This one is a little more obscure, but it has something of a cult following. The main character is Richard Fountain, a brilliant young Cambridge scholar who travels to Greece and becomes tangled up with a mysterious, mesmerizing, dangerous woman named Chriseis. Soon, he'staking part in twisted, sadistic rituals, and his friends, growing concerned, set out in search of him.

Instead of playing that premise as pulp and relying on conventional Gothic imagery, the book distinguishes itself through its unusual combination of intellectual sophistication and provocative subject matter, especially for 1960. Doctors Wear Scarlet explores the psychological dimensions of vampirism, leaning hard into obsession, control, forbidden desires, and the darker impulses concealed beneath respectable social masks.

"The world was gone, and he was alone." This classic greatly influenced both vampire and zombie fiction. Most notably, it was the first vampire story to strip away the magic and make its bloodsuckers the result of a global pandemic, a conceit that pretty much spawned a new subgenre unto itself. At the center of the plot is survivor Robert Neville, who lives alone in a fortified house, spending his days gathering supplies, researching the disease, and hunting the infected.

At night, he barricades himself indoors while the vampires gather outside, attempting to lure him into their clutches. Much of the suspense comes from watching Neville's attempts to understand the biological mechanisms behind the creatures' behavior. In this approach, I Am Legend takes the themes of superstition-versus-science even further than Dracula originally did, culminating in a punchy, unforgettable ending that remains subversive and iconic.

"Some nights the darkness comes down so thick you can almost taste it." Set in 1857, Fevre Dream follows Abner Marsh, a struggling steamboat captain whose fortunes change when he is hired by a mysterious gentleman named Joshua York. However, Abner becomes increasingly suspicious of Joshua's peculiar habits, particularly his secretive conversations and aversion to sunlight.

Long before finding mainstream success with A Game of Thrones, George R. R. Martin penned one of the richest and most immersive vampire novels of the late 20th century. While some of the plot mechanics are familiar, the backdrop is unique: the action unfolds on boats navigating the Mississippi River in the antebellum era. That setting feels really authentic. Not to mention, Martin also hits hard with the themes. For instance, he presents philosophies concerning the relationship between humanity and its supernatural predators.

"To flee is life. To linger, death." Most readers will be familiar with the brilliant film adaptation, but many won't be aware that Let the Right One In was originally a book. Set in the Stockholm suburb of Blackeberg during the early 1980s, the novel follows Oskar, a bullied twelve-year-old boy whose miserable existence begins changing when he befriends Eli, a mysterious child who has recently moved into his apartment complex. Needless to say, she turns out to be a vampire.

In contrast to most vampire fiction in the 2000s, Let the Right One In does not romanticize the monster. Eli's existence is defined by violence and isolation, becoming a mirror to the ordinary people around her, who also struggle with addiction, exploitation, despair, and inner darkness. The relationship between Oskar and Eli forms the heart of the story, developing into a complicated friendship at once tender and deeply unsettling.

"The town knew about darkness." This book has been described as "Peyton Place meets Dracula", and that's exactly right. Stephen King's sophomore (published) novel is one of his strongest, fusing vampire mythology with realistic small-town drama. It's an ensemble piece, but the central character is Ben Mears, a novelist who returns to the town of Jerusalem's Lot, Maine, hoping to confront traumatic memories from his childhood. However, his arrival coincides with the appearance of two sinister newcomers, Richard Straker and Kurt Barlow.

Soon afterward, residents begin disappearing or exhibiting strange behavior, slowly becoming an army of the undead. Again, that could easily have become a schlocky penny dreadful, but King makes it vastly more interesting because the community feels real. He paints a sprawling, convincing portrait of ordinary people, marked by complicated relationships and private resentments. This meticulous development makes the town's gradual destruction all the more horrifying.

#3363. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.
