Elden Ring may very well be FromSoftware's magnum opus, a feat that has, consequently, led to it getting numerous spin-offs, expanded media releases, and merchandise, all of which are treasured by fans worldwide. From its game-sized DLC to the highly anticipated big-budget Elden Ring movie, there truly is no escaping the magnitude of this incredible game. So, perhaps it should come as no surprise that fans are being treated to yet another Elden Ring release in 2027.

It comes at a rather opportune moment, as fans have been left waiting for the next FromSoftware game and the ever-elusive Bloodborne sequel that will, surely, release at some point. This new release, aptly titled Raging Wolf, looks absolutely incredible and will almost assuredly be the centerpiece of any fan's collection. However, as is often typical of Elden Ring merchandise, it comes with a rather significant caveat that fans should be aware of.

The Raging Wolf release joins a pantheon of upcoming Elden Ring merchandise that has fans excited, if only because it means even more statues to adorn one's shelf with. It is a 1/6 scale statue of the game's protagonist, the Tarnished, wearing the iconic Raging Wolf armor set as seen on the game's box art. Produced by premium figurine manufacturer GECCO with close supervision from FromSoftware, this is a premium statue, packed with details that fans are sure to appreciate.

The Elden Ring: Raging Wolf statue comes fully painted, with everything from the scales on the metal armor to the leather straps beneath expertly sculpted. Even the statue's base has had additional consideration given to it, as it has been designed to resemble the path leading to the legendary Stormveil Castle. This is truly a piece of Elden Ring merchandise designed for and aimed at fans, something that is unequivocally represented in the Raging Wolf statue's exorbitant price.

If you want to pick up this 1/6 scale statue (which is approximately 12.9 inches tall), you'll need to spend an eye-watering $469.99. Of course, you're getting an intricately detailed and painted statue for that price, something that typically does not come cheap. Still, it's an expensive purchase, and one that is definitely targeting dedicated fans with a lot of disposable income. For those ready to take the plunge, you can pre-order it right now via the official Bandai Namco website.

The Elden Ring: Raging Wolf statue has a tentative release date of January 30, 2027. This is according to the countdown on the official Bandai Namco store listing for the statue. However, this is, as always, subject to change, and the statue's release date could be further delayed.

Regardless, there isn't too long to wait until you can get your hands on this incredible new Elden Ring statue. Of course, one can hope that, beyond the likes of these highly detailed and niche collectibles, FromSoftware elects to release another game within the Elden Ring series, or, indeed, elevates its ideas in an altogether new IP.

#3360. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

#3359. IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More

IndieWire, the definitive outlet for creative independence in film and TV, announced on Friday, November 13 the lineup for the Winter 2026 edition of our IndieWire Honors event, featuring our largest lineup yet of film honorees. Curated and selected by IndieWire’s editorial team, IndieWire Honors is a celebration of the filmmakers, actors, and artisans key to crafting some of the most exciting cinematic works this year.

The event will take place on Thursday, December 3 in Los Angeles, starting with an intimate cocktail reception and awards ceremony. IndieWire will also begin rolling out exclusive editorial content, including honoree profiles, on Friday, November 27 through the lead-up to the awards night. Throughout the ceremony, into the next day, IndieWire will publish photos and exclusive social content from the event as well. The ceremony’s host will be announced at a later date. Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

“It’s thrilling to be able to recognize the artists behind so many of this year’s most exciting and compelling films,” said Brent Lang, IndieWire’s editor-in-chief. “They dazzled us with their talent, inspired us with their willingness to take risks, and left an indelible mark on cinema. We are excited to celebrate their accomplishments.”

“It’s exciting to celebrate such an eclectic group of film talent for this year’s IndieWire Honors,” said James Israel, IndieWire’s SVP and Publisher. “We are also pleased to continue to celebrate top craft artisans in entertainment.”

The Winter 2026 IndieWire Honors honorees are:

The fact that he is known for being a frequent collaborator of both Spike Lee and the Coen brothers conveys just how expansive an actor Turturro is. The Brooklyn native is quintessentially New York, as most recently proven in Sony Pictures Classics’ acclaimed Sundance premiere “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” written and directed by Noah Segan. Yet, a filmmaker can still drop the performer into the corporate dystopia of sci-fi series “Severance,” or have him go on a Southern odyssey in “O Brother, Where Art Thou?,” and he just as well hits it out of the park.

With nearly five decades of film work under his belt, starting with an uncredited role in “Raging Bull,” Turturro manages to be one of the few veteran actors who continues to best himself year after year.

The pair of Madrid-based directors colloquially known as Los Javis are not shy about cluing the audience in on the shoulders upon which they stand on. They cast Penélope Cruz and Lola Dueñas, two muses of auteur Pedro Almodóvar, as the most important women within their epic adaptation of an unfinished play by Federico García Lorca, another one of Spain’s queer artist forefathers. That reverence is balanced by the confidence in their own eye for new talent, weaving together three different timelines led by three relative unknowns, including most notably, indie musician Guitarricadelafuente, who also contributed the poignant original song “La Nieve” to the project.

Made outside the Hollywood system and chosen to represent Spain in the Best International Feature Oscar race, the Netflix release “La Bola Negra” is a film of immense scale. If viewers knew nothing of the director duo before seeing the film, they come away with a crash course in everything they are about. Considering how they won both the Best Director Award at Cannes, and the coveted People’s Choice Award at TIFF, it seems to be an experience most cinephiles enjoy.

“Tallgrass” is the code word that unlocks what makes the creative collaboration between “Paper Tiger” writer-director James Gray and star Adam Driver such a feat. Though the Neon release, which premiered at Cannes, is their first time ever working together, the filmmaker imbues the two-time Oscar nominee with such a specific vision of what it feels like to realize one’s time has gone by. Though the film is another deeply personal work in the oeuvre of the Queens-born auteur, Driver adds a more broad portrait of a figure wrapped up in crime, slowly feeling the overwhelming situation constrict and constrict.

“Josephine” was not made to be an easy watch, but boasts the rare feat of winning both the Grand Jury Prize and Audience Award at the Sundance Film Festival. Written and directed by Araújo, and starring Gemma Chan and Mason Reeves as mother and daughter, the drama is a bold exploration of how little control parents have over their children being confronted by certain horrors in life that there’s no guarantee of avoiding.

An early release for new distributor Sumerian Pictures, “Josephine” has only felt more necessary as the year has gone on, and news stories like the Cornell rape case have come to the forefront. It is a conversation piece about a subject many wish to evade, that puts forth the effort to reach meaningful discourse.

The most bold artistic choice in “Artificial,” the latest film from prolific director Luca Guadagnino, is to not proffer any romance in becoming one of the Promethean figures. The repeated refrain of “Feel the AGI” rings as a benevolent threat by the time the two hours and 20 minutes of the Neon release are over. Garfield, Borisov, Barbaro, and Barinholtz, all four playing key figures in the genesis of OpenAI, play incredibly off of each other as tech titans forcing a smile as they convince their audience artificial technology is inevitable. Join or die. Their joint efforts to invoke a common sense of humanity would be funny if the reality of the situation weren’t so uncanny.

Re-teaming with her “Secret Sunshine” director Lee Chang-dong almost 20 years later, the “Possible Love” star is unmissable as a woman caught in a class divide between her blue collar, out-of-work husband, and the couple that hosts them as a means to interview them for a documentary. It is a role that she said uses “the whole entirety of her body” to push back against the weight of capitalism. The Netflix film chosen to represent South Korea in the Best International Feature category at the 2027 Oscars offers a feast of ideas, with Jeon’s layered turn as Mi-ok alone being enough fodder for many conversations to come.

All sorts of biopics enter theaters each year, but few task their leads with the difficult job of playing someone still actively in the public eye. In Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” from Amazon MGM Studios, newcomer Ippolito deftly captures the distinctive look and sound of a young and hungry Sylvester Stallone. But what is more impressive than that form of transformation is how the 27-year-old actor captures the spirit of the unlikely star and scribe of the 1977 Best Picture winner. How some of his best moments come when he himself plays Rocky is a meta element we are still unpacking, but add it to the overwhelming evidence that Ippolito is one to watch.

There is a standout moment in Oscar winner Siân Heder’s “Being Heumann” in which Madeley, as trailblazing disability rights activist Judy Heumann, asks a well-meaning congressman what he means by calling her “inspiring.” “Inspired to do what?,” she says. It is a moment that clarifies that the film about Heumann leading the successful protest to get the government to sign Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act is not standard fare about a woman in a wheelchair overcoming odds, but a film about her refusing to let those odds overcome her.

Madeley embodies a fight against circumstances that applies to more than just the disability community. May casting directors take notice of the limitless potential she offers as part of any type of ensemble.

As the President and CEO of Laika Studios, Knight has spent over 20 years educating audiences on the artform of stop-motion animation. And still, in his latest film “Wildwood,” a fantasy epic taking place in the forests outside Portland, Oregon, Knight directs scenes that seem inexplicable. It is hard enough to animate one bird flying, using that technique, yet the Fathom Entertainment release sees whole flocks fly off toward a war between species. The film’s commentary on parents and children is as heartrending as the craft behind how the film was made is genuinely inspiring to filmmakers of all types.

Talk about legacy. Decades after his father, noted documentarian William Greaves, hosted a party for the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” co-directed finished the film, one of the gems of Sundance 2026. To listen to Black luminaries from the ‘20s speak about how their work has endured into the ‘70s, with the dramatic irony of watching the film through a modern lens, is a singular cinematic experience. In a year where there is so much conversation around what pushes the documentary artform forward, the Neon release delivers both necessary context and innovation.

There is humor in having puppetry, one of the world’s oldest artforms, at the center of a conversation around innovation, but come on. Ortiz’s performance as Rocky in “Project Hail Mary,” supported by the work of visual effects team leaders Scanlan, Lambert, and Sarnowska, made us fall in love with a spidery alien rock that has no mouth or face. Puppetry’s forebearers would have still found that to be an insurmountable challenge. Hence, why the artist behind the fan favorite character opposite Ryan Gosling in the Amazon MGM Studios blockbuster deserves their flowers for helping viewers go beyond their earthly imaginations.

#3358. Marvel's New Villains Are The Game-Changing Opposite Of Hydra

Warning! This post contains SPOILERS for Captain America #17

Marvel has just debuted the game-changing opposite of Hydra. Of course, Hydra has been one of the Marvel Universe's most enduring villain organizations and a classic foe of Captain America. However, it looks as though Steve Rogers will soon be facing an all-new threat, one that hits much closer to home in the pages of Marvel Comics.

In the past, Hydra's primary mission has been global dominance in a bid to assert its fascist ideals and order across the entire globe. They've existed for millennia, a cabal that refuses to die even in the Marvel Universe's modern era. However, a brand-new villain organization has just been revealed in the pages of the new Captain America #17 by writer Chip Zdarsky with art by Ton Lima.

Having already kidnapped a major Avenger with teases about their dark leader, here's everything we know about Marvel's new villain group known as the Knomads, and how they differ from Hydra.

As seen in Captain America #17, the Knomads' debut quickly establishes them as a significant threat with the reveal that they've kidnapped Tony Stark's Iron Man, explaining why Steve Rogers has been unable to contact his fellow Avenger. Its members are shown wearing simple white masks, with one of the Knomads claiming that people like Stark are a symptom of a dying United States. They then threaten to "drag his corpse through the streets of the country he's fed off for far too long" if Iron Man doesn't provide the intel they're after.

Combined with some synopses and promotional material, it seems the Knomads are motivated by an American nationalist agenda to "make their country great again", as opposed to Hydra's wider goals of full worldwide supremacy.

While both factions seem to share a focus on imposing their respective versions of order, the Knomads are specifically focused on one nation in particular (their own). Likewise, kidnapping an Avenger as powerful and influential as Tony Stark indicates that they're well organized and have major plans to enforce their vision beyond just being a fringe political movement. This is likely thanks to the man who's already been teased as their dark leader in the Marvel Universe: Grant Rogers.

The Knomads' introduction goes hand in hand with the ending twist in Captain America #17, with the reveal that it is not Steve Rogers on the run and protecting the young clone of Victor von Doom, but Grant Rogers, the former Hydra Captain America from Marvel's Secret Empire storyline. While he had most recently been a Flag-Smasher, it seems Grant has started impersonating Steve once again, having taken Steve's shield and sharing his twisted takes on American values with Vic throughout, likely in a bid to corrupt and shape the young clone into a Doctor Doom for America.

Identify the cover art while scratching off as little foil as possible.

Sure enough, the cover art for Captain America #18 sees Grant dressed as Captain America with Knomds flanking either side. Seeing as how Nomad was once a name used by Steve himself when he was a "man without a country", it's more than likely that even the Knomads' name is another weapon to tarnish and corrupt Steve's legacy. Rather than leading Hydra as he once did, Grant is shifting his tactics to leading an aggressive nationalist faction, which should prove darkly fascinating.

Across the board, all signs are pointing to the next issues of Captain America having a heavy focus on the corruption of patriotism, its symbols, and American values overall. With Tony Stark's Iron Man already in the Knomads' hands, Marvel's newest villain organization feels perfectly positioned to make their presence felt across the entire superhero community at large, especially with a global ban on superpowers having just been instigated by the United Nations (except for America).

#3356. Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

From the misty seaports of Massachusetts seaports to the otherworldly town of Twin Peaks and even the distant shores of Troy, Ruth De Jong has spent the past twenty years transporting audiences into the unforgettable worlds created by auteur directors like Paul Thomas Anderson, Terrence Malick, Kenneth Lonergan, David Lynch, Jordan Peele, and Christopher Nolan.

“My goal in my work is to always paint the most authentic pictures,” De Jong shared with IndieWire at the Virginia Film Festival, where the production designer received the festival’s Craft Award. The town of Charlottesville has a special place in De Jong’s heart.

It’s here where legendary production designer Jack Fisk, father of De Jong’s high school friend Schuyler Fisk, suggested she forgo attending the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts for grad school in favor of working on the set of Paul Thomas Anderson’s 2007 Oscar-winning film “There Will Be Blood” instead. Recalling that fateful conversation, De Jong said that Fisk told her he saw the younger version of himself in her, sharing, “I think what the world continually needs are mentors [like Fisk] showing up.” Related Stories After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More

De Jong fell in love with filmmaking as she continued to work with Fisk on Anderson’s “The Master,” and a handful of films by Terence Malick, including his Palme d’Or winner “The Tree of Life.” Eventually she spread her wings and took on her first film as production designer: Kenneth Lonergan’s “Manchester by the Sea.” Looking back on these early days and everything she learned on those sets, De Jong said that she believes “a body of work like that is built upon itself. I think I’m constantly pulling from the past, but also pulling from the future.”

Whether designing a fishing village in modern-day Gloucester, recreating the White House Oval Office, or crafting the iconic Trojan horse, all of De Jong’s work comes in service of the characters and story being told. While crafting a film’s world, De Jong asks herself, “How do I make this tangible and alive and real and authentic?”

To capture undertones of the real working-class people in the fishing community at the center of “Manchester by the Sea,” this meant spending time with local fishermen. “We asked if we could go into their houses. We asked if we could use their fishing boats. We asked if we could use their lobster cages and rope everything, and then we would,” De Jong recalled. All of this research helped De Jong nail the subtle nuances and layers of the region. “You’re always striving to not make it cliché,” De Jong told IndieWire.

The first step involves breaking down the script. At this phase of her process, De Jong attaches an image to each scene. “It may be a piece of art. It could be a photograph. It could be a texture. It could be a piece of cloth. It could be anything,” she shared, adding, “Then from that, I add physical locations, and we start putting the whole thing together and seeing our film.”

Sometimes these images come from the director themselves. While working on “Twin Peaks: The Return,” David Lynch gave De Jong some of his own artwork for inspiration. “He would hand me some of his paintings, his drawings, his work, and say, ‘Here, this is this set. Build that,,’” De Jong revealed, adding that even if it was “a flat 2D painting, the colors were wild and it’s textural.” These came in handy for the new worlds of the series, like the landmark Episode 8 (also known as “Gotta Light?”), in which De Jong designed the radio station and other eerier riffs on the atomic age 1950s.

For the more iconic aspects of “Twin Peaks, ” De Jong also dug up the original plans for the Red Room from the 1990s. “David remembered in his mind’s eye,” De Jong said, “and I’m there to continue to be David’s conduit on the new work. It was just a beautiful, beautiful dance.”

Along with reviving iconic sets from pop culture’s past, De Jong herself has created work that has become part of the entertainment firmament. The set she created for the “Jupiter’s Claim” theme park in Jordan Peele’s “Nope” has been added to the Studio Tour at Universal Studios Hollywood, a unique feat for an aspect of filmmaking that is often binned as soon as a production wraps. On the honor of her set being preserved in such a way, De Jong said, “It’s pretty incredible, because in the act of doing it, you aren’t thinking about what this is going to turn into.”

After receiving her first Oscar nomination for her work on Christopher Nolan‘s Best Picture-winning biopic “Oppenheimer,” De Jong re-teamed with the writer-director this year for his ambitious take on Homer’s epic poem “The Odyssey.” For this film, her process began at Nolan’s home, where she spent hours reading the script. Afterwards, De Jong asked for the parameters. “He said, ‘There are none,'” De Jong recalled.

This allowed the designer the freedom to “take the audience on the same journey that Odysseus (Matt Damon) was on,” she said. Starting with seven countries, De Jong and Nolan began searching for the film’s faraway locations, the only edict being that Nolan wanted the film to start in the Mediterranean and end in the Mediterranean. Without the barriers of realism, De Jong found inspiration in locations across the globe. “We didn’t care that we were shooting the Laestrygonians in Scotland. It didn’t matter. It just had the topography we were interested in. Same with Iceland and the same with Morocco,” De Jong said. Once the locations were determined, then came building sets that reflected the characters who inhabit them.

For the ominous stone house owned by Circe (Samantha Morton), who beguiles Odysseus’ men and turns them into pigs, De Jong shared that Nolan “was very clear about not wanting Circe’s home to be a Hansel and Gretel in the woods type cottage. She’s so peculiar and unique and bizarre and a witch.” With this in mind, the duo decided she should live on the edge of a cliff, finding the perfect craggy rocks in Scotland. Soon, a whole backstory informed the building of her dwelling. “She formed her house out of those craggy rocks,” De Jong said, adding, “We just made up all these stories and created the sets from there.”

The same attention to character informed the creation of the iconic Trojan horse, an imposing image of which opens the epic film. Nolan envisioned a rearing horse, telling De Jong that “it has to be iconic and it has to be larger than life.” For Nolan, De Jong said, the question at the center of this opening scene is, “Are the Trojans going to accept the gift?” Thinking about what kind of horse would be accepted, Nolan wanted their horse to be “the antithesis” of the one in Wolfgang Petersen’s 2004 film “Troy.” “We didn’t want the clunky wheels,” she said, adding that “these were master shipbuilders.”

“They’re master craftsmen,” De Jong insists, “If they collected all this wood, why don’t we shiplap the entire body, shiplap the tail? They hand-carved the legs and the head. That leaves the body all hollow like a ship, so all the men could all go inside and cut a trap door.” Once they agreed on the backstory for the building of the horse, the next step was figuring out how to make multiples out of fiberglass (and later out of plastic as one of the summer’s hottest collectible popcorn buckets).

As “The Odyssey” marches its way into awards season, De Jong is looking towards her future – and her next gig. With every project she takes, De Jong is looking to push herself as an artist. “It’s that space of being uncomfortable that is how you know you’re in the right place,” she said, adding, “The minute I find comfort, I realize I’m in the wrong place. So I’m always pushing to get back into that area of discomfort.”

Thinking back to her conversation with Fisk all those years ago, De Jong feels that what he taught her was “The act of physically doing and going and staying in momentum,” adding, “That’s something that Christopher Nolan has. All of these directors; They don’t stop producing work. They don’t do it in vain. They do it because that’s their language and their medium. They’re all artists at heart.”

Although De Jong looks back at her past fondly, she doesn’t regret forgoing art school to join the movie business. What she learned after all these years is that, “You need to go forward, and even if you go forward and you hit a wall, then just keep pivoting a little bit. Stay open and don’t be fearful. You can’t fear. I’d rather screw up royally and have tried than not tried at all.”

#3355. The 10 Most Hopeless Christmas Movies, Ranked

There’s no shortage of feel-good Christmas movies. Some will have dramatic moments, sure, but you can’t really call It’s a Wonderful Life downbeat or hopeless when it ends up feeling life-affirming and hopeful by the end. So, it’s not a movie that you'll see mentioned below, nor will you see other movies that have a lot of drama but wholly inspiring endings (see also most adaptations of A Christmas Carol).

Instead, what you'll see below are the most hopeless Christmas movies of all time. They generally work as good anti-Christmas movies, telling darker stories that just so happen to play out during the holiday season. They're not all 100% heavy, because some are more cynical than tragic, though in one way or another, they do ultimately stand out against the more conventional Christmas movies out there that you’ve probably seen discussed (and recommended) to death.

The Ref is a well-made comedic crime film that just so happens to take place on Christmas Eve, and mostly concerns a bunch of generally unlikable characters clashing, and then it’s kind of funny because no one’s sympathetic. If you take a step back, or try to imagine yourself stuck in this film, then it would be miserable, and that sense of it all being cynical is what makes it clash with most Christmas movies and the sentiments found within them.

There is certainly a time and place for anti-Christmas movies, especially if you're not someone who feels like engaging with the season this year, for whatever reason.

The antagonist here is a burglar who takes a family hostage, but the family is a dysfunctional one, and everyone ends up making everyone feel worse. There is certainly a time and place for anti-Christmas movies, especially if you're not someone who feels like engaging with the season this year, for whatever reason, and so something pessimistic like The Ref has got your back, in that instance.

What do you want, or what were you expecting? It’s a movie called Bad Santa. Okay, Bad Santa is good, but it’s not really feel-good; that’s the unsurprising part. It’s one of the better R-rated Christmas movies out there, and it might also be one of the “most R-rated” Christmas movies, too, because it's about a miserable conman who robs department stores while dressed up as a mall Santa, and then things change for him to some extent when he meets a young kid who’s struggling socially.

Only “to some extent,” since it’s not really warm and fuzzy, by any means. There is a tiny bit of heart here that stops this from being utterly depressing and nihilistic, yet a lot of the humor comes from that, and Billy Bob Thornton is very much the right person to cast if you want that kind of energy, too. It might not be the kind of dark Christmas movie that'll appeal to everyone, for obvious reasons, but it will likely appeal to you if you're after a Christmas-themed dark comedy.

There were a ton of great movies released in 1984, including Gremlins. This is also an all-timer if you're looking at subversive and possibly "edgy" Christmas movies, and sure, while it’s not as dark or twisted as some other films here, it’s a pretty wild one for something that’s kind of family-friendly. It’s grisly for something that older kids could probably still watch, and the way it goes from being very jolly and cozy to violent and chaotic is great.

The plot… you know the plot, right? It’s Gremlins. It’s a creature feature, and one of the best ever made. It's a dark and very funny film that's willing to strip away some of the typical magic of Christmas, in turn crafting something wilder and weirder than most Christmas movies. And it memorably ruins the magic of Christmas for potential younger viewers, thanks to having a character monologue about the awful event in her life that made her realize Santa wasn’t real. Merry Christmas!

This one is only slightly a Christmas movie, lacking the iconography and warmth you'd associate with such a film, but still, The Lion in Winter is worthy of getting a shout-out here. The premise does ultimately concern a dysfunctional family coming together for the holiday season and arguing a great deal, since they're not just any family, but the royal one, and the King, Henry II, has a few heirs who are power-hungry.

It’s like Succession but set a bit over eight centuries ago, though it doesn’t really feel like your average period drama, because there’s a lot of energy here and an incredible script that feels more modern (but not in a distracting way). The Lion in Winter is excellent as a film on its own, and so maybe the Christmas stuff kind of comes second, but the quality of it overall makes it feel hard to overlook. And, once more, it’s a good anti-Christmas movie, especially if you don’t particularly love the yearly requirement to come together as a family.

There’s one other Christmas-themed slasher movie that’ll be mentioned further down, because it is admittedly more intense and harrowing than Black Christmas. To some extent, Black Christmas is slightly cozy, but it is also tense for its time, not to mention important in the overall history of the slasher genre, since Black Christmas pre-dated other slashers like the original Halloween and Friday the 13th movies by a few years.

Pretty wild to consider there was an essential Christmas slasher movie before there was a true “Halloween” slasher movie; not the holiday you'd expect to be prioritized. Anyway, it’s about the members of a sorority house getting tormented and eventually hunted down by a mysterious killer. Simple stuff, but it’s a slasher movie, so of course it’s not going to be complicated. Black Christmas does what it needs to, and it also did so before a good many other slasher films. Much of it holds up, too (don’t bother with the more recent remakes/updates).

Batman Returns confirms that Gotham City celebrates Christmas. The film plays out when things are snowy and festive, and then it’s notably also quite dark for a superhero movie of its era. 1989’s Batman was already more intense than much of what came before, but Batman Returns is next-level in that regard, pushing things about as far as they can go while (just) retaining a PG-13 rating.

It’s almost a bit much. And sure, other movies here have more violence and profanity, but all this unpleasantness feels a little different in a film like this. So, Batman Returns is more of a cult thing, but the people who do feel this is a cult classic are passionate about Batman Returns; make no mistake. And even if you don’t love it, or enjoy it, it’s not hard to admire how gutsy this one was, and how effectively anti-Christmas it feels among Christmas movies.

Eyes Wide Shut was the final film Stanley Kubrick ever directed, and it came out posthumously. It is kind of a Christmas movie, taking place at the end of the year and having some of the iconography you'd expect to see, but thematically, it’s not very Christmassy. Nor does it really scream Christmas narratively, since it’s about a man putting himself in great danger psychologically and physically when he spirals after learning his wife once thought about cheating on him.

What happens around the middle of Eyes Wide Shut is absolutely horrifying, and then the final act is about the aftermath of all that, and unsettling in more subdued ways. It’s one of the more anxiety-provoking movies of its era for sure, but it is great, both for its direction and for how well-acted it is (Tom Cruise especially seems willing to do just about anything Kubrick asked of him, so he gives one of his most committed performances here).

With Terrifier 3, you get more Terrifier, for better or worse. It’s Terrifier set around Christmastime, so Art the Clown does some of his rampage while being dressed like Santa Claus, and after doing something (expectedly) horrifying to another person dressed up as Santa. You know the drill. Art torments people. Art tortures people. Art (eventually) kills people, after they’ve experienced the most pain possible.

Beyond the bloodshed, there are a few things going on narratively, at least more so than the first movie, and as a continuation of the second movie (also better than the first), Terrifier 3 works pretty well. You shouldn’t watch it if you're even a tiny bit squeamish, and there is a whole lot of gore and stress here, but these are all extreme horror movies, so if you’ve been fooled by Terrifier three times now, hoping for something different each time a new one comes out… like, come on.

The main reason to watch Spencer is Kristen Stewart’s performance as Princess Diana, though you could also watch it if you like Christmas movies but don’t want to watch a nice/happy Christmas movie. It takes place during the holiday season, and is focused on Diana struggling with her marriage and being wrapped up in the royal family, with no one in the institution coming away from things looking particularly good (other than Princess Diana and maybe her two songs).

It's an unrelenting historical drama, but it gets heavy and feels intensely solemn for a good reason, demystifying things and being empathetic toward Diana. Spencer is no ordinary biopic, both because it’s quite dark and also because the timeframe here is rather narrow, but it’s pretty great for what it does and how intense it ends up being. And, once more, Stewart hasn’t even been better than she is here in the lead role.

You have to squint more than usual to see this as a Christmas movie, even compared to some of the other films here, but Brazil takes place at the year’s end, and there’s some Christmas-like imagery. It’s easier to describe as an essential cult classic sci-fi film, and also a very dark comedy, being about a bureaucrat whose life absolutely spirals out of control, largely due to his world being terrible and his luck being even worse.

The line between reality and fantasy breaks down, though not to the extent that you ever entirely forget just how horrible the dystopian world Brazil takes place in truly is. The way it wraps up is especially soul-crushing, and though before that point, much of Brazil is comedic, it’s also an exhausting sort of comedy. If you don’t like feeling more stressed than usual around Christmas, maybe it’s better to wait and watch this one at a different point in the year.

#3354. These M5 MacBook Air Laptops Are up to $250 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Apple announced a slew of products in March, including the MacBook Air with the M5 chip, which ended up increasing in price in June due to the RAM shortage. These MacBooks come in both 13-inch and 15-inch sizes, and if you're interested in either, it's a good time to buy: In the leadup to Black Friday, Amazon is selling both at a $200 discount, and the 1 TB storage versions for $250 off.

Those discounts bring the 13-inch MacBook Air to $1,099.99 (down from $1,299) and $1,349.99 (originally $1,499.99) for the 512GB and 1 TB versions, respectively. The 15-inch MacBook Air is down to $1,299 (originally $1,499), and the 1TB version is $1,549.99 (originally $1,799.99). All versions are at their lowest prices since the June price hikes.

The M5 MacBook Air is the best laptop for most people looking for a new machine in 2026. In comparison to the already excellent M4 Airs, the M5 base model has double the storage at 512GB. #3353. Grey's Anatomy: Why TR Knight's George O'Malley Was Killed Off In Season 6

The George O’Malley death in Grey's Anatomy season 6 and T.R. Knight's departure from the show were shocking — so how did George O'Malley die, and why was he killed off in the first place? The series is led by Meredith Grey, who started her journey as an intern along with many other characters that won the audience over before Grey's Anatomy killed them off. One of those Grey's Anatomy characters was George O’Malley (T.R. Knight), who struggled a bit but became a very skilled and talented surgeon, and the best friend of Izzie Stevens. George dies in Grey's Anatomy in season 6 due to complications from an accident.

Just when George seemed to have found his path in medicine, he planned to leave Seattle Grace in season 5 to join the U.S. Army in Iraq. But on his way home, he jumped in front of a bus to save a woman’s life and was left severely disfigured. None of Grey’s Anatomy’s doctors recognized George, and it wasn’t until he traced “007” on Meredith’s hand that they knew who the “John Doe” patient was. His brain fatally swelled during surgery. The George O’Malley death in Grey's Anatomy was a tragic ending that saw T.R. Knight leave the series in season 6 without much understanding as of why.

George left Grey's Anatomy due to some behind-the-scenes creative differences. Knight’s Grey’s Anatomy season 6 departure was announced in June 2009, and he revealed (via EW) not long after that the reason behind it was a gradual “breakdown of communication” between him and Rhimes, who he also said tried to discourage him from coming out. This led him not to ask what was going on with Grey's Anatomy's George O’Malley storylines anymore, and he simply asked to be released from his contract, leading to the George O'Malley death.

In addition, Knight wasn’t comfortable with where his character was being led to before his Grey's Anatomy season 6 (the same season when Katherine Heigl left) death and struggled with the storyline where George cheated on his wife, Callie Torres (Sara Ramirez), with Izzie. So, they killed George O'Malley to come up with a proper reason for T.R. Knight to leave the show. Knight later said he was at peace with his decision to leave Grey’s Anatomy in season 6 and end his time with the George O'Malley death scene, saying there “comes a time when it’s so clear that moving on is the best decision.”

He may have fallen prey to Grey’s Anatomy's shortfall in handling character exits, with their go-to solution being to kill them off. However, Grey’s Anatomy's George O’Malley death stands out for how abrupt and cruel it was. George dies in season 6 of Grey's Anatomy, and while it brought a lot of drama to the series, it was also a reflection of all the behind-the-scenes issues around the character, and how his ending was handled didn’t do justice to him.

While T.R. Knight found solace after the show in George O'Malley's death and his decision to exit Grey’s Anatomy in season 6, the actor and character have since returned to the series. In Grey’s Anatomy season 15, George O’Malley made a posthumous return in the episode “Flowers Grow Out of My Grave,” briefly appearing as a ghost who visits Meredith Grey on the Day of the Dead. However, this was accomplished through archived footage.

T.R. Knight later reprised his Grey’s Anatomy role in season 17, appearing in one of Meredith’s unconscious beach visions while suffering from COVID-19, in which they reflect on George O’Malley’s season 6 death. Several figures from Meredith's past visited her while on the beach, all people who were incredibly important to her, like her sister and her husband as well.

People were happy yet incredibly surprised to see T.R. Knight's George O’Malley return in a season 17 episode of Grey's Anatomy. While his reappearance was welcomed with open arms, it was difficult to imagine that the star would return given his reasoning for exiting the show and Isaiah Washington's homophobic comments towards the actor. Despite the George O'Malley death scene, he did come back in Grey's Anatomy, this time as a product of Meredith's mind. The purpose of George's reappearance on the show came down to one thing for showrunner Krista Vernoff: closure.

The George O'Malley death in season 6 was a shock to many, and some felt that the character was wronged for it. Bringing George back on Grey's Anatomy was meant to act as closure for people who thought that the character wasn't given a fair shot. Knight was originally a bit dubious when Vernoff approached him with the idea of returning to the program. However, his husband, Patrick Leahy, convinced him to return as George O’Malley. In an interview (via Deadline), Knight is able to look back fondly at the experience, recounting, "It was incredible, it was just an overwhelming feeling of love in that moment."

After the George O'Malley death in Grey's Anatomy, T.R. Knight has been in numerous movies and television programs. In 2013 he appeared in the movie 42 as Harold Parrot, and in 2015 he was in the feature film A Year and Change as Kenny. His last movie was in 2017, called Hello Again, where he played Carl. He's also appeared in numerous television programs, such as The Good Wife, the Will and Grace reboot, and Law & Order: SVU, but his most famous property is being cast in The Flight Attendant as Davey Bowden.

The George O'Malley death on Grey's Anatomy was one of the saddest moments of the show, but T.R. Knight had such an impact as the character that he was the first person that showrunner Krista Vernoff thought of to visit Meredith in her dreams as she battled with COVID-19. The thought of Meredith and George walking on the beach together through troubling times warmed her heart (via E! News). Vernoff said:

Right now in our lives, in this pandemic, pure joy is rare, and so I'm so grateful to T.R. for coming and playing, and offering that to everyone, because I think it's meaningful.

T.R. Knight essentially echoed these sentiments in an Instagram post shortly after the fated Grey's Anatomy episode. Knight mentioned how much he enjoyed working with the fellow Grey's Anatomy cast. He stated that George would "always claim [his] heart," proving that there's still a ton of love there, despite the Goerge O'Malley death. He also said that while Meredith and George love each other, it doesn't hold a candle to the love he has for Pompeo. Knight had nothing but thanks for the cast, saying, "Thank you to Ellen, Chandra, Jim, Krista, and all the familiar faces for once again sharing your beautiful light."

George wasn’t the first major death in the show. Instead, that honor went to Denny, the patient Izzy had fallen in love with. Denny, however, was a recurring character, not a member of the main cast. His death had also been telegraphed from his introduction on the show, unlike George, whose death blindsided fans since they didn’t even initially know the man hit by the bus was George.

George’s death made it clear that writing a character out of the show didn’t just mean doctors leaving for other jobs or taking a trip that never ended. A character leaving the show could truly be permanent. Killing them off became the easiest way for Grey’s Anatomy to do that once George became the first main character to get that final farewell.

If the show hadn’t killed George off, it’s entirely possible the series wouldn’t have such a brutal track record for character exits today. Fans often worry their favorite character is going to be killed when they find out an actor is leaving the show now. Beyond the audience realizing that no character is safe and that there are genuine stakes in the dramatic storylines, George’s death also had an impact because so many of the main characters had a strong connection to him and the show allowed each of them to grieve in different ways.

Izzie and Meredith were his best friends and had past romantic relationships with him. While Izzie’s grief came in waves, Meredith tried to avoid it completely. Bailey claimed him as her favorite intern and named her child after him, and following his death, she became a bit harder on those around her, putting up a wall again. Though Callie and George had divorced, they were still close. She nearly immediately broke down at the news. They were all given a spotlight without Grey’s Anatomy having to center the show on George after he was gone.

The show made a smart decision in having several weeks take place in a single episode. It allowed the characters space to mourn without requiring them to grieve for the entire next season. While some fans might have found it rushed, it worked for the show because the compressed timeline made it clear that despite this tragic event, life continued, and Grey’s Anatomy had more stories to tell.

Created by Shonda Rhimes, long-running medical drama Grey's Anatomy depicts the professional and personal lives of the employees of a Seattle hospital.

#3352. After Returning to Spanish with ‘Bitter Christmas,’ Pedro Almodóvar Might Be Done with English-Language Movies

With Cannes entry “Bitter Christmas,” Oscar-winning Spanish auteur Pedro Almodóvar (“Talk to Her”) is back making movies in his native language. Since his debut “Pepi, Luci, Bom and Other Girls Like Mom” in 1980, Almodóvar has written singularly identifiable, heightened, rhythmic, and mellifluous Spanish dialogue.

While Tilda Swinton and Julianne Moore adeptly wrangled his translated English in Golden Lion-winner “The Room Next Door,” which deployed his usual bright Almodóvar colors and exacting mise-en-scène, the director did not enjoy dealing with the unions in New York. “In Spain everything is much more immediate, and also it is my language, it’s my culture,” he told me during the New York Film Festival. While he doesn’t rule out making another English-language movie, it would have to be small-scale. “I don’t find myself, anymore, capable of dealing with a production that is chaotic with a lot of people and a lot of characters.” Related Stories ‘Fatherland’ Wins Golden Frog at ToruńCAMERIMAGE 2026 — Full Winners List Production Designer Ruth De Jong on How to Build (Ancient) Worlds for Auteurs

Now he’s back in Spain in self-referential, meta autofiction mode in full force. The results are exhilarating. “Bitter Christmas” offers a movie within a movie, as writer-director Raúl (Leonardo Sbaraglia) crafts a script that lifts some key story points from his friends’ experiences. Even though Almodóvar considers the movie one of his riskiest, it’s the filmmaker’s biggest hit in Spain since “Volver.”

Almodóvar considers “Bitter Christmas” to be “twins” with Oscar-nominated “Pain and Glory,” which starred his old favorite Antonio Banderas as his alter ego. “‘Pain and Glory’ is more about the physical pain, right?,” he said. “The character [Raul] has had a lot of surgeries, and his fear is about that the fact that he’s not going to be physically able to to handle another another film shoot. Whereas in this film I deal with a different pain, which is the pain of writer’s block, of the blank page, or writing something that doesn’t quite come together for you. The character of Aitana in the film says to Raul, ‘you know we are all losers, you have lost grace.’ And by grace it means inspiration, something that is equally painful to that writer-director as the physical pain was to the writer director in ‘Pain and Glory.'”

Mostly when Almodóvar sits down to write, he’s making things up. He’s gotten into trouble in the past for raiding his friends’ stories. “There is not any law that creates the limits of the autofiction,” he said. “There is no law that’s going to define the limits of what you can appropriate and what you can’t appropriate. But if I’m inspired by the life of someone who’s close to me, who’s going through a difficult time, as a writer, you are selfish, because what propels you is the idea, even if it means going against the relationship. I don’t feel comfortable the two or three times that I did it. This is the limit: not to hurt anyone. But it’s normal that writers are influenced by everything in life you see, you talk to with others, you read, you see movies. So it’s impossible to renounce the influence of the life of others.”

And he’s passionate about making movies. As Raúl says in the film, “This is all there is to my life.” But Almodóvar has never suffered writer’s block. “I inspire myself because this is the profession that I know better than anyone, than any other,” he said. “The only thing that separates me from this alter ego is that I never lived a creative crisis. The experience I have had is more scripts that have taken me a long time to find the solution and to get them to gel together. But I’ve always succeeded ultimately.”

And he only recently discovered panic attacks, which took him by surprise. “I hadn’t previously experienced panic attacks, but now I have,” he said. “At that moment I was unconscious, and it was something awful, awful.”

Needless to say Almodóvar spends most of his days sitting at his desk at the computer. (Hence his legendary bad back.) Mostly he enjoys writing but also feels the clock ticking. “You always feel like time is lacking, right?” he said. “Especially that moment when you get that idea that’s going to become the motor of your story, you feel like there’s no time to breathe, because you want to get it all down as fast as possible. They’re quite intense days as we’re trying to get this. And then once I’ve started the story, my process is to get up in the morning and start writing. Those are some of the most pleasurable days in my life because you know where you’re going. But also, I have to pay attention to everything, because in that moment that you are possessed by the idea, you experience everything in your life filtered through the sensibility of the story that you’re writing.”

Listening to music feeds his creative beast. While he was writing “Talk to Her,” he listened to Caetano Veloso’s “Cucurrucucú Paloma,” a song that he had heard thousands of times, “but then it was like an epiphany. I discovered the song, and you feel it in a different way.” And in “Bitter Christmas,” his two actresses in the movie-within-the-movie listen to “Weeping Woman” from the filmmaker’s longtime muse, Mexican chanteuse Chavela Vargas.

Finally, the filmmaker had fun making himself the bad guy. “This was a new structure for me,” he said. “What I liked about it was that I could talk about myself as a writer-director, but mostly I also enjoyed the part of becoming the villain in a sense of that story. But the spectator does have to pay a lot of attention because if they go to the bathroom for two minutes, they’re going to miss something and be lost.”

In one scene, the filmmaker offers a close-up of the cursor on the computer screen. “Even though the cursor itself is not a very cinematic thing to see,” he said, “it’s his call to creativity, right? It’s the thing that calls him and pulls him in to have to tell his story. So it’s autofiction.”

Going forward, Almodóvar has no plans to put himself at the center of another film. “I promise not to talk about me anymore,” he said. “I was interested since the beginning of my career about the origin of creation and the relation with reality. Inspiration and life together, like the two sides of a coin. This mysterious question that so fascinates me is about not just where does creativity come from, how does it come, when does it come, how does it manifest? I have reached the end of my exploration around this.”

Up next: He’s writing, he said. “This is almost the opposite of this one. The new one will be very different.”

A Sony Pictures Classic release, “Bitter Christmas” is now playing in theaters in New York and Los Angeles. It expands nationally on November 25.

#3351. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

Credit: Marion Curtis/StarPix for Apple TV/INSTARimages

Timothy Olyphant and Brad Pitt's reunion continues a seven-year tradition.

Quentin Tarantino directed the 2019 hit drama Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, starring Leonardo DiCaprio, Pitt, and Margot Robbie. The story unveiled a fictionalized account of the Sharon Tate murders, in which Pitt portrays the stunt double Cliff Booth, who comes across the Manson Family. After the role won him an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor, his character now becomes the hero of his own story in the upcoming sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. The only other actor returning is Olyphant, who portrayed the real-life actor James Stacy.

Just weeks before its IMAX release, FilmRatings.com confirmed that The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth will officially be rated R, like the original 2019 movie. The certificate indicates that the upcoming sequel has "some strong/disturbing violence, bloody images, pervasive language, sexual content, nudity and drug use." The warning is not far off from Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, which had similar cautions of its violent content. Nevertheless, the R-rating was expected, given that Netflix released a red-band trailer earlier this month.

It's the latest Olyphant movie to get an R rating. Since Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, only two of his films have avoided the restricted MPA rating; The Starling was rated PG-13, and LEGO Star Wars: The Mandalorian was TV-Y7-FV.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth takes place eight years after Tarantino's original hit, in which Cliff leaves the stunt world behind and becomes a studio fixer. Before that, the stunt double survived the Manson family attack at the end of Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, which hinted at Rick Dalton's acting struggles during the late 1960s. Although Tarantino wrote the story, the directorial duties were passed over to acclaimed director David Fincher.

The upcoming movie marks the fourth reunion between Pitt and Fincher after they previously worked on Se7en, The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, and Fight Club. Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, and Carla Gugino round out the supporting cast.

Olyphant provided details about his appearance and his collaboration with Fincher. He confirmed that his screen time is brief, having just filmed a day and a half of scenes. Nevertheless, he described the sequel as a "cool mix" of both filmmakers, with Tarantino's slick dialogue and Fincher's layered, distinct direction.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth will become the first Netflix movie to have an exclusive IMAX release. The sequel is Tarantino and Fincher's most expensive movie, with a $200 million budget. Although DiCaprio had a key role as Rick Dalton in Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, he will not reprise the fictional character in the sequel after turning down a cameo.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth will be exclusively in IMAX for two weeks, starting November 25, before going to Netflix on December 23.

#3347. These Like-New Kindles Are up to $75 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Amazon is offering early Black Friday discounts on like-new versions of its 2024 Kindles, with prices starting at $152.99 for the Paperwhite and savings of $27 to $75 across five models that include the color-screen Colorsoft and the pen-equipped Kindle Scribe. All five are a generation behind Amazon's current lineup: The company introduced redesigned Paperwhite and Colorsoft models (plus accessories) in October, with the new Paperwhite now starting at $199.99, and replaced the 2024 Scribe with a third-generation model in December 2025. As for its “like-new” label, it means these are pre-owned devices that Amazon has tested and certified to look and work like new.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite (16GB) is down to $152.99 from $179.99 and covers just about everything most people need for everyday reading, including enough storage for thousands of ebooks. Its seven-inch, 300ppi glare-free display is larger than the previous generation’s 6.8-inch screen, with faster page turns, an adjustable warm light, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. As PCMag notes in its review, it's a great option for readers who don't need color or handwriting features.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $190.99 from $224.99, making it just $38 more than the like-new Paperwhite (16GB). For that relatively small difference, you're doubling the storage to 32GB and getting wireless charging, an ad-free lock screen, and a front light that automatically adjusts to your surroundings—on top of the same sharp seven-inch display, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life as the standard Paperwhite, as noted by this PCMag review.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft (16GB) is down to $220.99 from $260.99 and offers something the Paperwhite models can’t: a color E-Ink display, which makes it well suited to comics, graphic novels, illustrated books, and travel guides. Its seven-inch screen shows that color content at 150ppi while keeping text at a sharp 300ppi, and you can mark passages in multiple highlight colors to keep your notes organized. That said, colors are noticeably more muted than on a conventional tablet, and battery life tops out at eight weeks, compared with 12 weeks on the Paperwhite.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $243.99 from $287.99, making it just $23 more than the standard like-new Colorsoft. For that modest increase, you're getting twice the storage at 32GB, which is particularly useful for comics, manga, and graphic novels that take up more space than regular ebooks, along with wireless charging, an automatically adjusting front light, and an ad-free lock screen. However, as PCMag notes in its review, the color display produces more subdued tones than a conventional tablet, so the Paperwhite remains the more economical choice if you primarily read novels.

The Like-New Kindle Scribe (16GB) is down to $284.99 from $359.99, the biggest dollar discount in this roundup. Unlike the other Kindles here, it's built for reading and writing, with a 10.2-inch, 300ppi glare-free display and a Premium Pen with an eraser and shortcut button—making it the most versatile option for readers who want an e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3346. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.

#3345. Prime Video's 62-Episode Sci-Fi Masterpiece Deserves Credit For Skipping To Book 2

According to conventional wisdom, the more faithful a live-action adaptation remains to its source material, the more acclaim will be headed its way. That's certainly true for The Expanse, which started on Syfy before moving onto Prime Video halfway through. The future-set space opera rendered James S.A. Corey's novel series in glorious live-action, knowing exactly which parts of the books could be trimmed out, condensed, or tweaked in ways that would remodel the story for a visual medium without feeling like huge deviations.

Generally speaking, TV series based on books and comics start off relatively close to the original story, then forge their own separate path as the show unfolds. The Umbrella Academy, Game of Thrones, and The Walking Dead are all examples of series that grew increasingly confident in ignoring the instruction manual.

The Expanse worked in the opposite direction. The show's six-season run covered Corey's first six books, averaging out at one book per season, and by the time Amazon got hold of it, The Expanse literally was adapting one specific book in each season. During the Syfy days, however, those lines were a little more blurred, and not without good reason.

The Expanse's TV incarnation is known for its blend of space adventuring and interplanetary politics that has earned it such accolades as 'Game of Thrones in space.' While the books adopt a similar mashup of styles, that wasn't the case in James S.A. Corey's debut, Leviathan Wakes.

That first book only followed the narratives of James Holden, leading his crew aboard the Rocinante, and Detective Miller, investigating the disappearance of Julie Mao before fatefully joining up with Holden. The Expanse's first book is actually very light on political intrigue, with characters such as Chrisjen Avasarala and Sadovir Errinwright forced to wait until the sequel, Cibola Burn, before making their respective bows.

Instead of leaving them hanging around for season 2, The Expanse's TV series got Avasarala and Errinwright involved right from the start, adding in new plot points (such as the character of Franklin DeGraaf) to show the unseen politics that happened entirely in the background of book one.

The Expanse's first season mixed the thriller-y excitement of Leviathan Wakes with the slow-burn conspiracies and careful maneuvering of Cibola Burn, and this was undoubtedly the right call. It gave The Expanse's early episodes a more balanced palette, and one that would feel consistent with the seasons to come. Had that initial run of episodes followed the book's full-throttle approach directly, viewers would've been in for an abrupt switch of genres when season 2 started taking a deeper interest in the nitty-gritty of diplomacy.

Bringing Earth politics into The Expanse season 1 inevitably meant parts of Leviathan Wakes were delayed until season 2, which was great news for a certain Josepheus Miller.

The Expanse's first book concludes with Miller crashing Eros onto Venus, and his physical form dying in the process. The Expanse season 1, however, merely ended with Miller escaping Eros alongside Holden and joining the Rocinante crew as a temporary member. Not only did this allow Thomas Jane an extra season on the show, it meant The Expanse retained the noir-ish, 'private detective with a grudge' vibe that tagged along behind Miller, at least for a little while longer.

The TV series enjoyed more tonal consistency as a result, and as great as they are, the first entries in the book series are a lot starker in their leaps between genres. It's not a huge issue on the page, but would have made for a jarring experience in a TV adaptation, and The Expanse deserves all the credit for spotting that potential pitfall in advance.

#3344. Amy Poehler’s ‘Parks and Recreation’ Replacement Officially Arrives Next Week

It's been over ten years since Amy Poehler left Pawnee, Indiana, and Parks and Recreation behind, and since then, she's been less of a defining presence in live-action television comedy. Her most recognizable role since starring in the beloved mockumentary sitcom for seven seasons has easily been as the emotion Joy in Disney's Inside Out movies, though she's also been quite busy behind the camera. She co-created the Netflix hit Russian Doll, as well as her own animated comedy series, Duncanville, and served as producer on everything from Broad City to Harlem and the recent Cinderella-twisting animated film Steps. In just over a week, however, she'll be back to bringing the laughs on-screen with help from a familiar collaborator.

Poehler is set to resurface at Peacock for the new series Dig, which she both leads and co-created with one half of the Parks and Recreation creative duo, Michael Schur​​​​. Based on Kate Myers' bestselling novel Excavations, it centers on four women at vastly different stages of their careers working on an archaeological dig site in Greece over the summer who set their differences aside after making the discovery of a lifetime. Their history-changing big break also puts them at the center of an international conspiracy that spans far wider than they could possibly imagine. All episodes are slated to drop on November 23, just in time for a holiday binge over Thanksgiving.

After leading Pawnee's Parks and Recreation department, Poehler leads the cast of Dig as the excavation site's lead archaeologist, Elise, with Hugh Laurie playing the long-standing source of her ire, Neville, a British scientist who sincerely loves archaeology but has simply refused to retire from the dig and always gets the credit for any discoveries. The main group is rounded out by Geraldine Viswanathan, Fina Strazza, and Antonia Thomas, though there's also a wealth of stars attached. Jason Mantzoukas, Noma Dumezweni, and Brennan Lee Mulligan are set to recur, while What We Do in the Shadows alum Kayvan Novak headlines a group of guest stars including Max Greenfield, Jon Pointing, Bonita Friedericy, and Dan Bucatinsky.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

Dig adds another high-profile comedy to Peacock's roster with The Office DNA after just debuting Season 2 of Greg Daniels' standalone spin-off series, The Paper, back in September. It's been a strong fall in terms of originals for the streamer, most recently including the thriller family drama The Good Daughter, led by Meghann Fahy and Rose Byrne.
