#3314. 'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

Grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

Now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro."

PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

In the post, Rockstar also announced that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

That's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar says that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the company hasn't explained why that is.

#3313. ‘Is This Supposed to Happen?’: How Matt Dike Dominated Eighties Hip-Hop Music

Set in 1980s Los Angeles, Peter Relic’s “Bust a Move: Matt Dike, Delicious Vinyl, and the Hip-Hop Hits that First Conquered Pop” chronicles the peculiar circumstances that led to the founding of independent record label Delicious Vinyl, and the creation of three of the biggest crossover singles of that era: “Wild Thing” and “Funky Cold Medina” by Tone Loc, and Young MC’s “Bust a Move.”

“The fact that those indelible hits — as well as Beastie Boys’ classic album ‘Paul’s Boutique’ — were created in Matt Dike’s dusty, second floor apartment using patched-together equipment makes this one of the great DIY success stories in music history,” Relic, a Rolling Stone and Vibe contributor says. “I had no idea how truly extraordinary this story would be going into it, never mind how the mystery of Matt Dike would drive my entire investigation.”

As the record label Dike cofounded with fellow nightclub DJ Michael Ross rose to global prominence, the charismatic producer was offered the chance to work with artists including Aerosmith and Brian Wilson. Instead, Matt Dike disappeared.

“All I had was his phone number, and the knowledge that Matt had not given an in-person interview to the press since 1990. What I never guessed was what was going to happen that night after he finally picked up the phone.”

In the following excerpt from the book, three of the key players find themselves at a miraculous, ridiculous tipping point in hip-hop and pop music history.

Tone Loc was stuck. Like a big, brawny genie trapped in a dusty bottle, the rapper in the wraparound shades needed to be freed to unleash his magic.

Here, onstage at the Fabulous Forum in Inglewood, California, with purple-and-gold Los Angeles Lakers championship banners dangling from the rafters and 18,000 teenyboppers baying for beats, the semi-reformed gangster could only blink through the tendrils of dry ice swirling around him, his heart thumping faster than the tom-tom turnaround of his big hit “Wild Thing.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Out in the crowd, two young dudes passed a flask of Jack Daniel’s and guffawed at the sight of Tone jammed in a giant prop bottle labeled FUNKY COLD MEDINA. “Oh my god, this is so Spinal Tap!” gasped the tall gangly one, his lank blond hair tented beneath a tied-back bandana. His buddy with the impressively dimpled chin could only glug in incredulity: “Is this supposed to happen?”

The answer was no. None of it. Not the ridiculous prop malfunction. Not rap music made in LA beating New York to the top of the pop charts. Nor any of the extraordinary circumstances that had led Matt Dike, Michael Ross, and Tone Loc to this moment.

The date was Aug. 13, 1989. Two years earlier, Dike and Ross had been battering away at a primitive drum machine in a grungy apartment in the wrong part of Hollywood. With a $5000 loan, they’d started a record label called Delicious Vinyl, recorded a couple of mildly lascivious songs with unknown local rapper Anthony “Tone” Smith, and pressed up a few hundred 12-inches to hawk at swap meets and local shops.

Within eighteen months, their fledgling label had sold nearly ten million records worldwide. They had shocked New York, and battered down the barriers of a recording industry still largely intent on keeping hip-hop out.  Related Content BigXthaPlug Wrestles With Success on ‘Better Over Time’ First They Found the Buried Treasure. Then Came the Sunken Slave Ship Jay-Z Deserves the Super Bowl Halftime Gig Drake ‘Janice STFU’ Copyright Lawsuit Is Withdrawn

Yet here was Tone Loc, headlining Club MTV Live Tour, a concert revue featuring a smattering of ready-to-serve stars of the moment: techno-poppers Information Society, funk goofballs Was (Not Was), dance queen Paula Abdul, and mime mannequins Milli Vanilli. No stranger to smoke inhalation, Loc had had enough of this guff, and in a moment of twin-fisted fury prepared to bash his way out of his Plexiglas coffin.

“We’ve gotta get up there!” Dike shouted at Ross. The two cofounders of Delicious Vinyl, ALL ACCESS passes gummed to their chests, began weaving their way toward the stage.

Covering the show that night for the Los Angeles Times was journalist Jonathan Gold. Two decades later, Gold’s fearless gastronomy and appetizing prose as LA Weekly food critic won him the Pulitzer Prize, but throughout the 1980s, Gold’s primary beat was music. He had penned multiple admiring stories documenting Dike’s hot string of underground dance clubs and the subsequent rise of Delicious Vinyl.

In his review in the morning paper, Gold chided Club MTV host Downtown Julie Brown and the night’s other acts before singling out Tone Loc for special praise: “In only a few months, the good-natured rapper seems to have made the transition to headlining a sold-out Forum with astonishing ease. The beats, kind of distorted with the other Club MTV performers, sounded richer and funkier played really loud, as if they were supposed to be that way. He shook hands with the audience, bantered with the audience — acknowledged that there is an audience, which is probably contrary to Club MTV house policy, but what the hey — and made rap clichés convincing for the first time since 1982. And that voice — whiskey-warm, rasping, insinuating, funny — is the best instrument in rap, cutting effortlessly through cranked guitar chords and bongo beats and cowbells.”

Finally free of his prop bottle, Tone delivered “Funky Cold Medina,” go-go joint “I Got It Goin’ On,” and pungent weed ode “Cheeba Cheeba,” while behind him onstage, next to the turntable riser manned by DJ M.Walk, Matt Dike and Mike Ross peered out at the crowd, facing down their unlikely demographic: pale adolescents whose orthodontic braces were hooked on the antenna of MTV.

Then came the money shot, a roof-rattling rendition of the year’s hottest jam. “Wild Thing” had been recorded on a patched-together tape machine in Dike’s apartment, with samples of a failed, decade-old Van Halen single, its accompanying video made for barely $400, but now Dike and Ross, dancing and deliriously drunk, were thinking the same thing as Jonathan Gold: This sounds awesome.

The moment was momentous. It couldn’t get any better. And then, sensing the profound nature of the occasion, Matt Dike turned his back, bent over, and mooned the crowd.

#3312. Lifehacker's Pick for the Best TV to Gift in 2026 Isn't Actually a TV

Welcome to Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, a collaborative multimedia project in which Lifehacker, CNET, ZDNET, and Mashable harness the power of our product testing laboratory and our editors' expertise to offer the best gift-buying recommendations possible. In this episode, we're talking televisions.

I recently did a deep dive into TV development history, checked out what was on shelves for 2026, and I concluded that the best gift TV you can give this year is, actually, a pair of sunglasses. The XBX by XReal video display glasses are basically a TV you can shove in your pocket. Check them out:

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.

#3309. What to Expect From Best Buy's 2026 Black Friday and Cyber Monday Sales

For all intents and purposes, Black Friday sales are already here. There are plenty of deals out already, even though we're weeks away from the actual event. One of the reasons for that is the competition retailers have with each other to be the first to get your money. One of the retailers that is making the biggest early splash is Best Buy, confirming their entire plan for the rest of the year. Here's what you need to know.

Best Buy has announced the following events:

DoorBoosters: A Halloween sale from Oct. 30 to Nov. 1.

Early Black Friday Deals and Doorbusters: The official start of early Black Friday deals on Nov. 6. New deals will drop every Friday.

Black Friday Doorbusters and Deals: Best Buy says this will be its main sale, starting on Thursday, Nov. 19 and running until Nov. 28 with deals on "computing, gaming, home theater, wearables, and more."

Cyber Sunday and Monday: Best Buy is extending Cyber Monday to five days and says you can find deals going up to 50% off select tech.

Last-minute savings: The Christmas sale will run from Dec. 18 until Dec. 24.

You don't need to be any kind of member to shop Best Buy's Black Friday in July sale; however, it is free to sign up for a My Best Buy membership, which will get you free shipping. If you join one of their paid subscriptions (My Best Buy Plus for $49.99 per year or My Best Buy Total for $179.99 per year), you'll get faster free shipping, exclusive prices and deals, an extended 60-day return window on most products, and access to select sales, like the Member Deals Days sale that is going on right now. Paid members will also earn extra rewards from both the current sale and the upcoming Black Friday in July sale.

You can find deals on TVs, laptops, headphones, video games, electric bikes, and more. There will be new deals every week in stores, on its website, and in the Best Buy mobile app. They'll offer price matching, meaning if the price drops further during the sale (Dec. 24), they will match it and offer a refund.

Here are the best deals I've found so far. I'll be updating these deals throughout the sale, so make sure to come back and see what's new. Remember that new deals drop every day.

Best Buy price matches its own products, so if a product drops in price later, you'd get those savings too, but it does not cover any deals coming from a competitor's Black Friday sale. There are some other important exceptions you can read in more detail here.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

The other major retailers doing Black Friday sales are Amazon, Target, and Walmart. Currently, Amazon has many early deals, seeing their lowest prices yet. Target has some week-long deals and a Deal of the Day. Walmart will have three Black Friday and Cyber Monday shopping events. Nowadays, large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3307. CMF Watch 3 Pro review

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is a sleek, budget-friendly entry-level smartwatch with effective workout tracking and almost two weeks of battery life. However, initial step counts can be inaccurate, sleep tracking is unreliable, the bulky design won't suit everyone, and there's no third-party app support.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

When it comes to finding the best cheap smartwatch, you want something that will suit everything about your lifestyle. Whether it’s sport or running errands, I know I don’t want my watch to get in my way — I need it to support me in my tasks.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is a good choice since it’s affordable and has a sleek design. Fitness tracking is effective, and the battery life is good too. But will it be for everyone? Not by a long shot.

I found the watch face very bulky on my small wrists, and the sleep tracking is inaccurate. The lack of third-party app support may also put off some users. To find out more, keep reading my full CMF Watch 3 Pro review.

Light Green, Orange, Light Grey, Dark Grey

Accelerometer, Gyroscope, Ambient light, Heart rate and SPO2 Blood Oxygen Saturation sensor

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is available to purchase on Amazon for $79 in the U.S. and £99 in the U.K. The watch comes in a range of colors, including Light Green, Orange, Light Grey and Dark Grey, which I tested.

This is a pretty cheap watch and is the same price as the Amazfit Bip 6. Sleep tracking in particular is far more accurate on the Bip 6 in comparison to the CMF, and the Bip 6 can also track more types of workouts.

A cheaper option is the Xiaomi Smart Band 10 for $51, which is much slimmer and will suit people with narrower wrists, as the CMF watch is very chunky.

If you don’t mind being without a screen and want some of the best fitness tracking out there, I’d recommend the Fitbit Air for $99. At just $20 more, it offers incredibly valuable fitness insights. For under $50, you can pick up the Amazfit Band 7, which has a very informative companion app to help improve training where needed.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

CMF is a sub-brand of Nothing, and as such, I expected some seriously stunning design work. Whether it’s headphones or milk carton-shaped speakers (CMF Speaker M), Nothing and CMF tech always stands out from the crowd. The CMF Watch 3 Pro is no different.

I tested the Dark Grey version, and I like how this looks for day-to-day wear. However, I felt that the watch face was far too large for my wrist. The circular AMOLED display has a 1.4-inch diameter, so it felt quite bulky. Unfortunately, the Watch 3 Pro doesn’t come in different sizes like the Apple Watch Series 12 or the SE 3 — these are available in multiple case sizes, making them more accessible.

With that said, the strap was secure thanks to the buckle closure. This strap can be removed with a small latch and swapped out for different colors, making customization easy. This was very easy to do when attaching the strap to the watch, but also very secure so it won’t come undone on its own.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro isn’t the brightest out there. The Amazfit Bip 6 can achieve 2,000 nits of brightness, but the CMF only reaches a maximum of 670 nits. It’s bright enough, but if you know you’ll be using the torch feature on the watch face frequently, definitely look at a brighter option like the Bip 6. It will also be hard to see the screen in bright lighting conditions, like running in direct sunshine.

The watch has a durability rating of IP68, meaning it is completely dust-tight and protected against water submersion beyond one meter. That means you can wear it anytime, whether you're working out or at the beach. However, most smartwatches have a durability rating of 5ATM, meaning they can withstand pressure underwater, so you can swim in them, but the CMF watch doesn’t have this level of protection.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro has 131 sport modes and uses built-in dual-band GPS to help you track your routes. It’s easiest to control this through the watch itself, as the app interface is very clunky, and I didn’t feel like I was getting a whole lot of detail, information, or control

I’ve been using the CMF Watch 3 Pro to track hikes, runs, and pilates sessions, and while I feel it’s been tracking my heart rate accurately throughout, I’m not entirely sold. Compared to my phone or Oura Ring 5, step counts, heart rate during workouts and sleep tracking weren’t accurate. This could also be because the watch face was so bulky on my wrist, and this meant that the sensors weren’t always in contact with my skin.

The watch tracks many metrics such as calories burned, step count, distance and of course heart rate, but the information is limited. I didn’t feel like I was getting feedback on my data as I do with other devices like the Amazfit Bip 6. Of course, this is a budget watch, but you get better workout analysis with Garmin, Apple, Amazfit, and even Xiaomi. This was missing from the CMF.

After using the watch for about a week, I started to notice that my movement tracking was improving, and my step counts were becoming more accurate. This likely happened as the watch used information like my height and GPS tracking for distance to affirm the count. It seems like the more it learns about my body, the more accurate it becomes. However, this has never been an issue for my Oura Ring, Apple Watch, or Xiaomi Smart Band, so there’s certainly some improvements to be made here.

The thing I get most excited about when I’m testing out a new fitness tracker is the health and sleep tracking. I track readiness and sleep almost to a fault, so it’s great to see how different devices can inform my health… I just don't think the CMF Watch 3 Pro is the one for the job.

The watch is a decent option for tracking heart health concerns, but shouldn’t be used as a diagnostic tool. It has automatic heart rate measurement that can run for 24 hours a day. It also tracks your resting heart rate throughout the day, and these readings were always about the same as I see with my Oura Ring 5.

You can set up heart rate reminders in the app settings. This means that if your heart rate goes above or below a specified number of beats, it will trigger an alarm. This is a great feature for anyone who may have a health condition. You can also set reminders for drinking water and standing up throughout the day.

I was disappointed by the sleep tracking on this watch. At first, I genuinely thought I was doing something wrong, but a quick look on Reddit and the Nothing community page showed me that this is a pretty common issue. I checked the firmware, battery, my wear position, and restarted the watch, but I was still having trouble logging sleep.

On my first night, the watch only detected three hours of sleep. My Oura Ring and Hatch Sleep clock both told me I was asleep for over eight hours. As I looked further into the data, I saw that the watch had also detected a nap at around eight o’clock in the evening. This was strange since I was cooking dinner, meaning I was moving around and my heart rate would have been slightly elevated.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro does not support any third-party apps; however, you can sync your data with your phone’s health app and directly sync with sports apps such as Strava. The watch also receives your phone's notifications, but you can’t reply to messages directly from the watch.

The dual-band GPS tracking is accurate, and I could see my route after my run. The watch also offers a custom running coach, and this is a great feature for those training towards shorter distances like a 5K or a 10K, but for longer distances I would recommend investing in a running programme that can be entirely tailored to you.

While the watch has some workout analysis, it’s not as in-depth as what you get from brands like Garmin, so if you’re seriously training towards a goal, I’d look into the Garmin Forerunner 70.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro has 13 days of battery life. This is pretty impressive, and about what I’ve come to expect with budget fitness trackers and smartwatches.

The Amazfit Bip 6 lasts for 14 days, and I got 15 days from the Xiaomi Smart Band 10. The CMF watch takes 99 minutes to charge.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is an affordable option for those new to smartwatches and who need something basic to track workouts. The design is sleek, and it’s effective in tracking most workouts, although step counting isn’t accurate at first. The battery life is good, giving almost two weeks of use with a single charge.

Although decent for tracking general health, it can’t track sleep as well as similarly priced rivals like the Xiaomi Smart Band 10. So if you’re someone who likes to make sure they’re getting enough rest, note that sleep tracking is wildly inaccurate. The bulky watch face was far too big for me and got in the way a lot, and unfortunately there isn’t support for third-party apps.

#3306. Can Chris Van Hollen Really Unseat Chuck Schumer?

The day after the Democrats notched the most impressive electoral performance by either political party in a generation, Chuck Schumer kicked off his own campaign, racing to shore up enough support to continue leading Democrats when they reclaim control of the Senate in January. His rationale was simple: He should be made majority leader because his efforts — recruiting and raising funds — created the new majority.

In podcast and television appearances, as well as an Atlantic story declaring him the “architect of a historic landslide,” Schumer made a point to emphasize his role in flipping several hard-fought seats, including in Mississippi, a state he boasted had long been his “white whale.” Schumer told told The Daily he scouted Scott Colom personally: “I went to him and said, ‘You’ve got to run.’’

But Schumer’s argument is undermined by the fact that many of the incoming senators disagree with the characterization that he contributed much to their victories at all.

Speaking to The Washington Post last week before his race was called, Colom ran through a long list of Democrats who helped him become the first Black senator to represent Mississippi since Reconstruction. Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse and Raphael Warnock, former Vice President Kamala Harris, and former President Bill Clinton were on that list; Schumer, the Post wrote, was “notably absent.” Colom was even more explicit on Friday, telling CBS it was “not accurate” to say that Schumer recruited him. “The people of Mississippi recruited me… You think I was listening to someone that lives in Brooklyn?” He declined to say whether he would back Schumer for majority leader.

Colom is not alone. Of 13 incoming Democrats, only Sherrod Brown, the once and future senator of Ohio, has publicly pledged to support the Senate’s current Democratic leader.

Abdul El-Sayed, the newly elected senator from Michigan, threw his support behind Schumer’s rival Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland shortly after Van Hollen publicly announced his bid to challenge the senator from New York on Thursday. Van Hollen, who represented the D.C. suburbs in the U.S. House for a decade and half before joining the Senate in 2017, won praise in 2025 for traveling to El Salvador and demanding to meet with a constituent, Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who was erroneously sent by the Trump administration to the sprawling CECOT prison complex. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

“I called on Sen Chris Van Hollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience. We need both right now,” El-Sayed wrote on X shortly after.

El-Sayed defeated Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens, Schumer’s preferred candidate, in the primary, before Stevens made the most dramatic heel-turn of the 2026 cycle and endorsed Republican Mike Rogers days before the election. (Schumer the move a “despicable betrayal.”)

El-Sayed is not the only new senator Schumer bet against. He backed centrist Rep. Angie Craig over Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota’s Democratic primary. Flanagan, who will take over the seat vacated by Sen. Tina Smith, has also announced her support for Van Hollen.

“Minnesotans are demanding change. Democrats need to deliver. That starts with new voices in our leadership,” Flanagan said Friday on X. “I believe Chris Van Hollen is the leader and fighter we need to bring about real change, so no American is left behind.”

Four other freshman Democrats — Sens. Troy Jackson of Maine, Juliana Stratton of Illinois, Adam Hamilton of Kansas, and Annie Andrews of South Carolina — have said explicitly they will not support Schumer, while six others have declined to say whether they would.  Related Content Kanye West Settles Lawsuit Over Sample Blocked by Descendant of Holocaust Survivors David Walliams: British Police Open Investigation Into Sexual Misconduct Allegations Trump’s Cabinet Is in Disarray Over Nvidia’s Honeypot Disaster Russell Brand: Six More Women Come Forward With Sexual-Misconduct Allegations

It is not a coincidence that Schumer’s most vocal opposition comes from recently elected senators, Ezra Levin, executive director of the progressive group Indivisible, tells Rolling Stone. “Those senators who just came through an election had to spend a lot of time with the public, and they understand where the public is [on Schumer],” Levin says.

“I don’t think anybody would deny that the people of this country want change,” adds Maurice Mitchell, national director of the Working Families Party. “People want government to do more, not less. People want immediate relief from the economic crisis that they’re in. They want accountability, and they also want new leadership. We’re listening to our folks, and we are embracing that change, and we are supporting Chris Van Hollen and his bid to be the next majority leader.”

Mitchell points to the blowout victories by newly elected Reps. Brad Lander of New York and Randy Villegas of California — primaries they won against centrist candidates closer to the Schumer mold — as evidence of the bold vision voters are looking for from Democrats. “They both ran on Medicare for All, they both ran against the war, they both were very clear about the need for us to change our relationship with the state of Israel,” Mitchell says. “Chris Van Hollen is aligned on all of those things.”

Sens. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) and Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen, as has Our Revolution, the political group that grew out of Sanders’ 2016 presidential run, and the Democratic Socialists of America, which kicked off a “Say No to Schumer” campaign this week.

The political advocacy group MoveOn has taken a stand against Schumer too, citing figures that indicate 82 percent of its membership wants to see him replaced. “Our members are tired of politicians content with incrementalism,” MoveOn’s Executive Director Joel Payne said in a statement. (A poll by Indivisible had worse results: just 10 percent of respondents want Schumer to remain in the leadership.)

Schumer has been regularly pilloried throughout the second Trump era for failing to do more to thwart the president’s scorched Earth agenda, provoking particular ire when he joined Republicans to pass a funding bill in March 2025. Indivisible first called on the Democratic leader to step down from his position after that vote.

“The argument, then as now, was not about ideology, it wasn’t about personalities, it wasn’t even about communication style,” Levin says. “It was about: Do you know what time it is? Do you know who is in the White House? Do you know what this regime intends to do? Are you willing to unify the caucus and strengthen the Democratic Party to get it done?”

Ahead of Van Hollen’s formal announcement on Thursday that he would seek the role, Schumer claimed that he already had the votes necessary to be reelected leader. Levin, for his part, is skeptical: “After Van Hollen announced, the fact that you did not see 29 senators, en masse, in a press release or at a press conference with Chuck Schumer means he doesn’t have the votes yet.”

Van Hollen has echoed some of the incoming senators in emphasizing that Democrats won big in the midterms in spite of, not because of, the party establishment. “I think if you look at this election, this was not a Washington, D.C.-orchestrated victory. This was a huge movement across the country,” he said this week. “That’s why we won in places like South Carolina. That’s why we won in Mississippi. #3305. 10 Google Privacy Hacks Everyone Should Know

Your Gmail account doesn't just have one email address. In fact, it has unlimited addresses, but you need a hack to utilize them. When you're signing up for a new service, you can add another word to your email address, as well as the "+" symbol, to create an alias. For example, if your email is "[email protected]," and you're signing up for an Amazon account, you can use "[email protected]" as your email address. The email will still end up in your main inbox, as if you simply used [email protected]. Not only can this trick turn one Gmail address into an unlimited number of addresses, but it also helps you identify who sold your email address to spammers, because those emails will have the alias in the "To" field.

Gmail's web view has a crucial security feature that lets you view session logs. This feature is inexplicably buried at the bottom of the inbox, and the font size is tiny, so it's easy to miss. To find it, log in to Gmail on the web, and scroll to the bottom of your inbox. Click the Details button in the bottom-right corner, below "Last account activity." This will show you a pop-up that lists the devices, apps, and locations you've recently logged in from. This makes it easy to see if there's been any suspicious activity in your Google account, and you can click the Security Checkup link in the pop-up to review this data. Just note that if you use a VPN or a service like iCloud Private Relay, you might not recognize your own device's location. To check if unwanted apps have access to your Google account, you can visit this settings page.

Google wants to show you personalized search results, which initially feels very helpful, but it also ends up trapping you in an algorithmic bubble. The best way to break out of your search bubble is to periodically use other search engines, but if you wish to stick to Google, you can disable personalized search recommendations in Google Search and the Play Store on Android. Go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized Recommendations and Play Personalization.

Google tracks your web and app activity by default, which includes your search history, voice data (if you use the speak-to-search feature), and activity from sites, apps, and devices that use Google services. However, associated information, such as your location data, is also saved to your Google profile, which you might not assume gets included in "Web & app activity." Fortunately, you can disable this tracking by going to this settings page, scrolling down to "Web & App Activity," and turning off all options in this section.

Google's Timeline feature saves your location in Google Maps to create a map of places you've visited. This is useful if you want to keep track of your recent stops; however, Google can use Timeline data to help businesses see how effective their ads were, or how likely you are to visit nearby stores. Its confirmation page confirms this: "Depending on your settings, activity saved as history in your Google Account, including ad interactions, may also be connected to Timeline data to help nearby businesses estimate the likelihood that people will visit their stores. No personal information is shared with businesses."

Timeline isn't enabled by default, but in case you enabled it a while ago, and are no longer using it, you can turn it off by going to this settings page. Click Turn off, and delete your activity to remove Timeline data from your Google account.

You can't fully escape Google's ads or tracking, but you can disable personalized ads to stop the company from using your account data to show ads. To do this, go to this settings page, and turn off Personalized ads.

While Google claims that it isn't using your emails to train AI, the company does offer AI features that make your emails feel more robotic than human. One of these is "Smart Reply," which offers email reply suggestions such as "Got it. See you soon." I can type that on my own, and I feel uncomfortable with Gmail analyzing the contents of my emails and replies to offer suggestions that I wouldn't use anyway. You can disable this by going to Gmail Settings > General, or by visiting this settings page. Scroll down to "Smart features," and turn off the checkbox next to it. This will disable Smart Compose, Smart Reply, suggestions for pending replies and follow-ups, spelling, grammar, and autocorrect.

A physical security key is a great security upgrade. It's a physical barrier that prevents most ways to hack into your account remotely. Even if someone discovers your email ID and password, and has access to your two-factor authentication code, they won't get in without physical access to that key. You can check out Google's support page for physical security keys for more information on compatibility and setting up your security keys.

Google uses data from Gmail and Google Drive to target ads, which means that your emails, files, and photos could be used for monetization. To stop this, you'll need to disable Personal Intelligence. To turn it off, visit this settings page, and click Turn off Personal Intelligence.

#3304. DHS Chief Markwayne Mullin Throws Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy Under Bus

Things got a little awkward during a press conference about the nationwide ground stop when DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin inadvertently laid blame on Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy ... before the FAA revealed they lost 12,000 flights.

It all went down Friday night ... when Mullin was asked if any cyberattack was responsible for the "extraordinary circumstances" that led to system malfunction.

Mullin said ... "What it appears to be right now, as Secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology and that new equipment and new technology just wasn't, it was overwhelming the older system."

As Mullin gave this response ... Duffy's system was seemingly overwhelmed too by what was said.

Hanging his head low, Duffy shook his head and at one point, may have even nudged Mullin from behind the podium. All in all ... it did not appear as if Duffy liked Mullin's response at all.

According to Duffy ... the "old legacy equipment" was to blame for the error and he warned there would be several more incidents in the future.

He said ... "This is an emergency. I want Congress to give us emergency funding. This is bipartisan. This is American. I want $50 billion."

Speaking with the press Saturday ... Duff said there's no better time than now to provide the much-needed funding ... while the FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford revealed 12,000 flights had been lost yesterday.

Saturday's press conference was a little tense too ... Bedford interrupting Duffy multiple times.

As you know ... the FAA lifted the ground stop -- that was implemented under "extraordinary circumstances" -- Friday night.

We've reached out to the Department of Transportation for comment ... so far, no word back. When reached, the DHS shared a press release about the press conference.

#3303. Garmin Cyclists Can Now Make Themselves Appear on Waze in Real Time

Cyclists who ride with Garmin gear can now appear as live, moving icons on the Waze driving app, and nearby drivers will receive an alert to slow down and watch for them on the road.

For riders already using Garmin devices, opting in costs nothing and adds a new layer of safety, particularly on roads where drivers may not expect cyclists. The feature is rolling out now, but you should be aware of its limitations.

Riders can simply opt in once through Garmin Connect. After that, sharing starts automatically when an outdoor cycling activity begins and stops when the ride ends. While a ride is underway, Waze users near the cyclist see a cyclist icon move along the road and receive a Live Cycling Alert reminding them to slow down and stay aware.

The feature runs on LiveTrack, Garmin's existing live location-sharing tool, which lets friends and family follow a rider's real-time location, speed, course, and more. Garmin says this collaboration extends that peace of mind to motorists, giving them greater awareness of their surroundings.

Garmin notes its location sharing is temporary and session-based. The rider's name, identity, and route are hidden, and no personal information is shared or displayed in Waze. Drivers see only an anonymous icon and the alert.

You'll need a few things to get this feature up and running:

A compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin watch

A phone running Garmin Connect with a data connection

An outdoor cycling activity (the feature doesn't apply to indoor rides)

The good news is using the feature is free: LiveTrack costs nothing on compatible Garmin bike computers and watches, and Waze is free for drivers.

This new feature is a great safety perk, but there are real-world caveats worth considering:

This feature is for Waze only. Alerts reach drivers only when Waze is open on their phone. Google Maps, which has far more users, is excluded, so a large portion of the drivers you share the road with won't see you this way.

It depends on your phone's signal. Your position travels from the Garmin to your phone, then to Garmin's servers, then to Waze, and finally to the driver's phone. On a patchy rural signal, a few seconds of lag could put the icon on the wrong side of a bend from where you actually are. A rider who leaves their phone at home or whose phone loses signal simply won't show up on a Waze map, as a ride without a data connection is invisible to Waze.

Finally, remember to treat this safety feature as an extra perk, not a guarantee. At the end of the day, it isn't a replacement for bike lights, bright clothing, and defensive riding.

#3301. The 15 Best ‘Hunger Games’ Soundtrack Songs

In the opening scene of The Hunger Games, before the battle and bloodshed, Katniss Everdeen comforts her sister Prim with a lullaby. “Deep in the meadow, under the willow,” she sings. “A bed of grass, a soft green pillow.” It only lasts a few seconds, enough to get out two simple lyrics, but it tells us what’s most important to Katniss, played by Jennifer Lawrence, and how she communicates. It tells us just how essential music is to the narrative about to unfold.

The Hunger Games franchise has grown considerably since the release of the first film in 2012. The four-part saga, adapted from the book trilogy written by Suzanne Collins, concluded in 2015. Since then, the franchise has expanded with two more book-to-film prequel pairings. The most musical of the batch, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, received a theatrical release in 2023, while the latest installment, Sunrise on the Reaping, was released in theaters on Friday, Nov. 20.

Each film has arrived alongside eclectic, star-studded soundtracks that recruit artists with distinct interpretations of the highly emotional, hotly volatile story at the heart of The Hunger Games. They aren’t all soothing lullabies, mockingjay calls, or political anthems. But they are genre-spanning, and rich with characters we’ve seen go from the page to the screen. With original releases created by artists from Lorde, Patti Smith, and the Weekend to Olivia Rodrigo, Taylor Swift, and Bella Kay, here are the 15 best Hunger Games soundtrack songs.

“Yellow Flicker Beat,” the first song released from the Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 1 soundtrack, opens with an unsettling hum. In 2014, Lorde described the song as her first attempt at getting inside of Katniss’ head. From the beginning, the character served as a flicker of hope for the districts, but the worst nightmare who leaders in the Capitol never saw coming. All over the song, you can hear the threads of teenage angst and rebellion that colored Lorde’s debut album Pure Heroine. It’s present in the opening verse, when she compares her blood to rubies and precious stones, but especially when the chorus hits: “This is the start of how it all ends/They used to shout my name, now they whisper it.” — Larisha Paul

Before Folklore and Evermore, Taylor Swift wrote from the perspective of one bow-slinging fictional character in particular: Katniss Everdeen. The result was “Safe & Sound,” a folky lullaby carried by plucky chords that pierce to the bone as they push against the salve-like lyrics. Swift and T-Bone Burnett, the architect behind the first Hunger Games soundtrack, captured the eerie energy of that initial film during an impromptu writing and recording session in Los Angeles with the help of the Civil Wars, who offer haunting harmonies. “The Civil Wars had a show that night so they raced right over to T Bone’s house,” Swift told Rolling Stone in 2012. “There’s so many things he could’ve done production-wise to make that song bigger sonically than it is, but I think that would have possibly been a mistake. For [Burnett] to have left the song as a lullaby is brilliant.” —M.G.

Olivia Rodrigo channels her songbird best on this acoustic taunt, sung from the perspective of The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds Snakes character, Lucy Gray Baird, “[She] is a character that I feel very connected to,” Rodrigo said in 2022. She packs the song with a convincing sense of vengeance atop the kind of gorgeous melody that a mockingjay would love to repeat. In fact, the closing credits song was inspired by the film’s final aerial scene of the fictional birds. “That was playing in a loop in my head over and over, and I was like, ‘I want to write a song that captures what that feeling is.’ That was the goal,” she said. —Maya Georgi

Tinashe didn’t originally write “The Leap” with the chaotic rebellion of The Hunger Games in mind. It was meant for one of her own albums, but at the time, Lorde — 17 at the time — was tasked with curating the Mockingjay – Part 1 soundtrack, and her team wanted to see what Tinashe might contribute. “The Leap” provides a sharp and chilling parallel to the film. “I’m gonna set it all ablaze, watch it burn to ash and dust,” calls to the destruction of Katniss’ home, District 12. “I was waiting on you, waiting on you” calls to Petta being stuck in the Capitol. And “hurry up, don’t miss your chance” nods to the harrowing secrets that come to light throughout the film. Even by accident, Tinashe hit her mark with “The Leap.” —L.P.

The first time we hear “The Hanging Tree” in the Hunger Games, it’s in the soft tone of Jennifer Lawrence’s voice. In Mockingjay, the rebellion begins to take full shape with Katniss at its heart. It’s a protest song for the ages. “Are you, are you/Coming to the tree/Where they strung up a man they say murdered three,” she sang. “Strange things did happen here/No stranger would it be/If we met up at midnight in the hanging tree.” In The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, when Rachel Zegler’s Lucy Gray Baird sings its sweet melody, we learn it was written following an execution in District 12. The prequel film takes place more than six decades before the events of the first film in the original trilogy. “The Hanging Tree,” like the mockingjay’s call, is the musical thread that ties them together. —L.P.

In Catching Fire, Katniss Everdeen and 23 other former Hunger Games victors head back into the arena. It’s an act of vengeance from President Snow, to show that even in victory, their lives still do not belong to themselves. The sob that breaks through when the format of the 75th Hunger Games is revealed in the film is unforgettable and devastating. On the sparse soundtrack cut “Devil May Cry,” the Weeknd offers a silver lining. “It won’t be in vain/To swallow all your pain,” he sings. “And learn to love what burns/And gather courage to return.” It’s all the tributes-turned victors-turned tributes again have to hold onto. —L.P.

The National originally titled their contribution to the Catching Fire soundtrack “Dying Is Easy.” On one hand, there’s some truth to the title, especially in the context of the Hunger Games. A momentary distraction in the arena, a step off of the starting line just a second early, any hesitation — it could all end in a flash. On the other hand, the final title, “Lean,” feels more apt to the theme of reliance that emerges throughout the song. “Dying is easy/I believe my love and my love relieves me,” Matt Berninger sings, later accepting the consequences of holding care in your heart in a battle as callous as the one in this story: “Love will lead us all to smithereens.” —L.P.

This is … the mocking as the jay, or rather, Patti Smith’s unique interpretation of Katniss as her character helps set the rebellion aflame in the Catching Fire film. The punk rock poet offers her best spoken-word couplets on this smoldering, folky take that’s less in the vein of “People Have the Power” and more of “Easter.” Leave it to Smith to tap into her political heart to speak truth to power, even when it’s about a fictionalized tyranny. —M.G.

Gigi Perez is somehow able to balance yearning, loss, and tenderness through the husky, low pitch of her voice, and she brought all those feelings to “Favor,” a haunting, folk-driven cut from The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping soundtrack. The acoustic track is emotional as it captures the goodbye between Haymitch and Lenore. Perez gets to the core of longing and missing someone, singing, “When you arе lonely, know I’m awake, listen for me and the song that we sang.” —Julyssa Lopez

Bella Kay continues the tradition of young, breakthrough singer-songwriters lending their musical and emotional expertise to The Hunger Games. “See It Coming,” from the Sunrise on the Reaping soundtrack, is a refusal to be blindsided: “Tell me you run, I’m beggin’ you, hide/They’re gonna hurt you, so give ’em a fight,” Kay sings, the distinct country twang that only occasionally slips through present in her tone. “A little revenge, an eye for an eye/We can call it a draw.” It cuts to the heart of the Hunger Games musical universe: to still feel and love deeply even in the face of impossible survival. The opening verse takes us back to the beginning while looking towards an uncertain future. “Swear to me now you’ll remember me hummin’,” she sings. —L.P.

Appearing on the Mockingjay Part 1 soundtrack, this Charli XCX contribution feels like an ember of hope hidden underneath the rubble of the Second Rebellion of Panem. Led by a cascading piano melody, Charli assumes the role of Katniss near the end of the original Hunger Games series; she’s bruised, beaten, and grief-stricken, but must go on. For a brief moment, Duran Duran’s Simon Le Bon appears to support her on the Rostam and Ariel Rechtshaid-produced rallying cry. “I’m lost, but I can’t slow,” Charli coos, before leaving the listener with an inspiring message: “I’m lost, but not alone.” —Jaeden Pinder

Ushered in like a gospel prayer, Miranda Lambert recruited her Pistol Annies bandmates Ashley Monroe and Angaleena Presley for “Run Daddy Run,” which appeared on the first Hunger Games soundtrack. It soon moves into a menacing warning: “Daddy, can you hear the devil drawing near” the trio sings in a gorgeous but unsettling harmony. “Like a bullet from a gun, run daddy run.” It’s a haunting warning that captures the alarm of the first film. —Marissa Moss

The Chemical Brothers and Miguel may seem an unlikely union, but the rebellious spirit of their Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 1 collaboration “This Is Not a Game” works despite the odds. The skittering electronic track opens with a whisper from Lorde, who extended her curatorial duties to include vocal contributions, singing, “There it is.” Miguel comes out swinging in the first verse with a quote from Charles Bukowski: “Find what you love and let it kill you.” He spends the rest of the song pouring gasoline on the fire of revolution, while the Chemical Brothers turn up the dial on their dark, warping production and pull trap influences into the fold. “I know what I’m doing,” Miguel spits. —L.P.

Before Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark were even born, there was Lucy Gray Baird. This District 12 tribute with a rebel heart knew that she had to charm the fake eyelashes off the Capitol if she wanted any chance at a victory, and so she did with this song. In The Ballad of the Songbirds and Snakes book, Gray Baird tells the devastating tale of her fated life with a guitar and Appalachian-inspired drawl during her pre-Games interview. With lyrics like “It’s sooner than later that I’m six feet under /It’s sooner than later that you’ll be alone,” it’s a sobering listen. Thankfully, Rachel Zegler does the pivotal moment justice with this soulful rendition, each bruised line made more powerful by her quivering soprano. —M.G.

Mckenna Grace joins the Hunger Games franchise in two roles, as both Maysilee Donner and Merrilee Donner in Sunrise on the Reaping. She holds the emotional anguish of both characters close on “Half Alive,” a sprawling soundtrack cut that confronts death and the destruction it brings, especially when it’s for the sake of entertainment. “I say I’m mean and tough and I don’t care ‘cause I’m not weak,” she sings. “But if tomorrow was my last, hope someone mourns me/Watch as they all applaud.” There are times during the song where Grace sounds breathless, grasping at a calmness that will always evade her. During the chorus, she pleads for whatever version of it she can get: “We feel the unspoken, the look in your eyes/Promise you’ll hold me when I’m half alive.” —L.P.

#3300. 10 Movies Like ‘Interstellar’ You Should Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Christopher Nolan’s 2014 megahit Interstellar has it all: big sci-fi ideas, cool robots, ugly crying, and a Matt Damon character in need of rescuing. Grounded in the intensity of the human experience, this story of humanity’s potential extinction and the sacrifice of one man to save it doesn’t just deliver exotic planets and thrilling spaceship maneuvers; it also provides all the feels as Joseph Cooper (Matthew McConaughey) sacrifices everything he has in an effort to save the entire human race. It’s one of the best science fiction films ever made, with Nolan’s signature complexity, time manipulations, and emotional wallop. If you love this movie, here are ten more that offer a similar viewing experience.

If you loved both the special effects in Interstellar that make space travel feel viscerally thrilling (and terrifying) and the mind-blowing concepts, this is the film for you. Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 epic (written by sci-fi master Arthur C. Clarke) traces humanity’s development from mildly smart apes to spacefaring capitalists who discover a mysterious obelisk on the Moon that sparks a mission to Jupiter. While it operates in a colder emotional key than Nolan’s film, 2001: A Space Odyssey absolutely delivers on the epic side of things (and the cool—if slightly deranged and deadly—artificial intelligences). Stream 2001: A Space Odyssey on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for more existential missions with somewhat reluctant heroes in space, Project Hail Mary is your next stop. When the Sun begins to dim due to the interference of an alien entity, scientists identify the one nearby star that isn’t being similarly affected. Brilliant molecular biologist Ryland Grace (Ryan Gosling) winds up forced to go on what is assumed to be a fatal, one-way mission into deep space to try to find a way to save humanity, unexpectedly assisted by a charming alien he names Rocky. It’s got the same emotional volume and big ideas as Interstellar, and fans of Nolan’s film will love it. Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+ or Philo, or rent it on Prime Video.

Part of what makes Interstellar so compelling is the stakes: The human race is slowly dying, and a handful of people must make incredible sacrifices to save it. That’s the vibe of Sunshine, set in a future where the Sun is dimming and a spacecraft is dispatched to deliver an enormous bomb designed to reignite the Sun’s fusion cycle. But the mission is the second attempt after the first ship vanished mysteriously seven years earlier, and when the new crew stumbles on the derelict wreck of the first mission, things quickly descend into violence and madness—but the crew remains determined to save the world, no matter the cost. Rent Sunshine on Prime Video.

Interstellar works in large part because of the emotional dynamics at play. McConaughey’s character leaves his children behind and is forced to witness them growing up without him, missing out on their lives and saddled with the knowledge that they resent him despite the necessity of his mission. Arrival is a First Contact story focused on language—linguist Louise Banks (Amy Adams) is drafted into an effort to understand the strange, complex language of the aliens. As she slowly builds to an understanding of how the aliens communicate and perceive time itself, her own heartbreak and loss come into play, giving this film a similarly devastating emotional punch. Stream Arrival on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Family dynamics and the toll of lonely space missions fuel Ad Astra, a film with the same emotional core as Interstellar. Twenty-nine years ago, famed astronaut Clifford McBride (Tommy Lee Jones) led the Lima Project, a space station around Neptune searching for intelligent life. Thirteen years ago, Earth lost contact with him. When bursts of energy emanating from Neptune threaten to end life on Earth, his son, Roy (Brad Pitt), is dispatched to try to make contact with his father. It’s an epic journey with a powerful climax that will satisfy fans of Interstellar in every way. Stream Ad Astra on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

Ridley Scott’s prequel to Alien has its flaws, but if you’re looking for a sense of epic spacefaring adventure in the same key as Interstellar, it’s perfect. When two scientists discover a star map apparently left behind by ancient aliens, they secure funding from the Wayland Corporation to organize a space expedition to the indicated planet. Accompanied by a colorful crew and the android David, they discover an apparently abandoned outpost of the species dubbed the Engineers. The story wrestles with questions about humanity’s origins, purpose, and potential—but this being an Alien film, things quickly turn horrifying. Rent Prometheus on Prime Video.

Adapted from Carl Sagan’s 1985 novel, Contact follows astronomer Dr. Ellie Arroway (Jodie Foster), who becomes involved with an effort to decipher a signal originating from the star Vega. The signal turns out to be a set of instructions for constructing a one-person spacecraft of some kind, and Arroway is eventually selected as the candidate to take the journey. There’s a sense of courage in the face of the unknown that’s similar to Interstellar, as well as the thrill of strapping into a spaceship and pressing the ignition. Plus, there’s the added bonus of seeing one of the greatest trick shots in cinematic history. Rent Contact on Prime Video.

Stanislaw Lem’s 1961 novel Solaris explores what Lem saw as the impossibility of ever understanding a truly alien life. The two major adaptations—Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 version and Steven Soderbergh’s 2002 take starring George Clooney—are both worth watching, but Tarkovsky’s film is a masterpiece of psychological horror. The story is set mainly aboard a space station orbiting a planet covered in what appears to be a sentient "ocean" and chronicles the strange haunting and inexplicable experiences of the humans living on the station. If your favorite part of Interstellar is the ending when things get trippy and weird, you’ll probably love Solaris. Stream Solaris on HBO Max, Plex, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

The story of a mission to Jupiter’s moon Europa to search for intelligent life, Europa Report has the same sense of terrifying excitement that accompanies Interstellar’s missions to the different candidate planets. Leaning into the fragility of life in an environment not designed to support it, the mission crew face a steady stream of loss and danger as they work to catch sight of alien life on the frozen, deadly moon, ultimately faced with making terrifying sacrifices in order to provide humanity with the answers that it seeks. Stream Europa Report on Netflix, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

A film based on a 1956 epic science fiction poem written by a Swedish Nobel Laureate might seem like an unlikely match for fans of Interstellar, but it’s actually perfect. As the Earth becomes uninhabitable, humanity begins launching ships to colonize Mars. When one such ship, the Aniara, is damaged and veers irreversibly off course, the passengers and crew are faced with the knowledge that they will sail off into the void without hope of rescue. Within a few years, despair has driven some to suicide and madness, while others cling to the possibility that they might yet find a way back. The film offers a different perspective on the existential crisis of humanity’s extinction, exploring the worst-case scenario to its bitter, bleak end. Stream Aniara on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3298. How the Biopic ‘Being Heumann’ Pulls Off Two Revolutions

Judy Heumann is just trying to cross the road in her wheelchair. It’s New York City in the 1970s, and the streets are chaotic. Traffic barrels past, pedestrians crowd the sidewalks, and the concrete curbs are steep cliffs. Unable to get her wheelchair up onto the sidewalk, she rolls in the middle of Madison Avenue, giving the middle finger to a city bus driver behind her who is laying on his horn.

Set to the propulsive guitar riff of Iggy Pop’s proto-punk anthem “The Passenger,” the opening sequence of Being Heumann — a new biopic about the disability-advocacy pioneer — introduces a woman who refuses to be dismissed and has zero patience for anyone standing in her way as she navigates through potholes, puddles, and pedestrians.

“You are not introduced quietly to this character,” says Ruth Madeley, who portrays Heumann. “You literally meet her in utter chaos and noise. She’s unfazed because she is doing that every damn day of her life.”

Denied access to school until she was nine years old because administrators considered her and her wheelchair a fire hazard, Heumann later sued the New York Board of Education for the right to become a teacher. Her fight for equal access grew into a lifelong crusade.

In 1970, she co-founded Disabled in Action, a grassroots advocacy organization, and went on to become a leading voice in the independent living movement. Her activism helped pave the way for landmark legislation including the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Audacious, confident, and fiercely determined, Heumann became known as the “mother of the disability rights movement,” helping to transform disability from a matter of charity into a question of civil rights.

Siân Heder, the 2022 Oscar-winning director of CODA, first encountered Judy Heumann in the 2020 Sundance-winning documentary Crip Camp. When she read Heumann’s memoir, from which the film takes its title, Heder saw a fascinating contradiction in a leader who demanded humanity from the world but sometimes struggled to recognize the limitations of those around her. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

In Being Heumann (now streaming on Apple TV), we see Judy charismatically inspire fellow disabled activists into action. And we also see when she pushes them to take on more risk than their bodies might be able to endure, like a hunger strike she urged others to take part in, even if that wasn’t wise considering their medical conditions.

“The title took on these other levels of meaning,” Heder says, “where it’s as much about Judy having to learn how to be human as it is about her asking the world to treat this marginalized group of people as human.”

For Madeley, portraying the fierce and complicated civil rights icon was “the biggest acting undertaking of my life. Finally, I get to play somebody who gets things wrong? Who is kind of brash sometimes? Who is so focused that she sometimes can alienate people,” Madeley says.

After the opening scene in New York City, we fast forward five years to April 1977 San Francisco. Rather than attempt to chronicle Heumann’s entire extraordinary life, Heder and her co-writer Rebekah Taussig focused the film on Heumann’s organization of a sit-in protest for Section 504, the first federal law that protects against discrimination based on disability. Heumann and her coalition of more than 100 disabled protesters staged the longest peaceful occupation of a federal building in U.S. history.

But Being Heumann isn’t your typical reverent biopic or a pedantic history lesson. Heder turns the fight for Section 504 and disability-rights legislation into a kind of high-stakes caper – an outrageous pursuit of an almost impossible prize.  Related Content Disabled Fans Say the Live-Music Industry Can Do Better: ‘We Are Not a Pain in the Ass’ The DOJ Is Stocking Its Civil Rights Division With Right-Wing Kooks ‘Un-American’: Dems Dig in as Southern States Try to Eliminate Black Representation Justice Department Guts Voting Rights Unit: Report

Heder recalls, “When I got to the section on the 504 [protest], I thought, ‘Oh, this is Dog Day Afternoon with disabled people. This is a bank robbery with people who don’t know how to rob a bank.'”

”This is a heist movie with a group of people who no one would expect to see in a heist movie,” Madeley says. “They weren’t going in for money or jewels. They were going for their rights. It was so much more expensive and so much more precious.”

EVERY GREAT HEIST HAS a plan within the plan, a twist the audience never saw coming. For Being Heumann, that second heist happened behind the camera. “Judy’s next mountain, her next mission, was Hollywood,” Madeley says.

Before her death in 2023, Heumann turned her attention toward the entertainment industry’s dismal record on disability representation. A 2019 Ford Foundation study authored by Heumann revealed “that disabled people were one in four in the population, and the media representation was under three percent,” according to Heder. “When disabled roles came up, they were played by non-disabled people.”

Some of this discrimination may be due, Heder says, to archaic ideas about the physical grit required for the job. “There’s an ethos around filmmaking where you die for the movie, and it’s like war, and it’s a badge of honor that you can’t walk at the end of every day. And what it’s done is exclude a lot of really talented people who can’t be on their feet for 14 hours,” Heder says.

Committed to upending that status quo, Heder hired widely from the disabled community. Being Heumann features 12 disabled leads and, at times, up to 60 disabled background performers. She was also determined to address inaccessibility on set. While the art department filled in modern curb cuts to recreate the inaccessible streets of the 1970s, the Being Heumann accessibility team was simultaneously building ramps, installing lifts and modifying trailers to make the set accessible.

For Madeley, who uses a wheelchair, the difference was transformative. “To have accessibility completely cared for, I was able to show up every day as an actor, and I didn’t realize how liberating that was.”

The film’s most powerful intersection of historical activism and present-day disability experience comes during a congressional testimony sequence. One by one, the disabled protesters share the indignities and injustices that have shaped their lives. Heder invited the actors to draw from their own experiences, blurring the boundaries between historical reenactment and personal testimony.

“I met with each actor and asked them what aspect of their experience they would be interested to share. What followed was one of the most powerfully cathartic experiences I’ve ever had on a set,” Heder says. “We rolled the camera in one long take, allowing actors to take turns coming up to the microphone. I sat by the camera and interviewed them, sometimes as their characters and sometimes as themselves.”

The scene transforms a decades-old debate about federal regulations into a profoundly contemporary portrait of discrimination, dignity, and belonging. “We were building something bigger than us. Whatever the outcome of the movie, we were allowing people who had been unseen and unheard to be centered,” Heder says.

AFTER 26 DAYS, THE protesters in San Francisco achieved what many believed impossible. Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare Joseph Califano (played in the film by Mark Ruffalo) signed the Section 504 regulations, establishing enforceable federal protections against disability discrimination and helping lay the groundwork for the Americans With Disabilities Act, passed 13 years later in 1990.

On the final day of filming, Madeley recalls when first assistant director Walter Gasparovic wrapped production by calling out the names of every cast member, including the background performers. Like the activists they portrayed, the cast and crew pulled off something Hollywood long considered impossible — an accessible production with one of the largest ensembles of actors with disabilities in history.

Madeley remembers thinking, “We did it. We pulled off the heist!”

But even in that triumphant moment, she could hear Judy urging them onward. “I could literally feel Judy being like, ‘That’s great! Now get in the edit.’” Because for Judy Heumann, a hard-won victory was never the end of the fight. It was simply the beginning of dismantling the next obstacle.

At the Los Angeles premiere of Being Heumann at AFI Fest, Heder discovered that the historic theater hosting the celebration had an inaccessible stage and backstage area, preventing members of her cast from participating onstage and forcing the Q&A to be relocated to the middle of the auditorium.

Even as Hollywood celebrated a film about disability rights, the building itself was excluding the very people whose story it was honoring. Heder publicly called out the theater during the premiere. “I had to say something because Judy would.” Trending Stories Noel Fielding Says He Regrets 'Horrible' Jokes He Made With Russell Brand After Old Clip Resurfaces Pink Floyd’s Roger Waters Files for Divorce From Fourth Wife Kamilah Chavis After 5 Years of Marriage Journey Go Their Separate Ways With Longtime Drummer The ‘You Can See Everything’ Interview You’ve Been Waiting For

“Hollywood’s all about world-building,” Madeley says. “We build buildings. We build car chases. We build things that we can set on fire. Things are done in the industry that are hard and expensive. Building a ramp is not that big a deal. Hollywood, no more excuses. We’ve done it.”

“Being Heumann” is now streaming on Apple TV, debuting alongside a new accessibility feature offering optional onscreen ASL and BSL interpretation. The film’s sign language interpretation was directed by “CODA” and “Being Heumann” cast member Daniel Durant.
